entries.name: Pythagorean theorem
entries.description: Euclid I.47: area comparisons and constructed squares; drop an altitude and use similar triangles; rearrangement/dissection; algebraic coordinates or vectors. Euclid also gives a broader similar-figures version in VI.31.

routes.title: Euclid I.47: area comparisons and constructed squares
routes.proofSketch: On the sides of right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $A$) construct squares $BDEC$, $GB$ and $HC$, and draw $AL$ through $A$ parallel to $BD$. Triangles $ABD$ and $FBC$ are congruent (two sides and the included angle are equal, since both equal a right angle plus $\angle ABC$). The parallelogram $BL$ is double triangle $ABD$ (same base $BD$, same parallels), and the square $GB$ is double triangle $FBC$ (same base $FB$, same parallels), so $BL = GB$. Joining $AE$ and $BK$ gives in the same way $CL = HC$. Hence the square $BDEC$ on the hypotenuse equals $GB + HC$, the sum of the squares on the legs.

routes.title: drop an altitude and use similar triangles
routes.proofSketch: Drop the perpendicular from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse $c$, cutting it into segments $x$ and $c-x$. The two small triangles and the original triangle have the same angles, so all three are similar. Equal ratios of corresponding sides give $x/a=a/c$ and $(c-x)/b=b/c$, that is $x=a^2/c$ and $c-x=b^2/c$. Adding, $a^2/c+b^2/c=x+(c-x)=c$, and multiplying by $c$ yields $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

routes.title: rearrangement/dissection
routes.proofSketch: Take two squares of side $a+b$, each containing four copies of the right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$. In one square the triangles are placed so that their hypotenuses enclose a central square of side $c$; its area is $(a+b)^2 = 2ab + c^2$. In the other square the triangles are moved into two $a\times b$ rectangles, leaving two squares of areas $a^2$ and $b^2$, so $(a+b)^2 = 2ab + a^2 + b^2$. Equating and cancelling the area $2ab$ of the four triangles gives $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

routes.proofSketch: Place the right-angle vertex at 0 and legs as perpendicular vectors u,v. The hypotenuse vector is u−v, so ‖u−v‖²=‖u‖²+‖v‖²−2u·v=‖u‖²+‖v‖² because u·v=0.

entries.name: Irrationality of √2
entries.description: Lowest-terms parity/divisibility; infinite descent on a smaller integer pair; geometric descent on an isosceles right triangle; rational-root theorem. The geometric/descent sources explicitly compare routes.

routes.title: Lowest-terms parity/divisibility
routes.proofSketch: Assume $\sqrt2=p/q$ with whole numbers $p,q$ having no common factor. Squaring gives $p^2=2q^2$, so $p^2$ is even and hence $p$ is even, say $p=2a$. Then $4a^2=2q^2$, so $q^2=2a^2$ and $q$ is even as well by the same reasoning. Thus $p$ and $q$ share the factor 2, contradicting the choice of lowest terms, so no such $p,q$ exist.

routes.title: infinite descent on a smaller integer pair
routes.proofSketch: Suppose $\sqrt2=x/y$ with positive integers; the plan is to produce another fraction $x_1/y_1$ for $\sqrt2$ with $0<y_1<y$, which would give an infinite decreasing sequence of positive denominators. Put $x_1=2y-x$ and $y_1=x-y$. From $x^2=2y^2$ one checks by cross-multiplication that $x/y=(2y-x)/(x-y)$. Also $0<y_1<y$ is equivalent to $y<x<2y$, i.e. $1<(x/y)^2<4$, which holds because $(x/y)^2=2$. So a fraction with smaller denominator exists, contradicting minimality (or well-ordering), and $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

routes.title: geometric descent on an isosceles right triangle
routes.proofSketch: Start from an isosceles right triangle with legs $q$ and hypotenuse $p$, both whole numbers, with $p$ taken as small as possible; then $p=\sqrt2 q>q$. By the algebraic proof $p$ is even, so the hypotenuse can be bisected into two lengths $p/2$ and its midpoint joined to the right-angle vertex. This yields two smaller isosceles right triangles each with hypotenuse $q$ and legs $p/2$. The ratio hypotenuse/leg is then $q/(p/2)$ with $q<p$, contradicting minimality of $p$.

routes.title: Euclid's product-plus-one
routes.proofSketch: If p₁,…,pₖ were all primes, N=p₁⋯pₖ+1 has a prime divisor q. No pᵢ divides N, so q is absent from the list.

routes.verbatimProof:
Elegant proof of Euclid's theorem runs as follows. Suppose that p1 =
2 < p2 = 3 < · · · < pk are all the primes. Take n = p1 p2 · · · pk + 1
and let p be a prime dividing n. Then p cannot be any of p1 , p2 , . . . , pk ,
otherwise p would divide the difference n - p1 p2 · · · pk = 1.
  The above proof is actually quite a bit different from what Euclid
wrote. Since ancient Greeks did not have our modern notion of infinity,
Euclid could not have written "there are infinitely many primes", rather
he wrote: "prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of
prime numbers." Below is a proof closer to that which Euclid wrote,
but still using our modern concepts of numbers and proof. An English
translation of Euclid's actual proof given by D. Joyce in his webpages
[145] also can be found in
http://primes.utm.edu/notes/proofs/infinite/euclids.html. It is a
most elegant proof by contradiction (reduction ad absurdum) that goes
as follows.
Euclid's theorem. There are more primes than found in any finite
list of primes.
Proof. Call the primes in our finite list p1 , p2 , . . . , pk . Let P be any com-
mon multiple of these primes plus one (for example P = p1 p2 · · · pk +1).
Now P is either prime or it is not. If it is prime, then P is a prime that
was not in our list. If P is not prime, then it is divisible by some prime,
call it p. Notice p cannot be any of p1 , p2 , . . . , pk , otherwise p would di-
vide 1, which is impossible. So this prime p is some prime that was not
in our original list. Either way, the original list was incomplete.

routes.title: Euler's harmonic-series/Euler-product argument
routes.proofSketch: For primes p≤x expand ∏(1−1/p)⁻¹ into geometric series. Unique factorization includes every reciprocal 1/n for n≤x, so the product is at least Hₓ, which diverges; a finite set of primes would bound the product, contradiction.

routes.title: Furstenberg's topology on the integers
routes.proofSketch: Let S=Z with the topology generated by all two-sided arithmetic progressions. Each progression is clopen, so any finite union of progressions is closed. Let A be the union of pZ over all primes p. Every integer except −1 and 1 is divisible by a prime, hence Z\A={−1,1}; this two-point set is not open in this topology, so A is not closed. Thus A cannot be a finite union of the closed sets pZ, and there must be infinitely many primes.

routes.verbatimProof: In this note we would like to offer an elementary "topological" proof of the infinitude of prime numbers. We introduce a topology into the space of integers S, by using the arithmetic progressions (from −∞ to +∞) as a basis. It is not difficult to verify that this actually yields a topological space. In fact under this topology S may be shown to be normal and hence metrizable. Each arithmetic progression is closed as well as open, since its complement is the union of other arithmetic progressions (having the same difference). As a result the union of any finite number of arithmetic progressions is closed. Consider now the set A = ⋃ A_p, where A_p consists of all multiples of p, and p runs though the set of primes ≥ 2. The only numbers not belonging to A are −1 and 1, and since the set {−1, 1} is clearly not an open set, A cannot be closed. Hence A is not a finite union of closed sets which proves that there are an infinite of primes.

routes.title: analytic counting arguments. A historical survey catalogs about 200 variants
routes.proofSketch: For s>1, unique factorization gives ζ(s)=∏ₚ(1−p^(−s))⁻¹. If there were finitely many primes, the right side would remain bounded as s↓1, whereas ζ(s)=Σn⁻ˢ diverges by comparison with ∫₁∞x⁻ˢdx. Contradiction. This is an analytic Euler-product proof and overlaps route 3-r2; it is not a distinct strategy unless the ζ-function argument is developed separately.

entries.name: Infinitely many primes in an arithmetic progression (selected cases)
entries.description: Euclid-style products with congruence control; algebraic norms/cyclotomic factors for suitable progressions. State the progression and hypotheses precisely; do not conflate these special cases with Dirichlet's theorem.

routes.title: Euclid-style products with congruence control
routes.proofSketch: For a fixed modulus m, let P be the finite set of primes dividing m or a₁⋯aₖ. Choose N divisible by m and by all listed primes, and consider aN+1; any prime divisor q is new and q∤aN. This alone controls only q∤m when q is chosen with additional congruence constraints; a general product-plus-one is insufficient to force q≡a (mod m). The route is valid only for specially engineered progressions, as the catalog says.

routes.title: algebraic norms/cyclotomic factors for suitable progressions. State the progression and hypotheses precisely
routes.proofSketch: For a suitable cyclotomic value Φ_n(A), any prime divisor not dividing nA has multiplicative order n modulo q, hence n|(q−1), so q≡1 (mod n). Taking A arbitrarily large yields new such prime divisors; exclude finitely many exceptional divisors by choosing A. This establishes infinitely many primes ≡1 mod n, not arbitrary reduced residue classes.

routes.verbatimNote: Typed by the assistant from the rendered PDF page image(s); wording, numbering and order follow the source; mathematics rendered in LaTeX-style plain text. Symbols were not corrected or modernized. The source's ledger locator said pp. 47–48; the proposition is on p. 49 of the PDF. Source: Introduction to functional analysis, lecture notes for 18.102, Spring 2025, Christoph Kehle (MIT), May 2025 — Section 5 'Hilbert spaces', Proposition 5.3 (Cauchy–Schwarz inequality) with proof, p. 49. Attribution: Christoph Kehle, MIT 18.102 lecture notes, Spring 2025 (no license stated in the PDF or on the hosting page). Route match: verified.
routes.verbatimProof:
Proposition 5.3 (Cauchy–Schwarz inequality). Let $H$ be a pre-Hilbert space. Then
$$|\langle v,w\rangle|\le\|v\|\|w\|$$
with equality if and only if $v$ and $w$ are linearly dependent.

Proof. For $t\in\mathbb{K}$ define $p(t)=\|v+tw\|^2=\|v\|^2+|t|^2\|w\|^2+2\mathrm{Re}(t\langle v,w\rangle)$. Assume WLOG that $w\neq 0$, and set
$$t_{\min}=-\frac{\overline{\langle v,w\rangle}}{\|w\|^2}$$
Hence,
$$0\le p(t_{\min})=\|v\|^2-\frac{|\langle v,w\rangle|^2}{\|w\|^2}$$
from which we obtain the conclusion. Clearly, if $v,w$ are linearly dependent, we have equality. If equality holds, then $0=p(t_{\min})$ but then $v$ and $w$ are dependent. $\square$

entries.name: Euclid's lemma: prime p dividing ab divides a or b
entries.description: Bezout identity; Euclid's gcd lemma; prime elements in a UFD/irreducible-is-prime in a PID.

routes.title: Bezout identity
routes.proofSketch: If prime p divides ab but not a, then gcd(p,a)=1. Bézout gives rp+sa=1; multiply by b: rpb+sab=b. Both terms on the right representation are divisible by p, so p|b.

routes.title: prime elements in a UFD/irreducible-is-prime in a PID

entries.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
entries.description: Existence by strong induction and uniqueness via Euclid's lemma; valuation/exponent functions and prime divisibility.

routes.title: Existence by strong induction and uniqueness via Euclid's lemma
routes.proofSketch: Existence: factor a composite n into proper factors and apply strong induction until all factors are prime. Uniqueness: if p₁⋯pᵣ=q₁⋯qₛ, Euclid's lemma makes p₁ divide some qⱼ, hence equal to it; cancel and induct.

routes.title: valuation/exponent functions and prime divisibility
routes.proofSketch: For each prime p define v_p(n), its exponent in n. Existence follows by repeatedly dividing out prime factors; uniqueness follows because Euclid's lemma makes the p-adic exponent of a product additive. Thus every positive integer has a unique finite prime-exponent vector.

entries.name: Fermat's little theorem

routes.title: Permute nonzero residues under multiplication by a
routes.proofSketch: Multiplication by a permutes nonzero residue classes mod prime p. Multiply all residues: a^(p−1)(p−1)!≡(p−1)! (mod p); cancel the invertible factorial to get a^(p−1)≡1, hence a^p≡a.

routes.title: Lagrange's theorem in the multiplicative group

entries.name: Wilson's theorem
entries.description: Pair each unit with its inverse, leaving ±1; use the structure of the finite multiplicative group (with the p=2 case handled separately).

routes.title: Pair each unit with its inverse, leaving ±1
routes.proofSketch: Pair each unit x modulo n with its inverse. All pairs cancel in the product of units except self-inverse units; in a prime field the only roots of x²=1 are ±1, so (n−1)!≡−1 (mod prime n). This proof applies to prime n (and for composite n the Wilson congruence generally fails).

entries.name: Euclidean algorithm terminates and computes gcd
entries.description: Strict descent of remainders; invariant ideals/generated subgroups; continued fractions.

routes.title: Strict descent of remainders
routes.proofSketch: Repeated division gives a=bq+r with 0≤r<b. Each nonzero remainder is a strictly smaller positive integer, so the process terminates. Since gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r), the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b).

routes.proofSketch: In Z, ideals satisfy (a,b)=(b,a−qb) whenever a=bq+r, reducing the pair to the Euclidean remainder sequence. The last nonzero generator is the gcd; termination follows from strict descent of positive remainders.

routes.title: Back-substitute Euclidean divisions
routes.proofSketch: Write the Euclidean divisions backward: the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a,b), and each remainder equals the previous dividend minus quotient times divisor. Back-substitution expresses gcd(a,b)=ax+by.

routes.title: least positive element of the ideal (a,b)
routes.proofSketch: Among positive elements of I={ax+by:x,y∈Z}, take least d. Division with remainder shows d divides both a and b (otherwise a remainder in I is smaller); every common divisor divides d. So d=gcd(a,b) and lies in (a,b).

routes.title: lattice-point/linear-combination argument
routes.proofSketch: The integer lattice points generated by vectors (a,b) in Z² project their first coordinates to the subgroup aZ+bZ. Every subgroup of Z is dZ; its least positive element d is an integer combination and is exactly gcd(a,b).

entries.name: Chinese remainder theorem (coprime moduli)
entries.description: Construct coefficients with Bezout identities; ring isomorphism via kernels/ideals; Lagrange interpolation/idempotents.

routes.title: Construct coefficients with Bezout identities
routes.proofSketch: For coprime m,n choose u,v with um+vn=1. Given residues a mod m,b mod n, x=a·vn+b·um has x≡a mod m and x≡b mod n. Any two solutions differ by a multiple of both, hence mn.

routes.title: ring isomorphism via kernels/ideals
routes.proofSketch: The map φ:Z/(mn)→Z/m×Z/n sending a residue to its pair of residues is a ring homomorphism. Its kernel is multiples of mn, hence trivial; finite sets have equal size mn, so it is an isomorphism.

routes.title: Lagrange interpolation/idempotents
routes.proofSketch: For pairwise coprime moduli n₁,…,nₖ, put N=∏nᵢ and Nⱼ=N/nⱼ. Choose yⱼ with Nⱼyⱼ≡1 (mod nⱼ), and set x=Σⱼ bⱼNⱼyⱼ. Modulo nᵢ, every summand except the i-th vanishes and the i-th is bᵢ, giving all required congruences. If x and x′ are two solutions, every nⱼ divides x−x′; pairwise coprimality implies N divides x−x′, proving uniqueness modulo N.

routes.verbatimProof:
Fix a \(k\in\NN\). Then given \(b_1,\dots,b_k\in\ZZ\) and \(n_1,\dots,n_k\in\NN\), the system of congruences \[\begin{aligned} x&\equiv b_1\pmod{n_1}\\ x&\equiv b_2\pmod{n_2}\\ &\vdots\\ x&\equiv b_k\pmod{n_k}\end{aligned}\] has a solution \(x\in\ZZ\) if the \(n_1,n_2,\dots,n_k\) are pairwise relatively prime. The solution is unique modulo \(N=n_1\,n_2\dots n_k\).

Proof

For \(j=1,\dots,k\), let \(N_j=N/n_j\). Since the moduli \(n_j\) are pairwise relatively prime, \(\gcd(N_j,n_j)=1\) – after all, \(N_j\) is the product of all the moduli except \(n_j\). Hence by Corollary 2.2.1, \(\exists y_j = N_j^{-1}\) modulo \(n_j\), satisfying \(N_jy_j\equiv 1\pmod{n_j}\). Consider now \[x=\sum_{j=1}^k b_j N_j y_j\] Since \[N_j\equiv 0\pmod{n_i} \ \ \forall i\neq j,\] we see that \[x\equiv b_j N_j y_j\equiv b_j\pmod{n_j}.\] Hence \(x\) is a solution to the system of congruences.

We have to show now that any two solutions are congruent modulo \(N\). Suppose that \(x\) and \(y\) are both solutions of the system of congruences. Then \(x\equiv b_j\equiv y\pmod{n_j}\), or \(n_j\mid x-y\), for all \(1\leq j\leq k\). But then, since the moduli are pairwise relatively prime, using Theorem 2.1.2 \(k\) times (formally, this needs to be done by induction!), we can conclude that \(N=n_1\dots n_k\mid x-y\) or \(x\equiv y\pmod N\).

routes.title: Triangulation and induction

entries.name: Euler's polyhedron formula V−E+F=2 (convex polyhedra/planar graphs)
entries.description: Remove edges/faces inductively in a planar graph; triangulate and count incidences; topological Euler characteristic.

routes.title: Remove edges/faces inductively in a planar graph
routes.proofSketch: Induct on the number of faces of a connected planar graph $G$. If $G$ has one face it is acyclic (Jordan curve theorem) and connected, hence a tree with $E=V-1$, so $V-E+F=2$. Otherwise pick an edge $e$ separating two different faces and delete it. Then $e$ appears only once on each adjacent face boundary, so any path through $e$ can be rerouted around one of the faces and the graph stays connected. The deletion lowers both $E$ and $F$ by one, leaving $V-E+F$ unchanged, so the formula follows by induction.

routes.title: topological Euler characteristic
routes.proofSketch: The Euler characteristic of a polyhedron's surface is defined as $\chi=V-E+F$. It is a homotopy invariant because it is computed from homology, which is homotopy invariant. A convex polyhedron is homeomorphic to the 3-ball, so its surface is homeomorphic to the 2-sphere, whose Euler characteristic is 2. Hence $V-E+F=2$ for every convex polyhedron.

entries.name: There are irrational numbers / R is uncountable
entries.description: Cantor diagonal construction; nested intervals avoiding a proposed enumeration; cardinality via binary sequences.

routes.title: Cantor diagonal construction
routes.proofSketch: Let $T$ be the set of infinite binary sequences and suppose $s_1,s_2,\dots$ enumerates it. Build $s$ by taking its $n$-th digit to be the complement of the $n$-th digit of $s_n$. Then $s\in T$ differs from every $s_n$ in the $n$-th place, so $s$ is not in the list, contradicting the assumption that the list is complete. Hence $T$ is uncountable. The uncountability of $\mathbb R$ then follows by injecting $T$ into $\mathbb R$ (reading a sequence as a decimal fraction $0.t$).

routes.title: nested intervals avoiding a proposed enumeration
routes.proofSketch: Given any sequence $x_1,x_2,\dots$ and an interval $[a,b]$, take the first two terms lying in $(a,b)$ as the endpoints $a_1<b_1$, then the first two terms in $(a_1,b_1)$ as $a_2<b_2$, and so on, producing nested open intervals with $a_n$ increasing and $b_n$ decreasing. If the process stops, the last interval contains at most one $x_n$, so another point of it is missing from the sequence. Otherwise let $a_\infty=\lim a_n$, $b_\infty=\lim b_n$. By induction $(a_n,b_n)$ excludes $x_1,\dots,x_{2n}$, so $x_n\notin(a_n,b_n)$. If $a_\infty=b_\infty$ this common point lies in every interval, so it is not on the list; if $a_\infty<b_\infty$ every point of $[a_\infty,b_\infty]$ is missing. Applying this to a supposed enumeration of $[a,b]$ gives the uncountability.

routes.title: cardinality via binary sequences
routes.proofSketch: The set $T$ of infinite binary sequences is uncountable by the diagonal argument. To transfer this to the reals, define an injection $f:T\to\mathbb R$ by reading a binary string as a decimal fraction, $f(t)=0.t$, which sends different strings to different numbers. Since $T$ is uncountable, its image is an uncountable subset of $\mathbb R$, so $\mathbb R$ is uncountable. A bijection $T\to\mathbb R$ can then be built by Cantor's method of removing countable subsets.

routes.title: Complex analysis: Liouville applied to 1/P
routes.proofSketch: If nonconstant complex polynomial P has no zero, 1/P is entire and tends to 0 at infinity, hence bounded. Liouville says 1/P is constant, contradiction. Factor out a root and repeat to count deg(P) roots with multiplicity.

routes.verbatimProof:
6.5.3 Liouville's theorem

Theorem 6.16. (Liouville's theorem) Assume $f(z)$ is entire and suppose it is bounded in the complex plane, namely $|f(z)|<M$ for all $z\in\mathbf{C}$ then $f(z)$ is constant.

Proof. For any circle of radius $R$ around $z_0$ the Cauchy inequality says $|f'(z_0)|\le\frac{M}{R}$. But, $R$ can be as large as we like so we conclude that $|f'(z_0)|=0$ for every $z_0\in\mathbf{C}$. Since the derivative is 0, the function itself is constant.

In short:

If $f$ is entire and bounded then $f$ is constant.

Note. $P(z)=a_nz^n+\ldots+a_0$, $\sin(z)$, $e^z$ are all entire but not bounded.

Now, practically for free, we get the fundamental theorem of algebra.

Corollary. (Fundamental theorem of algebra) Any polynomial $P$ of degree $n\ge 1$, i.e.
$$P(z)=a_0+a_1z+\ldots+a_nz^n,\quad a_n\neq 0,$$
has exactly $n$ roots.

Proof. There are two parts to the proof.

Hard part: Show that $P$ has at least one root.

This is done by contradiction, together with Liouville's theorem. Suppose $P(z)$ does not have a zero. Then

1. $f(z)=1/P(z)$ is entire. This is obvious because (by assumption) $P(z)$ has no zeros.
2. $f(z)$ is bounded. This follows because $1/P(z)$ goes to 0 as $|z|$ goes to $\infty$.

[Figure: a circle $C_R$ of radius $R$ in the plane; "|1/P(z)| small out here" outside, "M = max of |1/P(z)| in here" inside.]

(It is clear that $|1/P(z)|$ goes to 0 as $z$ goes to infinity, i.e. $|1/P(z)|$ is small outside a large circle. So $|1/P(z)|$ is bounded by $M$.)

So, by Liouville's theorem $f(z)$ is constant, and therefore $P(z)$ must be constant as well. But this a contradiction, so $P$ must have a zero.

Easy part: $P$ has exactly $n$ zeros. Let $z_0$ be one zero. We can factor $P(z)=(z-z_0)Q(z)$. $Q(z)$ has degree $n-1$. If $n-1>0$, then we can apply the result to $Q(z)$. We can continue this process until the degree of $Q$ is 0.

routes.title: topology: winding number/fundamental group or degree
routes.proofSketch: Let f(z)=P(z)/zⁿ on a large circle; by the argument principle the winding number of P(z) around 0 equals n for sufficiently large radius (dominant leading term). If P had no zero inside, its boundary winding number would be 0, contradiction. Rouché's theorem formalizes this comparison.

routes.verbatimProof:
We are interested in the derivative of the integral

 \[g(t) = \int_0^t \sin(x)dx\]

 with respect to the upper limit, \(t\).

 We can compute this derivative, roughly, by evaluating \(\frac{g(t+d)-g(t)}{d}\) for very small \(d\).

 But \(g(t + d)-g(t)\) is just

 \[g(t) = \int_t^{t+d} \sin(x)dx\]

 The region between \(x = t\) and \(x = t + d\) is just a sliver, in which \(\sin(x)\) is very near \(\sin(t)\).
 So the area in this sliver between \(y = \sin(t)\) and \(y = 0\) is just \(d \sin(t)\), where \(d\) is the width
 of the sliver and \(\sin(t)\) its height, to a first approximation.

 This tells us that the derivative of \(g(t)\), the derivative of the integral of the sine function at argument
 \(t\), is this area divided by \(d\), which is \(\sin(t)\).

Exactly the same result holds for any function whose values for arguments sufficiently close to \(t\)
 are as close as you like to its value at \(t\). (These are called continuous functions) for all \(t\) between
 the limits of integration.

 This result is called the fundamental theorem of calculus. It says: If you
 differentiate the integral of a function, \(f\), that is continuous at argument \(t\) in the closed interval
 including the endpoints of integration (this is the condition that if's values are as close as you like
 to \(f(t)\) at arguments sufficiently near \(t\)) you get back the value of the integrand, \(f\), at
 argument \(t\).

 Another way to say this is: the integral with upper limit as variable, an area as we have just
 defined it, is an antiderivative of its integrand, when that integrand is continuous.

 This means that integrating a function and then differentiating the result with respect to upper limit,
 gives back the function.

routes.verbatimProof:
Suppose we start with a differentiable function, \(f\), and form its derivative, \(f'(x)\), and integrate this
 derivative between somewhere, say \(a\), and \(t\).

 In other words suppose we form

 \[g(t) = \int_a^t f'(x)dx\]

 The fundamental theorem then tells us: \(g(t) = f(t) - f(a)\).

 To see this, recall that if \(f\) is differentiable at argument \(x\) then for \(d\) sufficiently small, we
 have, to any desired accuracy:

 \[f' = \frac{f(x+d)-f(x)}{d} \enspace\text{or}\enspace f'd = f(x+d)-f(x)\]

 If we chop the interval between \(t\) and a up into slices of widths given by \(d\) appropriate to each \(x\)
 value, we can sum up the contribution from either side of the equation \(f'd = f(x + d) - f(x)\) over all the
 slices. We use the same value \(d\) for each slice

 The sum of the positive and negative terms in the last equation above will give us the sum of the areas in the
 little slices. This sum will "telescope". The left term from one slice will be the right term from the previous
 slice with the opposite sign; the two will cancel each other out, and we will get contributions only from the
 first and last slices. This means:

 \[f(t) - f(a) = \int_a^t f'(x)dx\]

 This is the standard form for the fundamental theorem.

routes.title: Rolle's theorem via extrema
routes.proofSketch: If f(a)=f(b)=k and f is constant, its derivative is zero throughout (a,b). Otherwise f takes a value above or below k. In the above case, continuity on [a,b] gives an absolute maximum; it cannot occur at an endpoint, so it occurs at an interior point and Fermat’s theorem gives f′(c)=0. The below case uses an interior minimum.

routes.verbatimProof:
Let f be a continuous function over the closed interval [a,b] and differentiable over the open interval (a,b) such that f(a)=f(b). There then exists at least one c∈(a,b) such that f′(c)=0.

Proof

Let k=f(a)=f(b). We consider three cases:

f(x)=k for all x∈(a,b).

There exists x∈(a,b) such that f(x)>k.

There exists x∈(a,b) such that f(x)<k.

Case 1: If f(x)=k for all x∈(a,b), then f′(x)=0 for all x∈(a,b).
Case 2: Since f is a continuous function over the closed, bounded interval [a,b], by the extreme value theorem, it has an absolute maximum. Also, since there is a point x∈(a,b) such that f(x)>k, the absolute maximum is greater than k. Therefore, the absolute maximum does not occur at either endpoint. As a result, the absolute maximum must occur at an interior point c∈(a,b). Because f has a maximum at an interior point c, and f is differentiable at c, by Fermat’s theorem, f′(c)=0.

Case 3: The case when there exists a point x∈(a,b) such that f(x)<k is analogous to case 2, with maximum replaced by minimum.

□

routes.title: subtract the secant line and apply Rolle
routes.proofSketch: Let ℓ be the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)), with slope m=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), and set g=f−ℓ. Then g(a)=g(b)=0 and g inherits continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b). Rolle’s theorem gives g′(c)=0, hence f′(c)=m.

routes.verbatimProof:
Let f be continuous over the closed interval [a,b] and differentiable over the open interval (a,b). Then, there exists at least one point c∈(a,b) such that

f′(c)=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).

Proof

The proof follows from Rolle’s theorem by introducing an appropriate function that satisfies the criteria of Rolle’s theorem. Consider the line connecting (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). Since the slope of that line is

(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a)

and the line passes through the point (a,f(a)), the equation of that line can be written as

y=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a)(x−a)+f(a).

Let g(x) denote the vertical difference between the point (x,f(x)) and the point (x,y) on that line. Therefore,

g(x)=f(x)−[(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a)(x−a)+f(a)].

Figure 
4.26

The value g(x) is the vertical difference between the point (x,f(x)) and the point (x,y) on the secant line connecting (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)).

Since the graph of f intersects the secant line when x=a and x=b, we see that g(a)=0=g(b). Since f is a differentiable function over (a,b), g is also a differentiable function over (a,b). Furthermore, since f is continuous over [a,b], g is also continuous over [a,b]. Therefore, g satisfies the criteria of Rolle’s theorem. Consequently, there exists a point c∈(a,b) such that g′(c)=0. Since

g′(x)=f′(x)−(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a),

we see that

g′(c)=f′(c)−(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).

Since g′(c)=0, we conclude that

f′(c)=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).

□

routes.title: Cauchy mean value theorem as a paired-derivative generalization
routes.proofSketch: For differentiable f,g with hypotheses ensuring a zero of g′, consider H(x)=(f(b)−f(a))(g(x)−g(a))−(g(b)−g(a))(f(x)−f(a)). Since H(a)=H(b)=0, Rolle yields the Cauchy mean value relation H′(c)=0. Taking g(x)=x gives MVT.

routes.verbatimProof:
Proof of the spectral theorem
November 5, 2013

1 Spectral theorem

Here is the definition of selfadjoint, more or less exactly as in the text.

Definition 1.1. Suppose $V$ is a (real or complex) inner product space. A linear transformation $S\in\mathcal{L}(V)$ is selfadjoint if
$$\langle Sv,w\rangle=\langle v,Sw\rangle\qquad(v,w\in V).$$

The point of these notes is to explain a proof (somewhat different from the one in the book) of

Theorem 1.2 (Spectral theorem). Suppose $V$ is a finite-dimensional real or complex vector space. The linear operator $S\in\mathcal{L}(V)$ is selfadjoint if and only if $V$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the eigenspaces of $S$ for real eigenvalues:
$$V=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}V_\lambda.$$
Here by definition
$$V_\lambda=\{v\in V\mid Sv=\lambda v\}$$
is the eigenspace for the eigenvalue $\lambda$. The orthogonality requirement means
$$\langle v,w\rangle=0\qquad(v\in V_\lambda,w\in V_\mu,\lambda\neq\mu).$$

The theorem says first of all that a selfadjoint operator is diagonalizable, and that all the eigenvalues are real.

The orthogonality of the eigenspaces is important as well. Orthogonal decompositions are easy to compute with, and they are in a certain sense very "rigid" and stable. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are distinct lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$, then automatically $\mathbb{R}^2=L_1\oplus L_2$. That is, any vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^2$ can be written uniquely as
$$v=\ell_1+\ell_2,\qquad(\ell_i\in L_i).\qquad(1.3)$$
If the two lines point in nearly the same direction, then writing a small vector $v$ may require large vectors in $L_1$ and $L_2$. For example, if
$$L_1=x\text{ axis}=\mathbb{R}\cdot(1,0),\qquad L_2=\mathbb{R}\cdot(1,1/10),\qquad(1.4)$$
then
$$(0,1/10)=(-1,0)+(1,1/10).$$
In a computational world, this means that small errors in $v$ may correspond to large errors in the "coordinates" $\ell_i$. If on the other hand the lines $L_i$ are orthogonal, then
$$\|v\|^2=\|\ell_1\|^2+\|\ell_2\|^2,\qquad(1.5)$$
so that small $v$ correspond to small $\ell_i$.

The proof that the conditions in the theorem imply selfadjointness is straightforward, and I won't do it. What's interesting and difficult is the proof that selfadjointness implies the eigenspace decomposition. This is based on the next two lemmas.

Lemma 1.6 (Orthogonal invariants). Suppose $S$ is a selfadjoint operator on an inner product space $V$, and $U\subset V$ is an $S$-invariant subspace:
$$Su\in U,\qquad(u\in U).$$
Then the orthogonal complement $U^\perp$ is also $S$-invariant.

Lemma 1.7 (Maximal eigenspaces). Suppose $S$ is a selfadjoint operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The function
$$s(v)=\langle Sv,v\rangle$$
takes real values on on $V$. If $v_0$ is a maximum for $s$ on the unit sphere
$$\text{sphere}=\{v\in V\mid\langle v,v\rangle=1\},$$
then $v_0$ is an eigenvector of $S$ with (real) eigenvalue $s(v_0)$.

We postpone the proofs of these two lemmas for a moment. Assuming them. . .

Proof of Spectral Theorem. Recall that we are proving only that a selfadjoint operator has the orthogonal eigenspace decomposition described. We proceed by induction on $\dim V$. If $\dim V=0$, then $S=0$ and there are no eigenvalues; the theorem says that the zero vector space is an empty direct sum, which is true by definition.

So suppose $\dim V>0$, and that the theorem is known for spaces of lower dimension. Because $V\neq 0$, there are nonzero vectors, so there are vectors of length one, and the unit sphere in Lemma 1.7 is not empty. The function $s(v)$ is continuous (if we choose a basis for $V$, $s$ is a quadratic polynomial function of the coordinates). Any continuous function must have a maximum on a closed bounded set like the unit sphere, so $s$ has a maximum at some point $v_0$. (This is a hard fact, proved in 18.100; you're not necessarily supposed to know it to understand this course. But the Spectral Theorem is a hard theorem, so you need to do something difficult somewhere. The proof in the text uses the existence of eigenvalues on complex vector spaces, which amounts to the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. That's hard too.)

According to Lemma 1.7,
$$v_0\in V_{s(v_0)};\qquad(1.8)$$
so the eigenspace is not zero. Because an eigenspace is obviously an invariant subspace, Lemma 1.6 implies that
$$V=V_{s(v_0)}\oplus V_{s(v_0)}^\perp,\qquad(1.9)$$
an orthogonal direct sum of $S$-invariant subspaces. Because $V_{s(v_0)}$ is not zero, it has positive dimension, so
$$\dim V_{s(v_0)}^\perp=\dim V-\dim V_{s(v_0)}<\dim V.\qquad(1.10)$$
By inductive hypothesis, $V_{s(v_0)}^\perp$ is an orthogonal direct sum of eigenspaces of $S$. Inserting this orthogonal decomposition in (1.9) gives the complete orthogonal decomposition into eigenspaces that we want. $\square$

The proof of Lemma 1.6 is extremely easy: you just write down what the lemma says is true, and see (using the definition of selfadjoint) that it's obviously true.

Proof of Lemma 1.7. Assume that $v_0$ is a maximum for $s$ on the unit sphere. We are going to show that
$$\text{if }\langle v_0,u\rangle=0,\text{ then }\mathrm{Re}\langle S(v_0),u\rangle=0.\qquad(1.11)$$
If we can prove this, then (applying it in the complex case to all the vectors $e^{i\theta}u$) we will know also that
$$\text{if }\langle v_0,u\rangle=0,\text{ then }\langle S(v_0),u\rangle=0.$$
This says that everything orthogonal to the line $F\cdot v_0$ is also orthogonal to $S(v_0)$: that is
$$u\in(F\cdot v_0)^\perp\implies\langle u,S(v_0)\rangle=0.$$
That is,
$$S(v_0)\in\big((F\cdot v_0)^\perp\big)^\perp=F\cdot v_0.$$
This last equation is precisely the statement that $v_0$ is an eigenvector of $S$:
$$S(v_0)=\lambda v_0\qquad(\text{some }\lambda\in F).$$
The eigenvalue $\lambda$ is
$$\frac{\langle S(v_0),v_0\rangle}{\langle v_0,v_0\rangle}=\langle S(v_0),v_0\rangle=s(v_0),$$
as we wished to show.

It remains to prove (1.11). This condition is true for $u$ if and only if it is true for any multiple of $u$, and it is true for $u=0$; so it is enough to prove it for vectors $u$ of length 1. We want to use the fact that $v_0$ is a maximum for $s$ on the unit sphere, so we need to cook up more vectors on the unit sphere. Because $u$ and $v_0$ are orthogonal unit vectors, the Pythagorean Theorem says that
$$v_t=\cos(t)v_0+\sin(t)u\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R})\qquad(1.12)$$
are all unit vectors. The notation is chosen so that the new definition of $v_0$ is equal to the old definition of $v_0$; so the function of one real variable
$$f(t)=s(v_t)=\langle Sv_t,v_t\rangle\qquad(1.13)$$
has a maximum at $t=0$. We're going to use calculus on the function $f$. The formula is
$$f(t)=\langle Sv_t,v_t\rangle=\cos^2(t)\langle Sv_0,v_0\rangle+\sin^2(t)\langle Su,u\rangle+\cos(t)\sin(t)\left[\langle Sv_0,u\rangle+\langle Su,v_0\rangle\right].$$
The selfadjointness of $S$ says that
$$\langle Su,v_0\rangle=\overline{\langle Sv_0,u\rangle},$$
so we get
$$f(t)=\cos^2(t)\langle Sv_0,v_0\rangle+\sin^2(t)\langle Su,u\rangle+2\cos(t)\sin(t)\left[\mathrm{Re}\langle Sv_0,u\rangle\right].$$
Consequently $f$ is differentiable, and
$$f'(0)=2[\mathrm{Re}\langle Sv_0,u\rangle].$$
Since 0 is a maximum for the differentiable function $f$, the derivative must be zero at 0; and this is (1.11). $\square$

routes.title: Group action on cosets/subsets
routes.proofSketch: For existence, let G act on k-element subsets of itself where |G|=pᵐs and p∤s. The binomial coefficient C(pᵐs,pᵐ) is not divisible by p, so some orbit has size prime to p; its stabilizer has p-part pᵐ and contains a Sylow p-subgroup. For conjugacy, act on cosets G/H; an orbit-count modulo p yields a fixed coset when H is p-subgroup, giving conjugate containment. Conjugation on Sylow subgroups then gives n_p≡1 mod p and n_p||G|.

routes.verbatimProof:
23.3 Proof of Sylow Theorems

The main idea to prove all of these theorems is to find a useful action of $G$ on a set and exploit it. This is a continuation of what we have been doing in the last few weeks, in geometric situations with symmetries as well as with the conjugation action of $G$ on itself. The striking part about these three proofs is that unlike rotational symmetries of the cube, where there are lots of sets to think about, such as vertices and faces and so on, here, there is no prior knowledge about $G$, and the only group action we have for any arbitrary group is $G$ acting on itself, and not much else.

Theorem 23.4 (Sylow I). Given $G$ such that
$$|G|=n=p^e\cdot m,$$
where $p^e$ is the largest power of $p$ (that is, $\gcd(p,m)=1$), then there exists a subgroup $H\le G$ such that
$$|H|=p^e.$$

Proof of Sylow I. Take $G$ such that
$$|G|=p^e\cdot m.$$
Let $S$ be the subsets of $G$ of size $p^e$ and let $n$ be the order of $G$. By basic combinatorics, there are $\binom{n}{p^e}$ such subsets, so
$$|S|=\binom{n}{p^e}.$$
Let $G$ act on $S$ by left translations: given an element $g\in G$ and a subset $U\in S$, we map
$$U\longmapsto gU.$$
Our eventual goal is to find a subgroup of $G$ of size $p^e$ by looking at stabilizers, as they are always subgroups of $G$. We find the size of a stabilizer by trying to find an orbit of size $m$, as we then know that the stabilizer will be order $p^e$.⁸³ We begin with some lemmas. The first lemma provides information about the size of the set modulo $p$.

Lemma 23.5. Where $n=|G|=m\cdot p^e$, we have that
$$|S|=\binom{n}{p^e}\neq 0\pmod p.$$
Furthermore,
$$\binom{n}{p^e}\equiv m\pmod p.$$

Sketch of Proof. The proof is not particularly relevant to group theory and can be proved by expanding the binomial coefficient and showing that the number of powers of $p$ in the numerator is the same as the denominator. Alternatively, one could expand $(1+x)^n$ and look at it modulo $p$. $\square$

To reiterate, $S$ consists of all subsets of $G$ of size $p^e$, and these subsets do not have to be subgroups.

Lemma 23.6. Suppose we have a subset $U\in S$ᵃ, which is a subset of $G$. Also, let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ that stabilizes $U$. Then, $|H|$ divides $|U|$.
ᵃNote that $U$ is an element of $S$ but is itself also a subset of $G$, so $U\subset G$.

Proof. Since $H$ stabilizes $U$, for any $h\in H$, we know $hU=U$. In other words, for each $u\in U$, we have
$$Hu\subset U.$$
Equivalently, for each $u\in U$, the corresponding right coset of $H$ is a subset of $U$. This implies that the right cosets partition $U$. Since the cosets have the same size, we know that $|H|$ divides $|U|$. $\square$

With these lemmas in hand, we can continue with the proof of the main theorem. The first lemma tells us that $|S|\neq 0\pmod p$. We know that the orbits partition $S$, so
$$|S|=|O_1|+\cdots+|O_r|.$$
Since $p$ does not divide the LHS, there must exist an orbit $\theta$ where
$$\gcd(p,|\theta|)=1.$$
Let the size of $\theta$ be $|\theta|=k$.

Now, consider some element $u$ of $\theta$. By the counting formula, we also know that
$$|G|=|\theta|\cdot|\mathrm{Stab}(u)|.$$
And so $p^em=k|\mathrm{Stab}(u)|$ and $p^e\mid|\mathrm{Stab}(u)|$ because $\gcd(k,p)=1$. By the second lemma, $|\mathrm{Stab}(u)|$ divides $|u|=p^e$.

Thus,
$$|\mathrm{Stab}(u)|=p^e$$
and we have found a Sylow $p$-group. $\square$

The proof of the second Sylow theorem is similar.

Theorem 23.7 (Sylow II). There are two parts; part a) is what is usually referred to as the second Sylow theorem.
(a) Given $H\le G$, where $H$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup, any other Sylow $p$–subgroup $H'\le G$ is conjugate to $H$; i.e. there exists $g$ such that $H'=gHg^{-1}$.
(b) Given any subgroup $K\le G$ such that $|K|=p^d$, for any Sylow subgroup $H$, there exists $g$ such that $gKg^{-1}\le H$.ᵃ
ᵃNotice that $|K|$ does not have to be the maximal prime power, and can have order smaller than $|H|$. Every prime power order subgroup, up to conjugation, sits inside a Sylow subgroup.

Proof of Sylow II. We approach this proof similarly, finding a nice set and an action on it. Fix $H$ to be a Sylow subgroup. Our set is $X=G/H$, the left cosets of $H$. The index of $H$ is the same as $|X|$, so $|X|=m$.

Let $K$ be the subgroup we want to show is a subgroup of $H$ up to conjugation, where $|K|=p^f$. We will look at how $K$ acts on $X$ by left translation, the mapping:
$$k(aH)\longmapsto kaH.$$
We decompose into orbits, $|X|=|O_1|+\cdots+|O_r|$. Note that these orbits are with respect to the action of $K$, not the action of $G$, as that would be transitive and we'd only have one orbit. We have that $|O_i|$ divides $|K|=p^f$, but $p$ does not divide $m$. Thus this orbit decomposition can only work if some orbit $O$ has size 1. In other words, there exists some coset $aH$ that is fixed by all $k\in K$. Then,
$$kaH=aH$$
$$a^{-1}kaH=H$$
$$a^{-1}ka\in H$$
$$a^{-1}Ka\le H$$
which is what we needed to show. $\square$

A lot of the work done in these proofs are choosing some set and action, then looking at the orbits and seeing what we can do what them. The third proof is similar.

Theorem 23.8 (Sylow III). The number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$ divides
$$m=\frac{n}{p^e}$$
and is congruent to 1 modulo $p$.

Proof of Sylow III. Our set will be $Y$ as the set of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$. We will be trying to find the size of $Y$. $G$ acts on $Y$ by conjugation, $H\longmapsto gHg^{-1}$. By Sylow II, there is only one orbit. Pick a Sylow subgroup $H\in Y$. Then
$$|G|=|\mathrm{Stab}(Y)||\mathrm{orbit}(H)|=|Y||\mathrm{Stab}(Y)|.$$
This already tells us that $|Y|$ divides $|G|=n$, but we can say more.

The stabilizer here has a name, the normalizer of $H$. It turns out that $H\le\mathrm{Stab}(H)$ because for all $h\in H$, $hHh^{-1}=H$. So $|\mathrm{Stab}(H)|$ is divisible by $p^e=|H|$. The counting formula then says that $|G|=p^em=|Y|\cdot(p^e\cdot\text{stuff})$ which implies that $|Y|$ divides $m$.

The last part is showing that $|Y|\equiv 1\pmod p$. We now use the action of $H$ on $Y$ by conjugation.

Fact 23.9. Suppose we have another Sylow subgroup $H'\in Y$, $H'$ is fixed by $H$ if and only if $H=H'$. In other words, under the action of $H$, there is only one fixed point.

By looking at orbits, there is only one orbit of size 1 because there is only one fixed point. The rest are powers of $p$ because the size of $H$ is a power of $p$. Thus the decomposition into orbits looks like
$$Y=1+p+\cdots+p^2+\cdots+p^3+\cdots\equiv 1\pmod p.$$

Proof of fact. If we look at the stabilizer/normalizer, $\mathrm{Stab}_G(H')=N(H')$, we know that $H\le N(H')$ because $H'$ is fixed by $H$, and that $H'\le N(H')$ by what we said above about normalizers.

Now $N(H')$ is a subgroup of $G$ as well, so the largest power of $p$ that divides $N(H')$ can only be $p^e$. So $H$ and $H'$ are Sylow subgroups of $N(H')$ as well. By Sylow II on $N(H')$, there exists $n\in N(H')$ such that $nH'n^{-1}=H$. But then by the definition of $N$, $nH'n^{-1}=H'$, and so $H=H'$. $\square$

Given this fact, we are done with the third proof. $\square$

⁸³The product of the size of an orbit and the size of the stabilizer is the size of the group $G$, which here is $m\cdot p^e$.

routes.title: Ratios of subtriangle areas and cancellation around the triangle
routes.proofSketch: Signs are handled first: the product of the three signed ratios is positive whether the concurrency point O is inside the triangle or outside. For magnitudes, triangles of equal height have areas proportional to their bases, so |BD|/|DC| = |BOD|/|COD| = |BAD|/|CAD|, and subtracting numerators and denominators gives BD/DC = |ABO|/|CAO| (adding instead if A and O lie on opposite sides of BC). The same argument gives CE/EA = |BCO|/|ABO| and AF/FB = |CAO|/|BCO|. Multiplying the three equations, the area ratios cancel cyclically and the product of the three ratios has absolute value 1.

routes.title: sine rule/trigonometric ratios
routes.proofSketch: The page states the trigonometric form: sin∠ABE/sin∠CBE · sin∠BCF/sin∠ACF · sin∠CAD/sin∠BAD = 1 for concurrent cevians AD, BE, CF. In its proof, the side-ratio product AF/FB·BD/DC·CE/EA = 1 is rewritten as a product of area ratios of triangles sharing the concurrency point K (e.g. AFK/BFK), since each pair has a common altitude from K. Each area is then written as (1/2)·side·side·sine of the included angle (e.g. AFK = AF·AK·sin∠BAD/2), and the common factors cancel, leaving the product of sine ratios equal to the inverse side-ratio product, hence 1.

routes.title: barycentric coordinates and a determinant condition
routes.proofSketch: Let O have barycentric coordinates (λ_A, λ_B, λ_C) with sum 1 and, since O is on no side line, all nonzero. Taking X = F (the intersection of AB and OC), the relation XO = λ_A XA + λ_B XB + λ_C XC rearranges to FO − λ_C FC = λ_A FA + λ_B FB. The left side is parallel to CF and the right side to AB, which are not parallel, so both vanish and λ_A FA + λ_B FB = 0, giving AF/FB = λ_B/λ_A. The same reasoning gives BD/DC = λ_C/λ_B and CE/EA = λ_A/λ_C, and the product is 1.

routes.title: Gaussian integer factorization
routes.proofSketch: For p = 4n+1, a lemma of Lagrange (or Euler's criterion) supplies an integer m with p | m^2+1. Since Z[i] is Euclidean, hence a UFD, and p divides (m+i)(m−i) but neither factor (their imaginary parts are ±1), p is not prime in Z[i]. So p has a nontrivial factorization, which by multiplicativity of the norm (N(p) = p^2) has exactly two factors, p = (x+yi)(x−yi), and hence p = x^2 + y^2. The first Dedekind proof on the same page uses the Frobenius map on Z[i]/(p) and splitting of the ideal (p) instead.

routes.title: Wilson's theorem and factorial congruences
routes.proofSketch: For p = 4m+1, Wilson's theorem gives that n = (2m)! is a square root of −1 modulo p (alternatively n = g^m for a primitive root g). Then p divides n^2+1 = (n+i)(n−i) in Z[i] but neither factor, so p is not irreducible there; to conclude it is not prime, the page shows Z[i] is Euclidean for the norm via a lattice argument, hence a UFD. So p = (a+bi)(c+di) with nonunits, and taking norms gives p^2 = (a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) with neither factor 1, so p = a^2+b^2.

routes.title: lattice-point/continued-fraction arguments
routes.proofSketch: Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, −1 is a quadratic residue mod p, so p | m^2+1 for some m. Take the lattice S spanned by u = (1,m) and v = (0,p). Any w = au+bv = (a, am+bp) has ||w||^2 ≡ a^2(1+m^2) ≡ 0 mod p. The fundamental parallelogram has area p, while the open disc of radius √(2p) has area 2πp > 4p and is convex and symmetric, so Minkowski's theorem gives a nonzero lattice point in it. Then 0 < ||w||^2 < 2p and p | ||w||^2, so p = ||w||^2 is a sum of two squares.

entries.name: Quadratic reciprocity

routes.title: Gauss's lemma and lattice-point parity
routes.proofSketch: For distinct odd primes p,q, Gauss's lemma says (q/p)=(-1)^N where N counts least positive residues of q,2q,…,((p−1)/2)q that exceed p/2. Counting lattice points in the rectangle 1≤i≤(p−1)/2, 1≤j≤(q−1)/2 below/above the line qi=pj gives N_p+N_q=((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2), yielding (p/q)(q/p)=(-1)^(((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2)).

routes.title: Eisenstein's lattice-point proof
routes.proofSketch: Count lattice points in the rectangle 1≤x≤(p−1)/2, 1≤y≤(q−1)/2 using the line y=(q/p)x; no lattice point lies on it. routes.title: algebraic closure and root splitting
routes.proofSketch: In an algebraic closure, repeatedly split any reducible polynomial into lower-degree factors until every factor is irreducible; degree strictly decreases, guaranteeing termination. Uniqueness follows because F[x] is a PID and irreducibles there are prime. Algebraic closure is unnecessary for the existence factorization and this route is therefore not as independent as it first appears.

routes.title: principal ideal generator
routes.proofSketch: The ideal (f,g) in the Euclidean domain F[x] is principal, say (f,g)=(d). Since d is in the ideal it is a combination af+bg; and because f,g lie in (d), d divides both. Thus d is a gcd and a Bézout combination.

routes.title: linear-algebra nullspace of a Sylvester matrix/resultant
routes.proofSketch: For polynomials f,g over a field, a common factor exists exactly when there are nonzero A,B with deg A < deg g and deg B < deg f such that Af+Bg=0. The forward direction uses f=f₁h and g=g₁h, taking A=−g₁, B=f₁. Conversely, if gcd(f,g)=1, Bézout gives Ãf+Ḃg=1; multiplying by B and substituting Bg=−Af forces f to divide B, contradicting deg B<deg f. Writing the bounded-degree relation coefficientwise gives the Sylvester matrix; its determinant is the resultant, which vanishes precisely when this system has a nonzero solution.

routes.title: Expand logarithmic derivative of the generating polynomial

routes.title: Indicator functions
routes.proofSketch: Use indicator functions, noting 1_A·1_B = 1_{A∩B}. For the union A of A_1,...,A_n, one wants 1_A = Σ_{k≥1}(−1)^{k−1} Σ_{|I|=k} 1_{A_I}, where A_I is the intersection over I. The product (1_A − 1_{A_1})···(1_A − 1_{A_n}) vanishes identically: at a point outside A every factor is 0 − 0, and at a point of some A_m the m-th factor is 1 − 1. Expanding the product gives the identity. Summing over x (or taking expectations, or integrating) gives the cardinality, probability, or measure form by linearity.

routes.title: classify elements by exact membership set
routes.proofSketch: Theorem 2.1.1 shows that the operator φ f(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T} f(Y) on functions on subsets of S is invertible with φ^{-1} f(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} f(Y); this is checked by composing and using Σ_{i}(−1)^i C(m,i) = δ_{0m}. In the combinatorial setting, f_=(T) counts objects having exactly the properties in T and f_≥(T) those having at least T, so f_≥(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T} f_=(Y) (2.3). Inverting gives f_=(T) = Σ_{Y⊇T}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} f_≥(Y) (2.4), and taking T = ∅ counts objects having none of the properties (2.5).

routes.title: Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
routes.proofSketch: The Boolean algebra B_n is the product of n copies of the 2-chain, so by the product theorem for Möbius functions μ(T,S) = (−1)^{#(S−T)}. Möbius inversion on B_n then says g(S) = Σ_{T⊆S} f(T) for all S iff f(S) = Σ_{T⊆S}(−1)^{#(S−T)} g(T), which is equation (2.8), the inclusion-exclusion principle. The direct check of the inverse is in the proof of Theorem 2.1.1: in the composite φψ, the coefficient of f(Z) is Σ_{T⊆Y⊆Z}(−1)^{#(Y−T)} = δ, so ψ = φ^{-1}.

entries.name: Cayley's formula: n^(n−2) labeled trees
entries.description: Prüfer codes; Matrix-tree theorem/determinant; weighted generating functions.

routes.title: Prüfer codes
routes.proofSketch: Encode a labelled tree by repeatedly deleting its least-labelled leaf and recording its neighbor; after n−2 deletions the recorded labels form a word of length n−2. To invert, scan the word from left to right, joining its first entry to the least label not appearing in the remaining word, deleting that label and the first entry at each step; finally join the two remaining labels. The procedures are inverse, so labelled trees correspond bijectively to the n^(n−2) words.

routes.verbatimProof:
In this lecture, we will prove Cayley’s formula, using the Prüfer code. In particular, we will give a map $PC$ that takes in a labelled tree with $n$ vertices, and returns a string of $n-2$ numbers, each between $1$ and $n$, and an inverse map $\mathbf{Tree}$ that takes in a string of numbers and returns a labelled tree.

The starting observation is that to write down a labelled tree is the same as writing down its $n-1$ edges. Since the vertices are ordered, each edge can be written down by a pair of numbers in $\{1,\dots,n \}$. The Prüfer code begins by writing down these edges in a clever ordering.

The Prüfer code

We are now ready to introduce the Prüfer code. We begin by writing down the edges of $T$. The two vertices of each edge will be written down in a column, with the parent vertex in the top row and the child vertex on the bottom row. We record the edges in the following specific order.

First, find the lowest numbered leaf, and record its number in the bottom row. Above it, write down the number of the vertex this leaf is adjacent to, which we call the parent vertex. Now, delete that lowest numbered leaf and the edge connecting it to the rest of the tree. Find the lowest leaf on the resulting vertex, and record its number, and the number of its parent, in the next column.

Iterate this procedure until we have written down all $n-1$ edges of our tree, with the leaf numbers in the top row, and the parent numbers in the bottom row.

The list of the first $n-2$ parent numbers (i.e., all but the last), is the Prüfer code of $T$.

Example

We illustrate the construction of the Prüfer code by finding the code for the following labelled tree:

The lowest leaf is 3, which is attached to 1, so the first column goes

 Parent node 
 1
 6
 6
 2
 2
 7

 Child node 
 3
 1
 4
 5
 6
 2

Thus, the Prüfer code for the above tree is 16622.

Reconstructing a tree from its Prüfer Code

It is clear from the above definition that the Prüfer code is a list of $n-2$ numbers between 1 and $n$; it is not clear that any such list of numbers is obtained, nor that any two trees give us a different set of numbers. To see this, we describe an inverse algorithm, that constructs a tree on $n$ vertices from a Prüfer code.

More explicitly, the inverse algorithm will take as input a Prüfer code, and from that Prüfer code it will reconstruct the full ordered table of edges we constructed in the Prüfer code algorithm. It should be clear from the description that the algorithm actually reproduces this table, and not some other table, and hence that the two algorithms are inverse to each other. This shows that the Prüfer code is a bijection, which proves Cayley’s formula, as there are $n^{n-2}$ valid Prüfer codes on $n$ vertices.

This algorith proceeds by figuring out the corresponding child nodes one by one. Recall that any number in our list appeared as a parent node, and so is not a leaf. At the first step, we deleted the smallest leaf. So the first child node is the smallest number that does not appear on our list.

After we recorded that edge, we deleted it; thus, the second child number is the smallest number that we haven’t

already used as a leaf number

doesn’t appear at or after the current spot as a parent.

Example

We first reconstruct the tree we did in the first example, from its code.
Recall, the Prüfer code was 1 6 6 2 2.

The lowest unused number is 3, so that is the first child.

To find the next unused number, we move to the second column. 1 only appears in the first column, and so it is now the lowest number that doesn’t appear, and so it goes underneath the first 6. Moving to the third column, we have already used 1 and 3 as child nodes. The number 2 is still to appear as a parent, and so can’t be a leaf yet, and so 4 is the first number that we haven’t used yet. Similar reasoning gives 5 and 7 for the 4th and 5th column.

Finally, the last remaining edge connects the two nodes we have not used as leaves yet; in this case 2 and 6.

routes.title: Matrix-tree theorem/determinant
routes.proofSketch: For the complete graph K_n, every Laplacian cofactor counts spanning trees by the matrix-tree theorem. Its Laplacian cofactor has diagonal n−1 and off-diagonal −1; its eigenvalues are n (multiplicity n−2) and 1, so the determinant is n^(n−2).

routes.title: weighted generating functions
routes.proofSketch: Let T(x) count rooted labeled trees as an exponential generating function. Decomposing a rooted tree into its root and an unordered set of rooted branches gives T=x exp(T). Lagrange inversion yields [x^n]T=n^(n−1)/n!, so there are n^(n−1) rooted labeled trees; forgetting the choice of root divides by n and gives n^(n−2).

routes.title: Alternating paths in maximum matchings
routes.proofSketch: Take a maximum matching M. If some left vertex is unmatched, follow alternating paths (unmatched edges left-to-right, matched edges right-to-left). No reached right vertex can be unmatched, or there is an augmenting path. The reached left set has fewer neighbors than vertices, contradicting Hall.

routes.title: Alternating-path construction
routes.proofSketch: In a maximum matching, start from unmatched left vertices and trace alternating paths. Let Z_L,Z_R be reached vertices. Then C=(L\Z_L)∪Z_R meets every edge; each matched edge has exactly one endpoint in C, so |C|=|M|, proving vertex-cover minimum equals matching maximum.

routes.title: linear-programming duality/integrality
routes.proofSketch: Formulate bipartite matching as the LP maximizing Σ_e x_e subject to incident-edge sums at each vertex ≤1 and x≥0; the dual minimizes Σ_v y_v subject to y_u+y_v≥1 on each edge and y≥0. The bipartite incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so optimal basic solutions of both programs are integral. The integral primal solution is a matching and the integral dual solution is a vertex cover. Strong LP duality makes their cardinalities equal, proving König’s theorem.

routes.verbatimProof:
[Slide: Vertex covers]
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph.
A set $C\subseteq V$ is called a vertex cover if every edge $e\in E$ has at least one endpoint in $C$.
Claim: If $M$ is a matching and $C$ is a vertex cover then $|M|\le|C|$.
Proof: Every edge in $M$ has at least one endpoint in $C$. Since $M$ is a matching, its edges have distinct endpoints. So $C$ must contain at least $|M|$ vertices. $\square$

[Slide: Vertex covers & matchings]
Theorem (Konig's Theorem): If $G$ is bipartite then there exists a matching $M$ and a vertex cover $C$ s.t. $|M|=|C|$.

[Slide: LPs for Bipartite Matching]
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a bipartite graph.
Recall our IP and LP formulations for maximum-size matching.
(IP) max $\sum_{e\in E}x_e$ s.t. $\sum_{e\text{ incident to }v}x_e\le 1\ \ \forall v\in V$; $x_e\in\{0,1\}\ \ \forall e\in E$.
(LP) max $\sum_{e\in E}x_e$ s.t. $\sum_{e\text{ incident to }v}x_e\le 1\ \ \forall v\in V$; $x_e\ge 0\ \ \forall e\in E$.
Theorem: Every BFS of (LP) is actually an (IP) solution.
What is the dual of (LP)?
(LP-Dual) min $\sum_{v\in V}y_v$ s.t. $y_u+y_v\ge 1\ \ \forall\{u,v\}\in E$; $y_v\ge 0\ \ \forall v\in V$.

[Slide: Dual of Bipartite Matching LP]
Note that any optimal solution must satisfy $y_v\le 1\ \ \forall v\in V$.
Suppose we impose integrality constraints:
(IP-Dual) min $\sum_{v\in V}y_v$ s.t. $y_u+y_v\ge 1\ \ \forall\{u,v\}\in E$; $y_v\in\{0,1\}\ \ \forall v\in V$.
Claim: If $y$ is feasible for IP-dual then $C=\{v:y_v=1\}$ is a vertex cover. Furthermore, the objective value is $|C|$.
So IP-Dual is precisely the minimum vertex cover problem.
Theorem: Every optimal BFS of (LP-Dual) is an (IP-Dual) solution.

[Slide, untitled]
Let $G=(U\cup V,E)$ be a bipartite graph. Define $A$ by
$A_{v,e}=1$ if vertex $v$ is an endpoint of edge $e$; $0$ otherwise.
Lemma: $A$ is TUM.
Claim: If $A$ is TUM then $A^T$ is TUM.
Proof: Exercise on Assignment 5.
Corollary: Every BFS of $P=\{x:A^Ty\ge\mathbf{1},y\ge 0\}$ is integral.
But LP-Dual is [min $\sum_{v\in V}y_v$ s.t. $y_u+y_v\ge 1\ \forall\{u,v\}\in E$, $y_v\ge 0\ \forall v\in V$] = [min $\sum_{v\in V}y_v$ s.t. $A^Ty\ge\mathbf{1}$, $y\ge 0$]
So our Corollary implies every BFS of LP-dual is integral
Every optimal solution must have $y_v\le 1\ \ \forall v\in V$
$\Rightarrow$ every optimal BFS has $y_v\in\{0,1\}\ \ \forall v\in V$, and hence it is a feasible solution for IP-Dual. $\blacksquare$

[Slide: Proof of Konig's Theorem]
Theorem (Konig's Theorem): If $G$ is bipartite then there exists a matching $M$ and a vertex cover $C$ s.t. $|M|=|C|$.
Proof:
Let $x$ be an optimal BFS for (LP).
Let $y$ be an optimal BFS for (LP-Dual).
Let $M=\{e:x_e=1\}$.
$M$ is a matching with $|M|=$ objective value of $x$. (By earlier theorem)
Let $C=\{v:y_v=1\}$.
$C$ is a vertex cover with $|C|=$ objective value of $y$. (By earlier theorem)
By Strong LP Duality:
$|M|=$ LP optimal value $=$ LP-Dual optimal value $=|C|$. $\blacksquare$

routes.title: Minimal-counterexample vertex of degree ≤5 plus recoloring
routes.proofSketch: Choose a vertex v of degree at most five (Euler’s formula guarantees one), color G−v with five colors. If its five neighbors use all colors, relabel cyclically and consider the 1/3 Kempe chain from the first to third neighbor. If they connect, the 2/4 chain cannot connect without crossing; swap one chain and free a color. If they do not connect, swap the 1/3 component. Color v.

routes.title: Supporting-line characterization of convexity

routes.verbatimProof:
Jensen's inequality statement

Let $X$ be random variable with finite mean $E[X]=\mu$.
Let $g$ be a convex function. This means that if you draw a straight line connecting two points on the graph of $g$, then the graph of $g$ lies below that line. If $g$ is twice differentiable, then convexity is equivalent to the statement that $g''(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$. For a concrete example, take $g(x)=x^2$.
Jensen's inequality: $E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X])$.
Proof: Let $L(x)=ax+b$ be tangent to graph of $g$ at point $(E[X],g(E[X]))$. Then $L$ lies below $g$. Observe
$$E[g(X)]\ge E[L(X)]=L(E[X])=g(E[X])$$
Note: if $g$ is concave (which means $-g$ is convex), then $E[g(X)]\le g(E[X])$.

routes.proofSketch: Prove finite Jensen by induction: combine the first n−1 points into their weighted mean, then apply the two-point convexity inequality. routes.title: Nested closed balls with radii→0
routes.proofSketch: Assume a complete metric space M is the union of closed sets C_n, each with empty interior. Starting with a point in C₁, choose a point outside C₁ and a small closed ball around it disjoint from C₁. Inductively choose nested centers and radii shrinking by a fixed factor, with the kth ball disjoint from C_k. The centers are Cauchy; completeness gives a limit lying in every nested ball, hence outside every C_k, contradicting the assumed cover.

routes.verbatimProof:
THEOREM 2 (Baire). If $M$ is a non-empty complete metric space and $C_n\subset M$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, are closed subsets such that
$$M=\bigcup_nC_n\qquad(1.82)$$
then at least one of the $C_n$'s has an interior point.

PROOF. We can assume that the first set $C_1\neq\emptyset$ since they cannot all be empty and dropping any empty sets does no harm. Let's assume the contrary of the desired conclusion, namely that each of the $C_n$'s has empty interior, hoping to arrive at a contradiction to (1.82) using the other properties. This means that an open ball $B(p,\epsilon)$ around a point of $M$ (so it isn't empty) cannot be contained in any one of the $C_n$.

So, choose $p\in C_1$. Now, there must be a point $p_1\in B(p,1/3)$ which is not in $C_1$. Since $C_1$ is closed there exists $\epsilon_1>0$, and we can take $\epsilon_1<1/3$, such that $B(p_1,\epsilon_1)\cap C_1=\emptyset$. Continue in this way, choose $p_2\in B(p_1,\epsilon_1/3)$ which is not in $C_2$ and $\epsilon_2>0$, $\epsilon_2<\epsilon_1/3$ such that $B(p_2,\epsilon_2)\cap C_2=\emptyset$. Here we use both the fact that $C_2$ has empty interior and the fact that it is closed. So, inductively there is a sequence $p_i$, $i=1,\ldots,k$ and positive numbers $0<\epsilon_k<\epsilon_{k-1}/3<\epsilon_{k-2}/3^2<\cdots<\epsilon_1/3^{k-1}<3^{-k}$ such that $p_j\in B(p_{j-1},\epsilon_{j-1}/3)$ and $B(p_j,\epsilon_j)\cap C_j=\emptyset$. Then we can add another $p_{k+1}$ by using the properties of $C_k$ – it has non-empty interior so there is some point in $B(p_k,\epsilon_k/3)$ which is not in $C_{k+1}$ and then $B(p_{k+1},\epsilon_{k+1})\cap C_{k+1}=\emptyset$ where $\epsilon_{k+1}>0$ but $\epsilon_{k+1}<\epsilon_k/3$. Thus, we have a sequence $\{p_k\}$ in $M$. Since $d(p_{k+1},p_k)<\epsilon_k/3$ this is a Cauchy sequence, in fact
$$d(p_k,p_{k+l})<\epsilon_k/3+\cdots+\epsilon_{k+l-1}/3<3^{-k}.\qquad(1.83)$$
Since $M$ is complete the sequence converges to a limit, $q\in M$. Notice however that $p_l\in B(p_k,2\epsilon_k/3)$ for all $k>l$ so $d(p_k,q)\le 2\epsilon_k/3$ which implies that $q\notin C_k$ for any $k$. This is the desired contradiction to (1.82).

Thus, at least one of the $C_n$ must have non-empty interior. $\square$

routes.title: complete metric space plus Cauchy construction
routes.proofSketch: Assume a complete metric space M is covered by closed sets C_n with empty interiors. Choose nested closed balls B_n with radii shrinking geometrically, where B_n avoids C_n and lies inside the preceding ball. Their centers form a Cauchy sequence; its limit lies in every B_n, so it avoids every C_n, contradicting the cover.

routes.proofSketch: In a locally compact Hausdorff space, suppose a nonempty open set is covered by countably many closed sets with empty interior. Choose a nonempty relatively compact open subset avoiding the first closed set; within it choose one avoiding the second, and so on, with nested compact closures. routes.title: Orthogonal projection onto kernel
routes.proofSketch: For a nonzero bounded functional f on a Hilbert space, ker(f) is a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement is one-dimensional. Choose nonzero x₀ in ker(f)⊥ and set z_f=f(x₀)x₀/||x₀||² (adjusting conjugation for the inner-product convention). On ker(f), both f and ⟨z_f,·⟩ vanish; on ker(f)⊥, which is spanned by x₀, they agree by construction. Hence f(x)=⟨z_f,x⟩ for all x.

routes.verbatimProof:
Theorem 5.17 (Riesz's representation for Hilbert spaces). Let $f\in H^*$ be a linear functional on a Hilbert space $H$. There exists a unique $z_f\in H$ such that
$$f(x)=\langle z_f,x\rangle\qquad(17)$$
for all $x\in H$ and $\|f\|=\|z_f\|$. In particular, the map
$$\mathcal{A}:H^*\to H,\ f\mapsto z_f$$
is an anti-linear isometric bijection with inverse
$$\mathcal{A}^{-1}:H\to H^*,\ x\mapsto\langle x,\cdot\rangle.$$

Remark 5.18. In quantum mechanics, one uses the bra-ket notation: $\langle\psi|$ is an element of $H^*$ and $|\psi\rangle$ is an element of $H$. Then the map $\mathcal{A}^{-1}:H\to H^*$ is the map $|\psi\rangle\mapsto\langle\psi|$.

Proof. Without loss of generality $f\neq 0$ so let $0\neq x_0\in\ker(f)^\perp$, where used that $\ker(f)$ is closed. Now define
$$z_f=\overline{f(x_0)}\frac{x_0}{\|x_0\|^2}$$
and note that $f(x)=\langle z_f,x\rangle=0$ for all $x\in\ker(f)$. Moreover, $\ker(f)^\perp$ is 1-dimensional³ so for any $y\in\ker(f)^\perp$, we have $y=\alpha x_0$ so
$$\langle z_f,y\rangle=\alpha\langle z_f,x_0\rangle=\alpha f(x_0)\frac{1}{\|x_0\|^2}\langle x_0,x_0\rangle=f(y).$$
For the uniqueness of $z_f$, let $z_f$ and $z_f'$ satisfy (17), then $\langle z_f-z_f',x\rangle=0$ for all $x\in X$ so in particular for $x=z_f-z_f'$ which shows $z_f=z_f'$. For the norm, we note that $\|f\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}|f(x)|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}|\langle z_f,x\rangle|\le\|z_f\|$. Moreover, $\|f\|\ge\frac{1}{\|z_f\|}|f(z_f)|=\|z_f\|$.

To see the anti-linearity of $\mathcal{A}$ we note that
$$\langle z_{\alpha f+\beta g},x\rangle=(\alpha f+\beta g)(x)=\alpha f(x)+\beta g(x)=\alpha\langle z_f,x\rangle+\beta\langle z_g,x\rangle=\langle\bar\alpha z_f+\bar\beta z_g,x\rangle.$$
Since $\mathcal{A}$ is isometric it is injective. It is also surjective as the $z\in H$, the map $f_z:x\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle$ is a bounded linear functional. $\square$

³Here we use that $H/\ker(f)\cong\ker(f)^\perp$ and $H/\ker(f)\cong\mathrm{range}(f)$ so $\ker(f)^\perp\cong\mathrm{range}(f)$.

routes.title: Baire category and nested balls
routes.proofSketch: It suffices to show T(B_X(0,1)) contains a neighborhood of 0. Surjectivity gives Y=⋃_n T(B_X(0,n)); Baire implies the closure of one such image has interior. By linearity and subtraction this yields a ball around 0 contained in the closure of T(B_X(0,1)). Repeatedly approximate a target y by T(x₁), then its residual by T(x₂), with ||x_k|| geometrically decreasing. The sum converges in X and maps to y, so a neighborhood of 0 lies in T(B_X(0,1)); scaling and translation show T is open.

routes.verbatimProof:
[§1.5, p. 14 — result relied on]

Theorem 1.51 (Baire category theorem). Let $X$ be a complete metric space and let $(A_n)_n$ be a family of open and dense sets. Then, $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n$ is dense.

Proof. Let $x_0\in X$ and $B_\epsilon(x_0)$ be an open ball around $x_0$. Since $A_1$ is open and dense and $B_\epsilon(x_0)$ is open, there exists $x_1\in X$ and $\epsilon_1>0$ such that $\overline{B}_{\epsilon_1}(x_1)\subset A_1\cap B_\epsilon(x_0)$. For $n\ge 2$ we use that $A_n$ is open and dense, to find $x_n\in X$ and $0<\epsilon_n<\frac1n$ such that
$$\overline{B}_{\epsilon_n}(x_n)\subset B_{\epsilon_{n-1}}(x_{n-1})\cap A_n\cap B_\epsilon(x_0).$$
Since the balls $B_{\epsilon_n}(x_n)$ are nested we have that $d(x_n,x_m)\le\frac{1}{\min(n,m)}\to 0$ as $n,m\to\infty$. Thus, $(x_n)_n$ is a Cauchy sequence and by completeness of $X$, there exists an $x\in X$ such that $x_n\to x$ as $n\to\infty$. By construction $x_n\in B_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)\subset A_m$ for all $n\ge m$ and since $\overline{B}_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)$ is closed we have that
$$x\in\overline{B}_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)\subset A_m\cap B_\epsilon(x_0)$$
for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ which concludes the proof. $\square$

Corollary 1.52. A complete metric space is not the countable union of nowhere dense sets.

Proof. Define $A=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n$, where $A_n$ are nowhere dense sets. In particular, $\overline{A_n}$ is closed and nowhere dense for every $n$. Hence, $\overline{A_n}^c$ is open and dense for every $n$ so by Baire's theorem, $\emptyset\neq\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{A_n}^c=(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{A_n})^c\subset A^c$ so $A\neq X$. $\square$

[§2.3, p. 22]

Theorem 2.32 (Open mapping theorem). Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces and $T:X\to Y$ be a surjective bounded linear operator. Then $T$ is open.

Proof. Since $T$ is linear, it suffices to show that $T(B_1^X(0))$ contains an open ball around the origin in $Y$.

Step 1. We will first show that $\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$ contains an interior point. Since $T$ is surjective, $Y=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}T(B_n^X(0))$ so by the Baire category theorem, there exists a $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\overline{T(B_N^X(0))}$ contains an interior point and by linearity so does $\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$. In particular, there exists an $\epsilon>0$ and $y_0\in\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$ such that $B_\epsilon^Y(y_0)\subset\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$.

Step 2. We will now show that $B_\epsilon^Y(0)\subset\overline{T(B_1^X(0))}$ which follows once we show that
$$\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}-y_0\subset\overline{T(B_1^X(0))}.$$
Let $y\in\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}-y_0$, i.e. $y+y_0\in\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$. For $y+y_0$ and $y_0$ we can write
$$y_0=\lim_{n\to\infty}Tx_n,\qquad y+y_0=\lim Tz_n$$
for $\|x_n\|<\frac12$ and $\|z_n\|<\frac12$. Thus, $y=\lim_{n\to\infty}T(z_n-x_n)$, where $\|z_n-x_n\|<1$ for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$. This shows that $y\in\overline{T(B_1^X(0))}$ and concludes the step.

Step 3. Using the linearity, we obtain
$$V_n\doteq B^Y_{\epsilon 2^{-n}}(0)\subset\overline{T(B^X_{2^{-n}}(0))}.\qquad(1)$$

Step 4. We will finally show that $V_1=B^Y_{\epsilon/2}(0)\subset T(B_1^X(0))$. Let $y\in V_1\subset\overline{T(B_{1/2}^X(0))}$ and choose $Tx_1\in T(B_{1/2}^X(0))$ such that $\|y-Tx_1\|\le\epsilon/4$. From (1) for $n=2$ we obtain that $y-Tx_1\in V_2\subset\overline{T(B^X_{2^{-2}}(0))}$. As before we find $x_2\in B^X_{2^{-2}}(0)$ such that $\|y-Tx_1-Tx_2\|\le\epsilon/8$. Continuing inductively, we obtain a sequence $(x_n)_n$ with $\|x_n\|<2^{-n}$ and for which
$$\Big\|y-\sum_{n=1}^NTx_n\Big\|\le\epsilon 2^{-N-1}.\qquad(2)$$
We note that $w_N=\sum_{n=1}^Nx_n$ is a Cauchy sequence because
$$\|w_N-w_M\|\le\sum_{n=\min(N,M)}^\infty\|x_n\|\le\sum_{n=\min(N,M)}^\infty 2^{-n}\to 0$$
as $\min(N,M)\to\infty$. Hence, by the completeness of $X$ we have $w_N\to w$ as $N\to\infty$. From (2) we obtain that $y=Tw$ and we are done once we show that $\|w\|<1$. Indeed,
$$\|w\|\le\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|x_n\|<\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n}=1.$$
This concludes the proof. $\square$

entries.name: Cauchy's integral theorem
entries.description: Goursat triangle subdivision; Green's theorem and Cauchy–Riemann equations; homotopy/primitive arguments on simply connected domains.

routes.title: Goursat triangle subdivision
routes.proofSketch: Prove the theorem first for a triangle C. Joining midpoints of the sides splits C into four positively oriented triangles whose interior edges cancel, so the integral over C is the sum of the four integrals, and one of them, C_1, has modulus at least a quarter of the total. Iterating gives nested triangles C_n with $|\int_C f| \le 4^n |\int_{C_n} f|$, shrinking to a point $z_0$ where f is differentiable. Writing $f(z)=f(z_0)+f'(z_0)(z-z_0)+\eta(z)(z-z_0)$ with $\eta\to 0$, the linear part integrates to zero over the closed triangle, so $\int_{C_n} f=\int_{C_n}\eta(z)(z-z_0)\,dz$. Since $L_n=2^{-n}L$ and $|z-z_0|<L_n/2$, the estimate gives $|\int_C f|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$, hence zero. Polygons follow by triangulating, and general simple closed contours by polygonal approximation (details omitted in the source).

routes.title: Green's theorem and Cauchy–Riemann equations
routes.proofSketch: Assume additionally that $f'$ is continuous. Writing $f=u+iv$, the contour integral splits as $\int_C u\,dx - v\,dy + i\int_C v\,dx+u\,dy$. Green's theorem turns the real part into $\iint_R(-v_x-u_y)\,dx\,dy$ and the imaginary part into $\iint_R(u_x-v_y)\,dx\,dy$, where R is the interior of C. The Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ make both integrands zero, so $\int_C f\,dz=0$.

routes.title: homotopy/primitive arguments on simply connected domains
routes.proofSketch: For f analytic on a simply connected domain D, fix $z_0$ and set $F(z)=\int_{z_0}^z f(\xi)\,d\xi$. Path independence: two contours $C_1,C_2$ from $z_0$ to $z$ give a closed contour $C_1-C_2$ whose integral vanishes by the Cauchy-Goursat theorem, so F is well defined. For the derivative, $F(z+\Delta z)-F(z)=\int_\Gamma f$ over the segment from z to $z+\Delta z$, and since $\int_\Gamma f(z)\,d\xi=f(z)\Delta z$, continuity of f gives $|(F(z+\Delta z)-F(z))/\Delta z - f(z)|<\varepsilon$. Hence $F'=f$.

routes.title: Maximal ideals and Zariski's lemma

entries.name: de Rham theorem
entries.description: Differential forms and local Poincaré lemma with partitions of unity; Mayer–Vietoris induction; sheaf/cohomological resolution.

routes.title: Differential forms and local Poincaré lemma with partitions of unity
routes.proofSketch: Consider the complex of sheaves $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\xrightarrow{d}\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$. The Poincaré lemma says closed forms are locally exact, so this sequence of sheaves is exact. Each $\Omega^k_M$ is fine, because local sections can be glued by a partition of unity (multiply by the partition functions and sum), and a fine sheaf has vanishing higher Čech cohomology by an explicit homotopy built from the partition of unity. Hence the sequence is a fine resolution of the constant sheaf, and the cohomology of its global sections, namely de Rham cohomology, equals the Čech (sheaf) cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$.

routes.title: Mayer–Vietoris induction
routes.proofSketch: Call a manifold de Rham if the integration map $H^p_{dR}(M)\to H^p(M;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism, and a cover a de Rham cover if its members and all their finite intersections are de Rham. Disjoint unions of de Rham manifolds are de Rham, and convex open sets in $\mathbb R^n$ are de Rham by the Poincaré lemma and homotopy invariance. For a finite de Rham cover, induct on the number of sets: compare the Mayer-Vietoris sequences of de Rham and singular cohomology for $U=U_1\cup\dots\cup U_k$ and $V=U_{k+1}$, and conclude with the five lemma. For a de Rham basis, an exhaustion function splits $M$ into two disjoint unions of finitely covered pieces, whose union and intersection are de Rham. Open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, hence every manifold, have such a basis of balls.

routes.title: sheaf/cohomological resolution
routes.proofSketch: Define a fine resolution of a sheaf $\mathcal F$ as an exact sequence $0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F^0\to\mathcal F^1\to\cdots$ with every $\mathcal F^k$ fine. Theorem 4.5 compares the Čech cohomology of a good cover with the cohomology of the complex of global sections of the resolution by chasing a double complex: rows below the first are exact because the $\mathcal F^k$ are fine, columns are exact by the hypothesis on the cover. Passing to the limit over covers (Leray) gives that the cohomology of $\mathcal F$ equals that of the global sections complex of any fine resolution. Applied to $0\to\mathbb{R}_M\to\Omega^0_M\to\Omega^1_M\to\cdots$, a fine resolution by the Poincaré lemma and partitions of unity, this identifies sheaf cohomology of $\mathbb{R}_M$ with de Rham cohomology.

routes.title: Radial homotopy operator
routes.proofSketch: Use Cartan's formula $L_\xi=d\,i(\xi)+i(\xi)d$. For a family of maps $f_t$ with velocity field $\xi_t$, differentiate $f_t^*\omega$ to get $\frac{d}{dt}f_t^*\omega=f_t^*L_{\xi_t}\omega$. Integrate over $t\in[0,1]$ and apply Cartan's formula to obtain $f_1^*\omega-f_0^*\omega=dJ\omega+Jd\omega$ with $J\omega=\int_0^1 f_t^*i(\xi_t)\omega\,dt$. On a ball centred at $x_0$ take the radial contraction $f_t(x)=t(x-x_0)+x_0$, so $f_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $f_0^*\omega=0$ for forms of positive degree; hence $\omega=dJ\omega$ when $d\omega=0$.

routes.title: integrate along straight-line contraction
routes.proofSketch: For a star-shaped open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ consider forms on $U\times[0,1]$ and define fiber integration $\pi_*$ by integrating the coefficient of $dt$ over $[0,1]$. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\pi_*(d\alpha)=\alpha_1-\alpha_0-d(\pi_*\alpha)$. Pull back along the straight-line contraction $h(x,t)=tx$ and set $J=\pi_*\circ h^*$ to obtain the homotopy formula $h_1^*\omega-h_0^*\omega=Jd\omega+dJ\omega$. For closed $\omega$ of positive degree, $h_1^*\omega=\omega$ and $h_0^*\omega=0$, so $\omega=dJ\omega$.

entries.description: Homotopy invariance of winding number; argument principle; perturbation estimate plus zero counting.

routes.title: Homotopy invariance of winding number
routes.proofSketch: The symmetric strict inequality $|f-g|<|f|+|g|$ on $\partial K$ implies $f,g$ have no zeros there and $g$ is never a negative real multiple of $f$. By the argument principle $N_f(K)$ equals the winding number of $f\circ C$ about $0$, and likewise for $g$. The segment homotopy $H_t=(1-t)f\circ C+t\,g\circ C$ avoids the origin, and the winding number $I(t)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{H_t}dz/z$ is continuous and integer-valued, hence constant. So $N_f(K)=N_g(K)$. The usual form $|g|<|f|$ follows by applying this to $f+g$ and $f$.
