routes.title: argument principle
routes.proofSketch: Apply the argument principle: since $f$ has no zeros on the boundary curve $C$, $N_f(K)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_C f'/f\,dz$, which equals the winding number of $f\circ C$ about $0$; the same holds for $g$. Because the hypothesis keeps the segment between $f(C(x))$ and $g(C(x))$ away from $0$, the family $H_t$ of curves has constant (integer-valued, continuous) winding number in $t$. Hence the winding numbers of $f\circ C$ and $g\circ C$, and so the zero counts, coincide.

routes.title: perturbation estimate plus zero counting
routes.proofSketch: The theorem is used by writing a function as a dominating part plus a perturbation: if $|g|<|f|$ on $\partial K$ then $f$ and $f+g$ have the same number of zeros in $K$ (for instance $z^5+3z^3+7$ has five zeros in $|z|<2$ because $|3z^3+7|\le31<32=|z^5|$ there). The informal explanation: with $h=f+g$ the condition says $f(z)$ is closer to $h(z)$ than to the origin all along $C$, so the two image curves wind around the origin the same number of times and the argument principle gives equal zero counts.

entries.name: Uniform boundedness principle (Banach–Steinhaus)
entries.description: Baire-category proof; gliding-hump construction on Banach spaces; weak compactness/duality route in suitable formulations.

routes.title: Baire-category proof
routes.proofSketch: For p∈N set S_p={x: ||x||≤1 and ||T_nx||≤p for every n}. These are closed and cover the closed unit ball by pointwise boundedness. Baire gives some S_p containing a relative ball. Taking differences of points in that ball bounds ||T_nw|| uniformly for w in a neighborhood of 0; rescaling yields ||T_n||≤2p/δ for every n, hence sup_n||T_n||<∞.

Symbols were not corrected or modernized. Two separate source passages (p. 14 and p. 21) are joined here in dependency order and labelled in brackets; the bracketed labels are the assistant's. The source itself says 'Baire's theorem (Corollary 1.52)'. Source: Introduction to functional analysis, lecture notes for 18.102, Spring 2025, Christoph Kehle (MIT), May 2025 — §2.3 'Cornerstones of functional analysis', Theorem 2.31 (principle of uniform boundedness) with proof, p. 21; relies on Theorem 1.51 / Corollary 1.52 (Baire), §1.5, p. 14, included first. Attribution: Christoph Kehle, MIT 18.102 lecture notes, Spring 2025 (no license stated in the PDF or on the hosting page). Route match: verified.
routes.verbatimProof:
[§1.5, p. 14 — result relied on]

Theorem 1.51 (Baire category theorem). Let $X$ be a complete metric space and let $(A_n)_n$ be a family of open and dense sets. Then, $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n$ is dense.

Proof. Let $x_0\in X$ and $B_\epsilon(x_0)$ be an open ball around $x_0$. Since $A_1$ is open and dense and $B_\epsilon(x_0)$ is open, there exists $x_1\in X$ and $\epsilon_1>0$ such that $\overline{B}_{\epsilon_1}(x_1)\subset A_1\cap B_\epsilon(x_0)$. For $n\ge 2$ we use that $A_n$ is open and dense, to find $x_n\in X$ and $0<\epsilon_n<\frac1n$ such that
$$\overline{B}_{\epsilon_n}(x_n)\subset B_{\epsilon_{n-1}}(x_{n-1})\cap A_n\cap B_\epsilon(x_0).$$
Since the balls $B_{\epsilon_n}(x_n)$ are nested we have that $d(x_n,x_m)\le\frac{1}{\min(n,m)}\to 0$ as $n,m\to\infty$. Thus, $(x_n)_n$ is a Cauchy sequence and by completeness of $X$, there exists an $x\in X$ such that $x_n\to x$ as $n\to\infty$. By construction $x_n\in B_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)\subset A_m$ for all $n\ge m$ and since $\overline{B}_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)$ is closed we have that
$$x\in\overline{B}_{\epsilon_m}(x_m)\subset A_m\cap B_\epsilon(x_0)$$
for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ which concludes the proof. $\square$

Corollary 1.52. A complete metric space is not the countable union of nowhere dense sets.

Proof. Define $A=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n$, where $A_n$ are nowhere dense sets. In particular, $\overline{A_n}$ is closed and nowhere dense for every $n$. Hence, $\overline{A_n}^c$ is open and dense for every $n$ so by Baire's theorem, $\emptyset\neq\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{A_n}^c=(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\overline{A_n})^c\subset A^c$ so $A\neq X$. $\square$

[§2.3, p. 21]

Theorem 2.31 (Principle of uniform boundedness, Banach–Steinhaus). Let $X$ be a Banach space and $Y$ be a normed space. Let $(T_n)_n\subset BL(X,Y)$ be a sequence of linear operators and assume that $\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_n(x)\|<\infty$ for all $x\in X$. Then, $\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_n\|<\infty$.

Proof. Define the set $A_m=\{x\in X:\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_n(x)\|\le m\}$ and note that each $A_m=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\{x\in X:\|T_n(x)\|\le m\}$ is closed and $\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}A_m=X$. By Baire's theorem (Corollary 1.52) there exists an $A_M$ with non-empty interior, i.e. there exists a ball $B_{2\epsilon}(x_0)\subset A_M$ for some $\epsilon>0$ and $x_0\in A_M$. Let $x\in X$ with $\|x\|\le 1$. Then,
$$\|T_n(x)\|=\epsilon^{-1}\|T_n(\epsilon x)\|\le\epsilon^{-1}\|T_n(\epsilon x-x_0)\|+\epsilon^{-1}\|T_n(x_0)\|\le 2\epsilon^{-1}M.$$
Thus, $\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\|T_n\|<\infty$. $\square$

routes.title: gliding-hump construction on Banach spaces
routes.proofSketch: Assume norms ||T_n|| unbounded; inductively choose unit vectors x_k with T_{n_k}x_k large while controlling earlier operators, and coefficients decreasing fast. A convergent series x=∑a_kx_k is constructed so ||T_{n_k}x||→∞, contradicting pointwise boundedness. The gliding-hump details require Banach completeness and careful subsequence selection.

entries.name: Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds
entries.description: Cellular dual decomposition; singular homology and cap product; differential forms/de Rham integration; Morse theory; Hodge star.

routes.title: Cellular dual decomposition
routes.proofSketch: Hatcher motivates Poincaré duality with dual cell structures C and C* on a closed manifold: each i-cell of C is dual to a unique (n-i)-cell of C* meeting it transversally in one point. Pairing cells with dual cells identifies the cellular chain groups C_i with C*_{n-i}. With Z_2 coefficients this identification is canonical, and the cellular boundary of C becomes the coboundary of C*, since boundary sends a cell to the sum of its faces while coboundary sends it to the sum of cells it is a face of. Hence H_i(C;Z_2) is isomorphic to H^{n-i}(C*;Z_2), and since C and C* are cell structures on the same space, H_i(M;Z_2) is isomorphic to H^{n-i}(M;Z_2). For Z coefficients one must choose compatible orientations of all cells when M is orientable. Hatcher treats this only as a sketch (worked for surfaces, then stated for dimension n) and abandons it, because constructing dual cell structures for general manifolds needs more manifold theory.

routes.title: singular homology and cap product
routes.proofSketch: Hatcher proves the stronger statement that the duality map D_M: H^k_c(M;R) -> H_{n-k}(M;R), x -> mu_K cap x (limit over compact K), is an isomorphism for every R-oriented n-manifold; for closed M it is cap product with the fundamental class. The key technical lemma gives a commutative-up-to-sign map between the Mayer-Vietoris sequences for compactly supported cohomology and for homology, built from excision and the classes mu_K, so by the five-lemma D_{U cup V} is an isomorphism if D_U, D_V, D_{U cap V} are. A direct-limit argument handles increasing unions of open sets. The base case M = R^n is read off from cap product on (Delta^n, boundary of Delta^n). One then passes to open subsets of R^n by induction over covers by convex sets, to manifolds that are countable unions of Euclidean opens, and in general by Zorn's lemma using a maximal open set on which duality holds.

routes.title: differential forms/de Rham integration
routes.proofSketch: Work with oriented M and the integration pairing H^q(M) x H^{n-q}_c(M) -> R, [w],[t] -> integral of w ^ t. The Mayer-Vietoris sequence of de Rham cohomology and the one for compactly supported cohomology (in reverse order) are linked by this integration pairing; the Main Lemma checks, square by square, that the pairings commute up to sign (the connecting-map square is the delicate one, comparing integrals of df_V ^ w ^ t). For M = R^n the Poincare lemmas leave only the pairing of constants with compactly supported top forms, which is obviously nondegenerate. The five lemma then shows that nondegeneracy for U, V and U cap V gives it for U cup V, and induction over a finite good cover (all intersections diffeomorphic to R^n) yields the result for manifolds with a finite good cover, in particular compact ones; finite dimensionality turns it into an isomorphism.

routes.title: Morse theory
routes.proofSketch: Define Morse cohomology with the pair (-f,g) instead of (f,g): the chain groups are again generated by the critical points of f, but since negating f turns the index p of a critical point into n-p and reverses flow lines, the Morse differential becomes an ascending coboundary delta of degree +1 counting flow lines. Because -f has the same critical points as f, C_i is isomorphic to C^{n-i}, and this identification intertwines the boundary and coboundary maps, giving MH^{n-*}(X) = MH_*(X) for the Morse (co)homology. Torres interprets this as 'looking at X upside down does not change its homology'. The argument is compressed and does not discuss orientations or the handle/intersection-pairing picture.

routes.title: Hodge star
routes.proofSketch: On a compact oriented Riemannian n-manifold, the Hodge star is defined by alpha ^ *beta = (alpha, beta) dvol and satisfies ** = +-1, giving the L^2 inner product <alpha,beta> = integral of alpha ^ *beta. By the Hodge theorem every de Rham class has a unique norm-minimising (harmonic) representative. The star maps harmonic i-forms isomorphically onto harmonic (n-i)-forms, so H^i and H^{n-i} have the same dimension. For the integration pairing, the induced map H^i -> (H^{n-i})* has zero kernel because the pairing of a nonzero harmonic alpha with *alpha is the squared norm, hence nonzero; equal dimensions then give a perfect pairing.

routes.title: Hook-walk probabilistic proof
routes.proofSketch: Run the Greene–Nijenhuis–Wilf hook walk from an outside corner: at each cell choose uniformly among cells strictly to its left or above in its hook, then move to the chosen cell. Compute the probability of terminating at each removable corner; the resulting recurrence matches the tableau count f^λ=|λ|!/∏h(c), with the hook factors emerging from transition probabilities.

routes.title: Syntactic proof via completeness/Henkin construction
routes.proofSketch: Assume every finite subset of the first-order theory T has a model. Expand the language in countably many stages by fresh constants witnessing each existential formula, while preserving finite satisfiability. The resulting Henkin theory has a model built from closed terms modulo provable equality: interpret functions on term classes and relations by membership in the theory. Its reduct satisfies T.

routes.verbatimProof:
Lecture 16

16.1 Compactness

We shall now prove the compactness theorem. The proof we give is by the so-called Henkin construction. Later in the course we will give a second proof making use of ultrafilters.

Definition. A theory $T$ is said to be finitely satisfiable if whenever $T_0\subseteq T$ is a finite subset of $T$ there exists a model $\mathfrak{A}$ of $T_0$.

Theorem 16.1 (The Compactness Theorem). Let $\tau$ be a signature and $T$ a $\tau$-theory. If $T$ is finitely satisfiable then $T$ is satisfiable, i.e. then there exists a model $\mathfrak{A}\models T$.

Remark. Compactness, as proved here, is a property of first-order logic, i.e. the sentences of $T$ are assumed to come from the first-order language $\mathcal{L}_{\omega\omega}(\tau)$.

We will use the technique of using the language itself to build a structure satisfying $T$.

We first prove some lemma's allowing us to reduce the problem of finding models of $T$ to that of finding models of a certain nice extension of $T$.

Definition. A $\tau$-theory $T$ has Henkin constants if for each formula $\varphi(x)\in\mathcal{L}(\tau)$ with one free variable $x$, there is a constant symbol $c\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$ such that
$$T\vdash\exists x\varphi(x)\longleftrightarrow\varphi(c).$$

Henkin constants act ass witnesses to all existential sentences, iff they are implied by $T$.

Proposition. For any signature $\tau$ there is a signature $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ expressible as $\bigcup_{i=0}^\infty\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|i)}$ and a theory $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ in $\mathcal{L}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}})$ such that
1.) $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ is an expansion by constants of $\tau$.
2.) $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ has Henkin constants.
3.) For each $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathrm{Str}(\tau)$ there is some non-zero $\mathfrak{A}'\in\mathrm{Str}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}})$ such that $\mathfrak{A}'\models T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}$ is the $\tau$-reduct of $\mathfrak{A}'$.

Proof. We define $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}$ and $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_n$ recursively in $n$. Let $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|0)}:=\tau$ and $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_0:=\emptyset$. At stage $n$ we expand $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}$ by adding constants only, indeed let
$$\mathcal{C}_{\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n+1)}}:=\mathcal{C}_{\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}}\cup\{c_\varphi:\varphi\text{ is in }\mathcal{L}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)})\text{ with exactly 1 free variable}\}.$$
We also expand $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_n$ to state that the new constants $c_\varphi$ act as witnesses, i.e. let
$$T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{n+1}:=T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_n\cup\{\exists x\varphi(x)\longleftrightarrow\varphi(c_\varphi):\varphi\in\mathcal{L}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)})\text{ with exactly 1 free variable}\}.$$
Then we define
$$\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}:=\bigcup_n\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad T^{\mathrm{Hen}}:=\bigcup_nT^{\mathrm{Hen}}_n.$$
Clearly $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ has Henkin constants and $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ is an expansion of $\tau$ by constants. This takes care of 1.) and 2.) in the proposition.

Now we show that $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ and $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ satisfy property 3.). Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be non-empty $\tau$-structure¹. We will find $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}\in\mathrm{Str}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)})$ such that $\mathfrak{A}_{|0)}=\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}=\mathfrak{A}_{|n+1)}|_{\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}}$ and such that $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}\models T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_n$.

For $n=0$ let $\mathfrak{A}_{|0)}:=\mathfrak{A}$, then have $\mathfrak{A}_{|0)}\models T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_0=\emptyset$.

Given $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}$, for each $\varphi\in\mathcal{L}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)})$ with free variable $x$ if $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}\models\exists x\varphi$ let $a_\varphi\in\varphi(\mathfrak{A}_{|n)})$, if $\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}\models\neg\exists x\varphi(x)$ then let $a_\varphi$ be arbitrary. Here we have used the axiom of choice to pick the witnesses $a_\varphi$. We interpret
$$c_\varphi^{\mathfrak{A}_{|n+1)}}:=a_\varphi.$$
This ensures that $\mathfrak{A}_{|n+1)}\models T^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{n+1}$.

Finally let $\mathfrak{A}'$ be the unique $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ structure with $\mathfrak{A}'|_{\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}_{|n)}}=\mathfrak{A}_{|n)}$. $\mathfrak{A}'$ is the desired structure. $\square$

Corollary. If $T$ is a finitely satisfiable $\tau$-theory then $T\cup T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ is a finitely satisfiable $\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}}$-theory.

Proof. Let $S'\subseteq T\cup T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ be finite. Then $S:=S'\cap T$ is finite. By hypothesis there is some $\mathfrak{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}\models S$. By the proposition there is some expansion $\mathfrak{A}'\in\mathrm{Str}(\tau^{\mathrm{Hen}})$ such that $\mathfrak{A}'\models T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ and such that $\mathfrak{A}'|_\tau=\mathfrak{A}$. This then implies that $\mathfrak{A}'\models S$. But since $S'\subseteq S\cup T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ we see that $\mathfrak{A}'\models S'$. $\square$

Thus given any finitely satisfiable theory $T$ we can canonically expand the language and the theory to get a finitely satisfiable theory $T^{\mathrm{Hen}}$ which has Henkin constants. So in proving the compactness theorem it will suffice to consider only the case where $T$ has Henkin constants.

We shall make one more reduction of the problem before proving the compactness theorem. This time we show how to extend to complete theories. Recall that we say a theory $T$ is complete if for every sentence $\varphi$ either $\varphi\in T$ or $\neg\varphi\in T$.

Proposition. If $T$ is a finitely satiable $\tau$-theory then there is a complete extension $\widetilde{T}\supseteq T$ which is still finitely satisfiable.

Proof. We use Zorn's lemma to find a maximal finitely satisfiable extension of $T$ and then argue by maximality that this extension must be complete.

Indeed let $\mathcal{P}$ be the partially ordered (by inclusion) set of extensions $T'\supseteq T$ which are finitely satisfiable. $\mathcal{P}$ is non-empty since $T\in\mathcal{P}$. Taking a non-empty chain in $\mathcal{P}$ then the union of the chain is also an element of $\mathcal{P}$ since any finite subset of the union is contain in one of the elements of the union and therefore satisfiable. Therefore by Zorn's lemma there is a maximal finitely satisfiable extension $\widetilde{T}\supseteq T$.

Now we claim that $\widetilde{T}$ is complete. Suppose by way of contradiction that $\varphi$ is a $\mathcal{L}(\tau)$-sentence and such that both $\varphi$ and $\neg\varphi$ are not in $\widetilde{T}$. Then both
$$\widetilde{T}\cup\{\varphi\}\supsetneq\widetilde{T}\supseteq T$$
and
$$\widetilde{T}\cup\{\neg\varphi\}\supsetneq\widetilde{T}\supseteq T$$
so neither $\widetilde{T}\cup\{\varphi\}$ nor $\widetilde{T}\cup\{\neg\varphi\}$ are elements of $\mathcal{P}$. Since they both contain $T$, the only way they can avoid being in $\mathcal{P}$ is if they are not finitely satisfiable. So there is some $U,V\subseteq\widetilde{T}$ such that $U\cup\{\varphi\}$ and $V\cup\{\neg\varphi\}$ are not satisfiable. But now $U\cup V\subseteq\widetilde{T}$ is finite hence satisfiable. Let $\mathfrak{A}$ be a model of $U\cup V$. Now either $\varphi$ or $\neg\varphi$ holds in $\mathfrak{A}$, either way we have a contradiction since one of $U\cup\{\varphi\}$ and $V\cup\{\neg\varphi\}$ will be satisfied by $\mathfrak{A}$. $\square$

So starting with any finitely satisfiable theory $T$ in any signature $\tau$ we can expand the signature and the theory to get a $\tau'\supseteq\tau$ and $T'\supseteq T$ which has Henkin constants. We can now extend further to another $\tau'$-theory $T''\supseteq T'$ which is complete. Then $T''$ still has Henkin constants and is also complete. If $T''$ is satisfiable then we can take a reduction back to $\tau$ to see that $T$ is also satisfiable.

Proposition. If $T$ is a finitely satisfiable theory with Henkin constants, then there exists a model $\mathfrak{A}$ of $T$. In fact we may take $\mathrm{dom}(\mathfrak{A})$ to be $\{c^{\mathfrak{A}}:c\in\mathcal{C}_\tau\}$.

Proof. Let $C:=\mathcal{C}_\tau$ be the set of constant symbols. We define a relation $\sim$ on $C$ by $c\sim d$ iff the sentence $c=d$ is in $T$. We will show that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation and then let $\mathrm{dom}(\mathfrak{A})$ be the set of equivalence classes.

First, to see that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation we check the three axioms. They all follow the same pattern so let us just show the reflexivity: Let $c\in C$. Since $T$ is complete either $c=c$ or $c\neq c$ is in $T$. But $T$ is also finitely satisfiable and since there is no model satisfying $c\neq c$ we must have $c=c\in T$, and so $c\sim c$.

We now define a $\tau$-structure $\mathfrak{A}$ with domain $C/\!\sim$. For $c\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$ let $c^{\mathfrak{A}}:=[c]_\sim$. For $f\in\mathcal{F}_\tau$ of arity $n$, then given $c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1}\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$ then
$$f^{\mathfrak{A}}([c_0]_\sim,\ldots,[c_{n-1}]_\sim)=[d]_\sim$$
if $T\vdash f(c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1})=d$ for $d\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$. For $R\in\mathcal{R}_\tau$ of arity $n$ and $c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1}\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$ then
$$([c_0]_\sim,\ldots,[c_{n-1}]_\sim)\in R^{\mathfrak{A}}\qquad\text{iff}\qquad R(c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1})\in T.$$
Of course we must check that $f$ is actually a function, and that it is well-defined. Likewise we must also show that $R^{\mathfrak{A}}$ is well-defined.

To see that $f$ is a function consider the formula $\varphi(x)$ given by $f(c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1})=x$. Since $T$ has Henkin constants we have
$$T\vdash\exists x\varphi(x)\longleftrightarrow\varphi(d)$$
for some $d\in\mathcal{C}_\tau$. Since $T$ is complete and finitely satisfiable it must be the case that $T\vdash\exists xf(c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1})=x$. Thus $T\vdash\varphi(d)$ and so $f^{\mathfrak{A}}$ is defined. To show that $f^{\mathfrak{A}}$ and $R^{\mathfrak{A}}$ are well-defined uses the same style of arguments.

We now have a $\tau$-structure $\mathfrak{A}$. Finally we show that $\mathfrak{A}$ is a model of $T$. We work by induction on the complexity of the sentence $\varphi$ to show that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi$ if and only if $\varphi\in T$. Without loss of generality we may assume $\varphi$ is unnested.

If $\varphi$ is an unnested atomic sentence then by construction of $\mathfrak{A}$ we see that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi$ if and only if $\varphi\in T$.

If $\varphi$ is $\theta\wedge\psi$, then $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi$ iff $\mathfrak{A}\models\theta$ and $\mathfrak{A}\models\psi$ which by the inductive hypothesis happens iff $\theta\in T$ and $\psi\in T$. But $\theta\in T$ and $\psi\in T$ iff $\theta\wedge\psi\in T$ since otherwise we violate the assumption that $T$ is finitely satisfiable and complete. A similar argument works for the other boolean combinations.

Now suppose $\varphi$ is $\exists x\theta$. Then
$$\begin{array}{lll}\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi&\text{iff}&\exists a\in A,\ \mathfrak{A}\models\theta(a)\qquad(16.1)\\&\text{iff}&\exists c\in\mathcal{C}_\tau,\ \mathfrak{A}\models\theta(c)\qquad(16.2)\\&\text{iff}&\exists c\in C,\ \theta(c)\in T\qquad(16.3)\end{array}$$
So if $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi$ then since $T$ is complete and finitely satisfiable we must have $\varphi\in T$. Furthermore if $\varphi\in T$ then by the above biimplications and using that $T$ has Henkin constants we see that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi$.

Thus, $\mathfrak{A}$ is a model of $T$. $\square$

¹If $\mathfrak{A}$ is empty then condition 3.) is vacuously satisfied since it is never the case that $\exists\varphi(x)$ is true.

routes.title: semantic proof via ultraproducts
routes.proofSketch: Let I be the finite subsets of Γ and choose a model A_i of each i. For each finite i let J_i={j∈I:i⊆j}; these cones have the finite-intersection property, so extend their generated filter to an ultrafilter U. In the ultraproduct Π_i A_i/U, for each φ∈Γ the indices whose structures satisfy φ include J_{ {φ} }, hence form a U-large set. Łoś’s theorem gives that the ultraproduct satisfies every φ.

routes.verbatimProof:
In this subsection, we prove the compactness theorem for first-order logic from Łoś’ Theorem.

We recall the definition of an ultraproduct and state the theorem. For a proof, see Chang and Keisler (1990, p. 217, thm. 4.1.9) or Hodges (1997, p. 241–242, thm. 8.5.3).

Let \((\mathfrak{A}_i)_{i \in I}\) be a collection of first-order structures of the same signature, indexed by \(I\), and \(U\) an ultrafilter over this indexing set \(I\). In this context, the Boolean algebra is \(\mathcal{P}(I)\) with the subset ordering \(\subset\), so a filter \(F \subset \mathcal{P}(I)\) is a set of subsets of \(I\) which does not contain the empty set and which is closed under finite intersection and upward containment. Denote the domain of each \(\mathfrak{A}_i\) by \(A_i\). When \(U\) is an ultrafilter over \(I\), defining \(a \sim_U b\) by \(\{i \in I: a(i) = b(i)\} \in U\) yields an equivalence relation over the product

$$

\prod_{i \in I} A_i = \Bigg\{f : I \to \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \mid \forall i \in I, f(i) \in A_i\Bigg\}.

$$

(We tend to view elements of the product as generalised sequences \((x_i)_{i \in I}\).) The characteristic function \(\mu_U\) of \(U\) is a finitely-additive full measure on \(I\) and thus intuitively the elements of \(U\) are `large subsets of \(I\)’: two functions in \(\prod_{i \in I} A_i\) are identified by this relation precisely when they agree `\(U\)-almost-everywhere’. We define a new structure \(\mathfrak{B} = \prod_{i \in I} \mathfrak{A}_i / U\) as follows:

Domain of \(\mathfrak{B} = \prod_{i \in I} A_i\) quotiented by \(\sim_U\); \([a]\) denotes the equivalence class of \(a\);

\(c^\mathfrak{B} = [(\cdots, c^{\mathfrak{A}_i}, \cdots)]\);

\(f^{\mathfrak{B}}([a_1], \cdots, [a_k]) = [(\cdots, f^{\mathfrak{A}_i}(a_1(i), \cdots, , a_k(i)), \cdots)]\);

\(R^{\mathfrak{B}}([a_1], \cdots, [a_k])\) if and only if \(\{i \in I: \mathfrak{A}_i \vDash R(a_1(i), \cdots, a_k(i))\} \in U\).

for any \(k\)-place function and relation symbols \(f\) and \(R\) and any constant \(c\) of the first-order language in question. As may be checked, the fact that \(U\) is a filter means that the definitions just given do not depend on the choice of representatives from \(\prod_{i \in I} A_i\). For \(\phi\) atomic we have by definition:

$$

\mathfrak{B} \vDash \phi(a_1, \cdots, a_n) \text{ if and only if } \{i \in I: \mathfrak{A}_i \vDash \phi(a_1(i), \cdots, a_n(i))\} \in U.

$$

Łoś’ theorem, which is proved by induction on the complexity of \(\phi\), extends this to all \(\phi\):

for all \(\phi\), \(\mathfrak{B} \vDash \phi(a_1, \cdots, a_n)\) if and only if \(\{i \in I: \mathfrak{A}_i \vDash \phi(a_1(i), \cdots, a_n(i))\} \in U\).

The induction step for the universal / existential quantifier step does require some Choice. In fact, the Ultrafilter Lemma together with Łoś’ theorem imply the full Axiom of Choice (Howard 1975).

To prove the compactness theorem for first-order logic from Łoś’ Theorem, let \(\Sigma\) be a finitely-satisfiable set of first-order sentences. Let \(I\) be the set of finite subsets of \(\Sigma\) and suppose we are given for each \(i \in I\) a model \(\mathfrak{A}_i\) for the sentences in \(i\). For \(i \in I\) let

\begin{gather*}

J_i \df := \{j \in I: i \subset j\}, \\

F \df := \{J \subset I: J_i \subset J \textnormal{ for some } i \in I\}.

\end{gather*}

The collection of \(J_i\) is closed under finite intersection because \(J_{i_1} \cap J_{i_2} = J_{i_1 \cup i_2}\), hence \(F\) is also closed under finite intersection; by definition, \(F\) is closed under upward containment, and clearly \(F\) does not contain the empty set. Thus \(F\) satisfies the conditions for being a filter and may therefore be extended to an ultrafilter \(U\). Now for any \(\sigma \in \Sigma\), we have \(\{\sigma\} \in I\) and \(J_{\{\sigma\}} \subset \{i \in I: \mathfrak{A}_i \vDash \sigma \}\), from which it follows that \(\{i \in I: \mathfrak{A}_i \vDash \sigma \} \in U\). By Łoś’ theorem, \(\mathfrak{B} \vDash \sigma\). This is true for every \(\sigma \in \Sigma\), so \(\mathfrak{B} \vDash \Sigma\), in other words if \(\Sigma\) is satisfiable. Intuitively, the model \(\mathfrak{B}\) was designed so as to agree with \(\mathfrak{A}_i\) on the `large subset’ \(J_i\) of \(I\) and in particular to agree with \(\mathfrak{A}_i\) on the truth-value of each element of \(i\); as this is true for all \(i\), \(\mathfrak{B}\) satisfies \(\Sigma\). This completes the ultraproduct proof of the compactness of first-order logic.

routes.verbatimProof:
The claim is that if triangles ABC and XYZ are perspective from
a point P, then they are perspective from a line (meaning that
the three points

AB⋅XY  BC⋅YZ  CA⋅ZX

are collinear) and conversely.

Since no three of A,B,C,P are collinear, we can lay down
homogeneous coordinates such that

A=(1,0,0)  B=(0,1,0)  C=(0,0,1)  P=(1,1,1)

By hypothesis, there are scalars p,q,r such that

X=(1,p,p)  Y=(q,1,q)  Z=(r,r,1)

The equation for a line through (x_1,y_1,z_1) and
(x_2,y_2,z_2) is

(y_1z_2-z_1y_2)x+(z_1x_2-x_1z_2)y+(x_1y_2-y_1x_2)z=0,

giving us equations for six lines:

:

y=0

As claimed, these three points are collinear, since the

routes.title: Galois action on primitive roots
routes.proofSketch: Let f be the minimal polynomial over Q of a primitive n-th root ζ. For a prime p∤n, suppose ζ^p is not a conjugate; let g be its distinct minimal polynomial. Then f and g are distinct monic integer factors of X^n−1. Modulo p, Frobenius gives the relevant pth-power relation between roots, forcing a repeated factor of X^n−1; this is impossible because p∤n makes X^n−1 square-free mod p. Thus ζ and ζ^p are conjugate. Factoring any a coprime to n into primes not dividing n and iterating shows every ζ^a is conjugate to ζ, so Φ_n is irreducible over Q.

routes.verbatimProof:
Theorem 3.1. The embedding $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbf{Q}(\mu_n)/\mathbf{Q})\hookrightarrow(\mathbf{Z}/(n))^\times$ is an isomorphism.

Proof. The number of primitive $n$th roots of unity is $\varphi(n)=\#(\mathbf{Z}/(n))^\times$, and the size of $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbf{Q}(\mu_n)/\mathbf{Q})$ is the number of $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugates of a primitive $n$th root of unity. So proving that $\#\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbf{Q}(\mu_n)/\mathbf{Q})=\#(\mathbf{Z}/(n))^\times$ is the same as showing all primitive $n$th roots of unity over $\mathbf{Q}$ are $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate, and that is what we will do.

Let $\zeta_n$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity. We want to show if $(a,n)=1$ that $\zeta_n$ and $\zeta_n^a$ are $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate. Since $\zeta_n^a$ only depends on $a$ mod $n$, we can take $a>0$, and in fact $a>1$. Write $a=p_1p_2\cdots p_r$ as a product of primes $p_i$, each not dividing $n$ (some $p_i$'s could coincide). To show $\zeta_n$ and $\zeta_n^a$ are $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate, it suffices to show for each prime $p$ not dividing $n$ that any primitive $n$th root of unity and its $p$th power are $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate, since then the successive primitive $n$th roots of unity
$$\zeta_n,\ \zeta_n^{p_1},\ \zeta_n^{p_1p_2},\ \zeta_n^{p_1p_2p_3},\ \ldots,\ \zeta_n^{p_1p_2\cdots p_r}=\zeta_n^a$$
are all $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate and each is a prime power of the previous one.

Let $f(X)$ be the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_n$ over $\mathbf{Q}$, where $\zeta_n$ is an arbitrary primitive $n$th root of unity. Assume $\zeta_n$ and $\zeta_n^p$ are not $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugate for some prime $p$ not dividing $n$. We aim to get a contradiction. The $\mathbf{Q}$-conjugates of $\zeta_n$ are the roots of $f(X)$, so $f(\zeta_n^p)\neq 0$. Let $g(X)$ be the minimal polynomial of $\zeta_n^p$ in $\mathbf{Q}[X]$, so $g(X)\neq f(X)$. The polynomials $f(X)$ and $g(X)$ are in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$ since they both divide $X^n-1$ and any monic factor of $X^n-1$ in $\mathbf{Q}[X]$ is in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$ by Gauss' lemma.

Since $f(X)$ and $g(X)$ are different monic irreducible factors of $X^n-1$ in $\mathbf{Q}[X]$, we have $X^n-1=f(X)g(X)k(X)$ for some $k(X)\in\mathbf{Q}[X]$, and by Gauss' lemma $k(X)\in\mathbf{Z}[X]$. Reducing this equation modulo $p$,
$$X^n-\overline{1}=\overline{f}(X)\overline{g}(X)\overline{k}(X)\qquad(3.1)$$
in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$. The polynomial $X^n-\overline{1}$ is separable in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$ since $p$ doesn't divide $n$, so $\overline{f}(X)$ and $\overline{g}(X)$ are relatively prime in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$.

Since $g(\zeta_n^p)=0$, $g(X^p)$ has $\zeta_n$ as a root, so $f(X)\mid g(X^p)$ in $\mathbf{Q}[X]$. Both $f(X)$ and $g(X^p)$ are monic in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$, so $f(X)\mid g(X^p)$ in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$ by comparing the division theorem for monics in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$ and $\mathbf{Q}[X]$. Hence $g(X^p)=f(X)h(X)$ for some $h(X)$ in $\mathbf{Z}[X]$. Reduce this equation modulo $p$ and use the formula $\overline{g}(X^p)=\overline{g}(X)^p$ in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$ to get
$$\overline{g}(X)^p=\overline{f}(X)\overline{h}(X)$$
in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$. This implies that any irreducible factor of $\overline{f}(X)$ in $\mathbf{F}_p[X]$ is a factor of $\overline{g}(X)$, which contradicts relative primality of $\overline{f}(X)$ and $\overline{g}(X)$. $\square$

routes.title: reduction modulo a prime and Frobenius
routes.proofSketch: For p∤n, every root α of Φ_n over F_p is a primitive n-th root: otherwise it would also be a root of X^d−1 for a proper divisor d|n, contradicting separability of X^n−1. Frobenius α↦α^p has orbit length ord_n(p), so each irreducible factor of Φ_n mod p has degree ord_n(p). Consequently Φ_n mod p is irreducible exactly when p mod n generates (Z/nZ)^×. This is a conditional modular criterion; such a prime need not exist for every n.

routes.title: Reflection principle/ballot paths
routes.proofSketch: Count monotone N/E walks with n N's and n E's that never have more E's than N's. Total walks number $\binom{2n}{n}$, so subtract the bad walks. For a bad walk, find the first step at which E's outnumber N's; interchange N and E in the segment up to and including that step. The result has $n+1$ N's and $n-1$ E's, and the map is reversible (first time N's exceed E's), so bad walks are in bijection with all walks in an $(n-1)\times(n+1)$ grid. Hence $C_n=\binom{2n}{n}-\binom{2n}{n-1}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

routes.title: first-return recurrence and generating functions
routes.proofSketch: Take a nonempty Dyck path and look at the first time after the initial up step that it returns to the diagonal, at $(k,k)$. Removing the first and last steps of the initial excursion leaves a Dyck path of semilength $k-1$, and the remainder is a Dyck path of semilength $n-k$; thus $C_n=\sum_{k=1}^nC_{k-1}C_{n-k}$ with $C_0=1$. Multiplying the recurrence by $x^n$ and summing gives $(C(x)-1)/x=C(x)^2$, i.e. $xC^2-C+1=0$; the minus sign in the quadratic formula is forced by $C(0)=1$, so $C(x)=(1-\sqrt{1-4x})/(2x)$. Extracting coefficients with the binomial series for $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ gives $C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$.

routes.title: triangulations of a polygon
routes.proofSketch: Show that triangulations of a polygon with $n+2$ sides (into $n$ triangles) satisfy the Catalan recursion. Fix a side as the base; in any triangulation it lies in exactly one triangle, the base triangle. That triangle splits the polygon into two smaller triangulated polygons, with $k+2$ sides on one side and $n-k+1$ sides on the other, with $k$ running over $0,\dots,n-1$ (extreme values when the base triangle uses two polygon edges). Hence $T_n=\sum_k T_kT_{n-1-k}$ with the same initial values, so $T_n=C_n$.

routes.title: parenthesizations/binary trees
routes.proofSketch: Let $C_n$ count the bracketings of a product of $n$ terms under a non-associative operation. The last application of the operation combines a bracketed product of the first $m$ terms with one of the last $n-m$ terms, giving $C_n=\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}C_mC_{n-m}$ with $C_1=1$. Hence $c(x)=x+c(x)^2$, solved by $c(x)=\tfrac12(1-\sqrt{1-4x})$ (sign fixed by $c(0)=0$); the binomial series gives $C_n=\frac1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ (i.e. $\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ for $n+1$ terms). Binary trees with $n$ leaves are parse trees of bracketed products, so they obey the same count.

routes.title: Parity count of boundary-labeled simplices
routes.proofSketch: Label a triangulated d-simplex Sperner-style. Count incidences between small d-simplices and their facets labeled {0,…,d−1}; interior facets contribute twice and cancel mod 2, while boundary facets reduce to the (d−1)-dimensional boundary simplex. routes.title: Pigeonhole using increasing/decreasing subsequence lengths
routes.proofSketch: For each sequence position k, let f(k) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at a_k. If any f(k)=n+1, the theorem follows. Otherwise f takes at most n values among n²+1 positions, so n+1 positions k₁<⋯<kₙ₊₁ share one value. Their entries must be strictly decreasing: if i<j and a_{k_i}<a_{k_j}, an increasing subsequence ending at k_i extends to k_j, contradicting equal f-values.

routes.verbatimProof:
The Erdős–Szekeres Theorem

In any sequence of $n^2+1$ real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length $n+1$.

Remark. Let $[a,b)$ denote the sequence $a,a+1,\ldots,b-1$. Then the sequence
$$[n^2-n,n^2)[n^2-2n,n^2-n)\ldots[0,n)$$
which is obtained by concatenating $n$ increasing sequences has length exactly $n^2$ and the longest monotone subsequence has length $n$.

Proof of the Erdős–Szekeres Theorem

Define the function
$$f(k)=\text{length of longest increasing subsequence ending at }a_k$$
If $f(k)=n+1$ for any $k$, then we are done. Otherwise, the range of $f$ has size at most $n$, so we can find values $k_1<k_2<\ldots<k_{n+1}$ such that
$$f(k_1)=f(k_2)=\ldots=f(k_{n+1})=a$$
for some $a\in\mathbb{N}$. Now $a_{k_1}\ge a_{k_2}\ge\ldots\ge a_{k_{n+1}}$ otherwise if $a_{k_i}<a_{k_j}$ where $i<j$ then $f(k_i)<f(k_j)$ by definition of $f$. $\blacksquare$

routes.title: poset-chain/antichain formulation
routes.proofSketch: Order pairs of rank data (longest increasing ending at i, longest decreasing ending at i). Distinct sequence entries make these pairs distinct: if i<j and a_i<a_j the increasing rank grows; if a_i>a_j the decreasing rank grows. With no monotone subsequence of length r or s, only (r−1)(s−1) rank pairs exist.

routes.title: Euler product and divergence of the harmonic series
routes.proofSketch: For each x, the finite Euler product P_x=∏_{p≤x}(1−1/p)^{-1} expands as a sum over integers whose prime factors are at most x, so P_x≥H_x and is unbounded. If Σ_p 1/p converged, then log P_x=Σ_{p≤x}log(1+1/(p−1)) would stay bounded, since log(1+u)≤u and 1/(p−1)≤2/p for p≥2. Thus P_x would be bounded, contradiction; hence Σ_p1/p diverges. This follows the source’s Euler-product/harmonic-series argument, using the corrected harmless constant bound for the logarithm.

routes.verbatimProof:
Euler first noted this fact, and one proof can be obtained by taking the natural logarithm of both sides of Euler’s Product Formula, (using s=1 in that formula) and noting that the right hand side consists of terms of the form 

Log(p/p-1) = Log(1 + (1/p-1)),

where Log denotes the natural log, and p is a prime. Using a Taylor series for Log, this term is itself bounded by 1/(p-1) < 1/p. Thus, if the sum of reciprocals for primes converge, then the harmonic series would converge, a contradiction.

routes.title: Erdős's elementary counting contradiction
routes.proofSketch: Assume ∑_p1/p converges and choose y so the tail sum over p>y is <1/2. Integers ≤x with a prime factor >y are at most x∑_{p>y,p≤x}1/p<x/2; those with all prime factors among the finitely many primes ≤y are O((log x)^k)=o(x). These cannot account for all x integers, contradiction.

routes.title: compare central binomial coefficients
routes.proofSketch: Put c_n=C(2n,n)/4ⁿ=(2n−1)!!/(2n)!!. The Wallis partial product is P_n=∏_{k≤n}(2k)²/((2k−1)(2k+1))=1/((2n+1)c_n²), so the product equals π/2 exactly when c_n∼1/√(πn). Caveat: if Stirling's constant √(2π) is itself obtained from Wallis' product the argument is circular, so the constant needs an independent derivation (for instance from the Gaussian integral).

routes.title: Bernstein polynomials and probabilistic binomial concentration
routes.proofSketch: For continuous f on [0,1], let B_n f be its Bernstein polynomial. Uniform continuity gives |f(x)−f(a)|≤ε when |x−a|≤δ; elsewhere bound it by 2M(x−a)²/δ², where M=||f||∞. Positivity and linearity of B_n then bound |B_nf(a)−f(a)| by ε plus (2M/δ²)B_n[(x−a)²](a). The Bernstein second-moment identity gives B_n[(x−a)²](a)=a(1−a)/n≤1/(4n), uniformly in a; hence B_nf→f uniformly.

routes.verbatimProof:
The following theorem, the Weierstrass approximation theorem, plays a central role in any discussion of approximations of functions. Loosely speaking, this theorem states that any continuous function can be approached as close as we want to with polynomials, assuming that the polynomials can be of any degree. We formulate this theorem in the $L^\infty$ norm and note that a similar theorem holds also in the $L^2$ sense. We let $\Pi_n$ denote the space of polynomials of degree $\le n$.

Theorem 4.1 (Weierstrass Approximation Theorem). Let $f(x)$ be a continuous function on $[a,b]$. Then there exists a sequence of polynomials $P_n(x)$ that converges uniformly to $f(x)$ on $[a,b]$, i.e., $\forall\varepsilon>0$, there exists an $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and polynomials $P_n(x)\in\Pi_n$, such that $\forall x\in[a,b]$
$$|f(x)-P_n(x)|<\varepsilon,\qquad\forall n\ge N.$$

We will provide a constructive proof of the Weierstrass approximation theorem: first, we will define a family of polynomials, known as the Bernstein polynomials, and then we will show that they uniformly converge to $f(x)$.

We start with the definition. Given a continuous function $f(x)$ in $[0,1]$, we define the Bernstein polynomials as
$$(B_nf)(x)=\sum_{j=0}^nf\!\left(\frac jn\right)\binom nj x^j(1-x)^{n-j},\qquad0\le x\le1.$$
We emphasize that the Bernstein polynomials depend on the function $f(x)$.

[Example 4.2 and Figure 4.1 omitted.]

We now state and prove several properties of $B_n(x)$ that will be used when we prove Theorem 4.1.

Lemma 4.3. The following relations hold:
1. $(B_n1)(x)=1$
2. $(B_nx)(x)=x$
3. $(B_nx^2)(x)=\dfrac{n-1}{n}x^2+\dfrac xn$.

Proof.
$$(B_n1)(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj x^j(1-x)^{n-j}=(x+(1-x))^n=1.$$
$$(B_nx)(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac jn\binom nj x^j(1-x)^{n-j}=x\sum_{j=1}^n\binom{n-1}{j-1}x^{j-1}(1-x)^{n-j}=x\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}x^j(1-x)^{n-1-j}=x[x+(1-x)]^{n-1}=x.$$
Finally,
$$\left(\frac jn\right)^2\binom nj=\frac jn\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-j)!(j-1)!}=\frac{n-1}{n-1}\frac{j-1}{n}\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-j)!(j-1)!}+\frac1n\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-j)!(j-1)!}=\frac{n-1}{n}\binom{n-2}{j-2}+\frac1n\binom{n-1}{j-1}.$$
Hence
$$(B_nx^2)(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\left(\frac jn\right)^2\binom nj x^j(1-x)^{n-j}=\frac{n-1}{n}x^2\sum_{j=2}^n\binom{n-2}{j-2}x^{j-2}(1-x)^{n-j}+\frac1nx\sum_{j=1}^n\binom{n-1}{j-1}x^{j-1}(1-x)^{n-j}$$
$$=\frac{n-1}{n}x^2(x+(1-x))^{n-2}+\frac1nx(x+(1-x))^{n-1}=\frac{n-1}{n}x^2+\frac xn.\ \blacksquare$$

In the following lemma we state several additional properties of the Bernstein polynomials. The proof is left as an exercise.

Lemma 4.4. For all functions $f(x),g(x)$ that are continuous in $[0,1]$, and $\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$
1. Linearity. $(B_n(\alpha f+g))(x)=\alpha(B_nf)(x)+(B_ng)(x)$.
2. Monotonicity. If $f(x)\le g(x)\ \forall x\in[0,1]$, then $(B_nf)(x)\le(B_ng)(x)$. Also, if $|f(x)|\le g(x)\ \forall x\in[0,1]$ then $|(B_nf)(x)|\le(B_ng)(x)$.
3. Positivity. If $f(x)\ge 0$ then $(B_nf)(x)\ge 0$.

We are now ready to prove the Weierstrass approximation theorem, Theorem 4.1.

Proof. We will prove the theorem in the interval $[0,1]$. The extension to $[a,b]$ is left as an exercise. Since $f(x)$ is continuous on a closed interval, it is uniformly continuous. Hence $\forall x,y\in[0,1]$, such that $|x-y|\le\delta$,
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le\varepsilon.\qquad(4.5)$$
In addition, since $f(x)$ is continuous on a closed interval, it is also bounded. Let
$$M=\max_{x\in[0,1]}|f(x)|.$$
Fix any point $a\in[0,1]$. If $|x-a|\le\delta$ then (4.5) holds. If $|x-a|>\delta$ then
$$|f(x)-f(a)|\le 2M\le 2M\left(\frac{x-a}{\delta}\right)^2.$$
(at first sight this seems to be a strange way of upper bounding a function. We will use it later on to our advantage). Combining the estimates for both cases we have
$$|f(x)-f(a)|\le\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}(x-a)^2.$$
We would now like to estimate the difference between $B_nf$ and $f$. The linearity of $B_n$ and the property $(B_n1)(x)=1$ imply that
$$B_n(f-f(a))(x)=(B_nf)(x)-f(a).$$
Hence using the monotonicity of $B_n$ and the mapping properties of $x$ and $x^2$, we have,
$$|B_nf(x)-f(a)|\le B_n\left(\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}(x-a)^2\right)=\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}\left(\frac{n-1}{n}x^2+\frac xn-2ax+a^2\right)$$
$$=\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}(x-a)^2+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}\frac{x-x^2}{n}.$$
Evaluating at $x=a$ we have (observing that $\max_{a\in[0,1]}(a-a^2)=\frac14$)
$$|B_nf(a)-f(a)|\le\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{\delta^2}\frac{a-a^2}{n}\le\varepsilon+\frac{M}{2\delta^2n}.\qquad(4.6)$$
The point $a$ was arbitrary so the result (4.6) holds for any point $a\in[0,1]$. Choosing $N\ge\frac{M}{2\delta^2\varepsilon}$ we have $\forall n\ge N$,
$$\|B_nf-f\|_\infty\le\varepsilon+\frac{M}{2\delta^2N}\le 2\varepsilon.\ \blacksquare$$

routes.title: Stone–Weierstrass algebra/separation theorem
routes.proofSketch: A subalgebra of C(K) containing constants and separating points is uniformly dense: its closure is closed under |f| via polynomial approximation to absolute value, hence under max/min; finite-cover patching then approximates any continuous target uniformly. This proves a general theorem, of which Weierstrass is a special case.

routes.title: Extremal derivative/maximization method
routes.proofSketch: Fix a simply connected region Ω≠ℂ and z₀∈Ω and maximize |f′(z₀)| over the univalent maps Ω→D. The family is nonempty (a square-root branch of z−a, with the two branches having disjoint images, composed with an inversion) and the derivative is bounded by the Cauchy estimate. Take a maximizing sequence; the family is bounded by 1, so Montel gives a locally uniformly convergent subsequence, and Hurwitz makes the limit univalent since its derivative at z₀ is nonzero. Composing with a disc automorphism shows the maximizer sends z₀ to 0, and rotating makes f′(z₀)>0. If f(Ω)≠D, a univalent map g on f(Ω) with g(0)=0 and |g′(0)|>1 (Lecture 17) gives g∘f with larger derivative, a contradiction, so f is onto. Uniqueness follows from the Schwarz lemma.

Lecture 18 — Date of Lecture: March 13, 2017

1. The Riemann Mapping Theorem

Let $\Delta$ denote the unit disc around $0\in\mathbf{C}$. Last lecture (Lecture 17) we showed the following (see Lemma 2.2.1 of loc.cit.):

Let $U$ be a simply connected open subset of $\Delta$ such that $0\in U$ and $U\neq\Delta$. Then there exists a univalent function $f:U\to\Delta$ such that $f(0)=0$ and $|f'(0)|>1$.

A little thought shows that if $f$ in the above has maximal derivative (in absolute value) at 0 amongst all univalent functions on $U$ taking values in $\Delta$ which take 0 to 0, then $f(U)=\Delta$. In other words if $f$ in the result in italics above is such $|f'(0)|=\sup_g|g'(0)|$, where the supremum is taken over univalent maps $g:U\to\Delta$ with $g(0)=0$, then $f(U)=\Delta$. If not, then we have a univalent map $h:f(U)\to\Delta$ with $h(0)=0$ and $|h'(0)|>1$. Then $g=h\circ f$ is such that $g$ is univalent on $U$, $g(0)=0$ and $|g'(0)|>|f'(0)|$, a contradiction. This leads us to the question, is there a $f$ as in Lemma 2.2.1 of Lecture 17 with maximal possible derivative (in absolute value) at 0? This an example of an extremal problem. We examine a slightly more general problem in the subsection that follows.

1.1. An Exremal Problem. We fix a simply connected region $\Omega$ such that $\Omega\neq\mathbf{C}$, as well a point $z_0\in\Omega$. Set
$$\mathscr{F}=\{f:\Omega\to\Delta\mid f\text{ is univalent}\}.$$
The extremal problem we pose is: Show there exists $f\in\mathscr{F}$ such that $f'(z_0)>0$ and if $g\in\mathscr{F}$ then $|g'(z_0)|\le f'(z_0)$.

Any solution of this extremal problem is called a Riemann mapping for $\Omega$ at $z_0$. As we will see a solution exists and it is unique. First let us observe the following.

Lemma 1.1.1. Suppose $V$ is a simply connected region of $\mathbf{C}$ such that $0\notin V$. Let $g_i:V\to\mathbf{C}$, $i=1,2$ be the two branches of the square root function $V$ (which exist because of our hypotheses on $V$). Then $g_1(V)\cap g_2(V)=\emptyset$.

Proof. Suppose $c\in g_1(V)\cap g_2(V)$. Then $c=g_1(a)$ and $c=g_2(b)$ for some $a$ and $b$ in $V$. Squaring, we see that $a=c^2=b$. Thus $g_1(a)=g_2(a)$, i.e., $g_1(a)=-g_1(a)$. This means $g_1(a)=0$, whence upon squaring $a=0$, contradicting the fact that $0\notin V$. $\square$

1.1.2. Solution to the Extremal Problem. Let us first show that $\mathscr{F}\neq\emptyset$. Let $a\in\mathbf{C}\setminus\Omega$. Then $h(z)=z-a$ is nowhere vanishing and univalent on $\Omega$. Let $V=h(\Omega)$. Then $V$ is simply connected and $0\notin V$. Hence if $\varphi:V\to\mathbf{C}$ is a branch of $\sqrt{z}$ on $V$, then by Lemma 1.1.1, $\varphi(V)\cap(-\varphi)(V)=set$. Let $D$ be disc of radius $\rho$ in $(-\varphi)(V)$ centred at $w_0\in(-\varphi)(V)$. Then, clearly $|z-w_0|>\rho$ for all $z\in V=h(\Omega)$. It follows that $\psi(z)=\rho/(z-w_0)$ is univalent map on $\varphi(V)$ which takes values in $\Delta$. If $H(z)=\psi\circ\varphi\circ h$, then $H$ is univalent on $\Omega$ and takes values in $\Delta$. Thus $H\in\mathscr{F}$, whence $\mathscr{F}\neq\emptyset$.

Let $M=\sup_{f\in\mathscr{F}}|f'(z_0)|$. Note that if $\varepsilon>0$ is so small that the disc $|z-z_0|\le\varepsilon$ lies in $\Omega$, then we have
$$|f'(z_0)|=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left|\int_{|z-z_0|=\varepsilon}\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z_0)^2}d\zeta\right|\le\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}(2\pi\varepsilon)\le\frac{1}{\varepsilon},\qquad(f\in\mathscr{F}).$$
Thus $M<\infty$. We can find a sequence $\{f_n\}$ in $\mathscr{F}$ such that $\{|f_n'(z_0)|\}$ converges to $M$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is locally bounded, in fact it is globally bounded by 1 since its members take values in $\Delta$, by Montel's Theorem $\{f_n\}$ has a convergent subsequence $\{f_{n_k}\}$ which converges uniformly on compact sets. Let $f=\lim k\to\infty f_{n_k}$. Then we know that $f\in\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$. Since each $f_{n_k}$ is univalent, by Hurwitz's Theorem, either $f$ is a constant or it is univalent. Further, we know that $f_{n_k}'\to f'$ uniformly on compact sets as $k\to\infty$. This means $|f'(z_0)|=M>0$. This means $f$ cannot be a constant. Hence $f$ is univalent. It clearly takes values in $\Delta$.

We claim $f(z_0)=0$. Suppose $f(z_0)=b$. Note $b\in\Delta$. Consider the function $\Phi_b(z)=\dfrac{z-b}{1-\bar{b}z}$. Then $\Phi_b\circ f\in\mathscr{F}$, and $(\Phi_b\circ f)(z_0)=0$. Moreover, $\Phi_b'(b)=\dfrac{1}{1-|b|^2}$. Hence we have
$$\frac{M}{1-|b|^2}=|\Phi_b'(b)||M|=|\Phi_b'(b)||f'(z_0)|=|(\Phi_b\circ f)'(z_0)|\le M,$$
giving,
$$\frac{1}{1-|b|^2}\le 1.$$
The above inequality implies $b=0$ since we know $|b|<1$. Thus $f(z_0)=0$ and $|f'(z_0)|=M$. It follows that $f'(z_0)=e^{i\theta}M$ for some real $\theta$. Replacing $f$ by $e^{-i\theta}f$ if necessary, we see that $f$ solves the Extremal Problem.

Lemma 1.1.2. Let $f$ be the solution to the above Extremal problem. Then $f(\Omega)=\Delta$.

Proof. If not, then $U=f(\Omega)$ is a simply connected region in $\Delta$ which is not equal to $\Delta$, whence we have a univalent map $g:U\to\Delta$ such that $|g'(0)|>1$. The composite $g\circ f$ is in $\mathscr{F}$ and $|(g\circ f)'(0)|>|f'(0)|$, a contradicton. $\square$

1.2. The Riemann Mapping Theorem. Here is the statement

Theorem 1.2.1 (The Riemann Mapping Theorem). Let $\Omega$ be a simply connected region such that $\Omega\neq\mathbf{C}$, and let $z_0$ be a point in $\Omega$. Then there exists a unique univalent onto map
$$f:\Omega\to\Delta$$
such that $f(z_0)=0$ and $f'(z_0)>0$.

Remark: Note that $f$ as in the Theorem gives us a biholomorphism between $\Omega$ and $\Delta$. In particular, $\Omega$ and $\Delta$ are homeomorphic, whence $\Omega$ is classically simply connected.

Proof. We have already seen the existence of such an $f$ (see Lemma 1.1.2 to see that the solution to the extremal problem in the last subsection maps $\Omega$ surjective on to $\Delta$). It only remains to prove uniqueness. So suppose $g$ is another biholomorphism from $\Omega$ to $\Delta$ which vanishes at $z_0$ and such that $g'(z_0)>0$. Then by Schwarz's Lemma there exists $\theta\in\mathbf{R}$ such that $(f\circ g^{-1})(z)=e^{i\theta}z$. Now $e^{i\theta}=(f\circ g^{-1})'(0)=f'(0)/g'(0)>0$. Hence $e^{\theta}=1$, whence $f=g$. $\square$

Maximize f′(z₀); if the image omits a point, compose with a disk automorphism and a square-root map to build a competitor with larger derivative, contradiction.

routes.title: Arzelà–Ascoli plus Cauchy estimates
routes.proofSketch: Local boundedness gives uniform equicontinuity on compact sets (Cauchy estimates, proved in the previous lecture). On each compact K, Arzelà–Ascoli then gives a subsequence converging uniformly on K. Taking an exhaustion K₁⊂K₂⊂… by compact sets, successively extract subsequences converging uniformly on K₁, K₂, … and take the diagonal sequence, which converges uniformly on every compact set. The limit is holomorphic as a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions.

Lecture 16 — Date of Lecture: March 6, 2017

1. Topology on the space of holomorphic functions

Last time we showed that if a non-empty family of holomorphic functions on a region is locally bounded then it is uniformly equicontinuous on compact subsets of that region. The two notions are actually equivalent, and equivalent to a few other related notions. It is most convenient to work with a topology (coming from a metric) on the space of holomorphic functions on a region.

1.1. The space $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$. Suppose $\Omega$ is a region. Let $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$ denote the space of holomorphic functions on $\Omega$. For each compact subset $K$ of $\Omega$ and each $f\in\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$ let us write $\|f\|_K$ for the supremum of $|f|$ on $K$. (In other words $\|f\|_K=\|(f|_K)\|_\infty$.) For each $n\in\mathbf{N}$, define a compact set $K_n$ by
$$K_n:=\{z\in\Omega\mid|z|\le n,\ \mathrm{dist}(z,\mathbf{C}\setminus\Omega)\ge 1/n\}.$$
Then one checks easily that
• $K_1\subset K_2\subset\ldots K_n\subset K_{n+1}\subset\ldots$, and
• $\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty K_n=\Omega$,
• if $K$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$ then $K\subset K_n$ for some $n\ge 1$.
A sequence of compact sets $\{K_n\}$ satisfying the above three properties is called an exhaustion of $\Omega$ by compact subsets. Let $\|f\|_n=\|f\|_{K_n}$ for $n\in\mathbf{N}$ and $f\in\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$. Define a metric $d$ on $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$ as follows:
$$(1.1.1)\qquad d(f,g):=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\|f-g\|_n}{1+\|f-g\|_n}\qquad(f,g\in\mathscr{H}(\Omega)).$$
We have the following

Lemma 1.1.2. The metric space $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$ is complete. A sequence $\{f_n\}$ in $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$ converges with respect to the metric $d$ if and only if it converges uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$.

Proof. We will first prove that convergence in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$ implies uniform convergence on compact sets.

Let $\{f_k\}$ be a convergent sequence in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$. Say it converges to $f\in\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$. We will show $f_k\to f$ as $k\to infty$ uniformly on each $K_n$. Since every compact set is contained in some $K_n$, this will show that $\{f_k\}$ converges uniformly on compact sets to $f$. Fix $n\in\mathbf{N}$. Given $\epsilon>0$ we can find $N\in\mathbf{N}$ such that
$$d(f_k,f)<\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\qquad(l,k\ge N).$$
From (1.1.1) it follows that
$$\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\|f_k-f\|_n}{1+\|f_k-f\|_n}\le\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}\qquad(k\ge N).$$
It follows that
$$\|f_k-f\|_n<\epsilon\qquad(k\ge N).$$
Thus $\{f_k\}$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $K_n$.

The above proof, with obvious modifications, also shows that if $\{f_k\}$ is Cauchy in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$, then it is Cauchy in $C(K)$ for each compact subset $K$ of $\Omega$ where $C(K)$ is the space of continuous functions on $K$ with supremum norm $\|\cdot\|_K$.

Now suppose $\{f_k\}$ converges uniformly on compact subsets on $\Omega$. Let $f$ be the limiting function. Recall $f$ must belong to $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$ in this case. Let $\epsilon>0$ be given. Let $n_0\in\mathbf{N}$ be chosen such that $\sum n=n_0+1^\infty 2^{-n}<\epsilon/2$. Since $f_k\to f$ uniformly on $K_{n_0}$ therefore there exists $N\ge 1$ such that $\|f_k-f\|_{n_0}<2\epsilon/(1-2\epsilon)$ for all $k\ge N$. In fact, since $K_n\subset K_{n_0}$ for all $n\le n_0$, we have $\|f_k-f\|_n<2\epsilon/(1-2\epsilon)$ for all $k\ge N$. Thus if $k\ge N$ we have
$$d(f_k,f)<\sum_{n=1}^{n_0}\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\|f_k-f\|_n}{1+\|f_k-f\|_n}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}$$
$$<\sum_{n=1}^{n_0}\frac{1}{2^n}\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}$$
$$=\epsilon.$$
The same proof with obvious modifications also shows that if $\{f_n\}$ is Cauchy in each $C(K)$, with $K$ compact in $\Omega$, then it is Cauchy in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$. This proves the Lemma. $\square$

The following is known as Montel's Theorem¹.

Theorem 1.1.3 (Montel's Theorem). Let $\Omega$ be a region and $\mathscr{F}$ a non-empty subset of $\mathscr{H}(\Omega)$. The following are equivalent:
(a) $\mathscr{F}$ is locally bounded.
(b) $\mathscr{F}$ is locally bounded and uniformly equicontinuous on compact subsets of $\Omega$.
(c) Every sequence in $\mathscr{F}$ has a subsequence which converges uniformly on compact sets.
(d) Every sequence in $\mathscr{F}$ has a subsequence which converges in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$.
(e) The closure $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ of $\mathscr{F}$ in $(\mathscr{H}(\Omega),d)$ is compact.

Proof. We have already proven (a)⇒(b). Lemma 1.1.2 yields (c)⇔(d)⇔(e).

We will now prove (b)⇒(c). For $K$ a compact subset of $\Omega$ let us write $\mathscr{F}|_K$ for the collection $\{f|_K\}_{f\in\mathscr{F}}$. Let $K$ be a compact subset of $\Omega$. Suppose (b) is true. According to Arzela-Ascoli this is equivalent to saying $\mathscr{F}|_K$ is relatively compact in $(C(K),\|\cdot\|_K)$, i.e., the closure of $\mathscr{F}|_K$ in $C(K)$ is compact. It follows that every sequence in $\mathscr{F}$ has a subsequence (depending upon the compact set $K$) which converges uniformly on $K$. Let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence in $\mathscr{F}$. Let $\{K_l\}_{l=1}^\infty$ be the exhaustion of $\Omega$ by compact subsets that we introduced earlier (to define the metric $d$). Let $\{g_{n,1}\}$ be a subsequence of $\{f_n\}$ such that $\{g_{n,1}\}$ converges uniformly on $K_1$. For $j\ge 1$, we recursively define $\{g_{n,j+1}\}$ to be a subsequence of $\{g_{n,j}\}$ such that $\{g_{n,j+1}\}$ converges uniformly on $K_{j+1}$. Set $f_{n_k}=g_{k,k}$. One checks easily that $\{f_{n_k}\}$ is a subsequence of $\{f_n\}$ which converges uniformly on each $K_j$, whence on each compact subset of $\Omega$. Thus (c) is true.

Finally we show that (c)⇒(a). Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ satisfies (c) and let $K$ be a compact subset of $\Omega$. The condition (c) is equivalent to saying that the closure of $\mathscr{F}|_K$ in $(C(K),\|\cdot\|_K)$ is compact. This means $\mathscr{F}|_K$ is bounded (in fact totally bounded) in $(C(K),\|\cdot\|_K)$, and hence there exists $M_K<\infty$ such that $\|f\|_K<M_K$ for every $f\in\mathscr{F}$. In other words $\mathscr{F}$ satisfies (a). $\square$

¹More precisely (a)⇔(c) is what is traditionally known as Montel's Theorem.

routes.title: diagonal compactness on compact subsets
routes.proofSketch: On each compact K⊂Ω, local boundedness on a slightly larger compact and Cauchy’s integral formula uniformly bound derivatives, hence give equicontinuity. Arzelà–Ascoli gives a uniformly convergent subsequence on K; diagonalize over an exhaustion K₁⊂K₂⊂… to get local uniform convergence, and the limit is holomorphic by the theorem on locally uniform limits.

routes.title: equicontinuity and holomorphic limit arguments
routes.proofSketch: Use equicontinuity only to upgrade pointwise convergence. Cauchy's estimate bounds |f′| by M/r on D(a,r) whenever |f|≤M on D(a,2r), so a locally bounded family is locally equi-Lipschitz. routes.title: Fourier-slice theorem and Fourier inversion
routes.proofSketch: Take the one-dimensional Fourier transform in the offset variable: the Fourier-slice theorem gives ℱ_t(Rf)(θ,σ)=f̂(σθ). Vanishing Radon data implies f̂ vanishes on every ray, hence everywhere; Fourier inversion gives f=0.

routes.title: filtered back-projection
routes.proofSketch: Back-project the line data Rf and apply the ramp filter |ξ| in Fourier space. The Fourier-slice theorem says each projection supplies the restriction of f̂ to a radial line; the ramp-corrected back-projection has Fourier transform a nonzero constant times f̂, so inversion recovers f and injectivity follows.

routes.title: moments/polynomial-density arguments. A MathOverflow answer links a lecture-note survey of proofs
routes.proofSketch: If Rf=0, every directional moment ∫t^m Rf(θ,t)dt equals ∫(x·θ)^m f(x)dx=0. As θ varies, these are all homogeneous moments, so every polynomial pairs to zero with f. Polynomials are dense on a compact set containing supp f; continuity then forces f=0.

routes.title: Construct a potential by path integration

routes.title: differential forms/closed-versus-exact 1-forms on simply connected sets
routes.proofSketch: The 1-form ω is path-independent on a simply connected domain iff all closed-loop integrals vanish. By Stokes, dω=0 makes integrals invariant under homotopy; simple connectedness contracts loops, so define φ(x)=∫_{x₀}^xω and differentiate to obtain dφ=ω. Conversely exact forms integrate to endpoint differences.

entries.description: Successive approximations/contraction mapping; Peano polygonal approximations plus equicontinuity for existence; differential inequalities/Gronwall for uniqueness.

routes.title: Successive approximations/contraction mapping
routes.proofSketch: Rewrite y′=F(t,y), y(t₀)=y₀ as y(t)=y₀+∫_{t₀}^tF(s,y(s))ds. On a cylinder |t−t₀|≤a, |y−y₀|≤b where F is continuous, |F|≤M and F is L-Lipschitz in y, the integral operator maps C([t₀−h,t₀+h], B̄_b(y₀)) into itself for h≤min(a,b/M), and is a contraction for h<1/L (or in the weighted norm sup e^{−2L|t−t₀|}|u| for the full h). Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique solution on that interval, and the Picard iterates converge uniformly to it.

routes.title: Peano polygonal approximations plus equicontinuity for existence
routes.proofSketch: Existence needs only continuity of F. On the cylinder with |F|≤M, build Euler polygons y_k with step 1/k on [t₀,t₀+h], h=min(a,b/M). They are uniformly bounded and M-Lipschitz, so Arzelà–Ascoli gives a uniformly convergent subsequence. Uniform continuity of F lets one pass to the limit in y_k(t)=y₀+∫F(s,y_k(s))ds+o(1), which yields a solution; the same works backward in time. This route gives existence without uniqueness (compare y′=√|y|), so the Lipschitz hypothesis enters only through a separate uniqueness step.

routes.title: differential inequalities/Gronwall for uniqueness
routes.proofSketch: Uniqueness: let y,z solve the problem on a common interval J∋t₀, and let K be a compact subinterval on which both stay in a set where F is L-Lipschitz in y. Then u=|y−z| satisfies u(t)≤L|∫_{t₀}^t u|, and Gronwall's inequality gives u≡0 on K. Local Lipschitz continuity makes the set {y=z} open (apply the argument near any coincidence point) and continuity makes it closed, so y=z on all of J by connectedness. Paired with an existence step (Picard iteration or Peano), this gives the local existence-and-uniqueness theorem.

routes.title: Hölder duality and integration

routes.title: convexity/Young's inequality
routes.proofSketch: Assume a=‖f‖_p and b=‖g‖_p are positive (otherwise the claim is trivial) and normalize F=f/a, G=g/b. Then f+g=(a+b)(λF+(1−λ)G) with λ=a/(a+b). Convexity of t↦|t|^p for p≥1 gives |λF+(1−λ)G|^p≤λ|F|^p+(1−λ)|G|^p pointwise. Integrating, ∫|λF+(1−λ)G|^p≤λ+(1−λ)=1, so ‖f+g‖_p≤a+b. Young's inequality xy≤x^p/p+y^q/q is the same convexity (weighted AM–GM) and is what underlies Hölder in the other route.

routes.title: interpolate from the triangle inequality for simple functions and pass by approximation. State the measure-space and p-range assumptions
routes.proofSketch: First take simple functions s,t on a common finite measurable partition E_1,…,E_N: then ‖s+t‖_p=(Σμ(E_j)|s_j+t_j|^p)^{1/p} is a weighted ℓ^p norm on ℝ^N, where Minkowski is the finite-sum inequality. For general f,g choose simple 0≤s_n↑|f| and 0≤t_n↑|g|; then ‖s_n+t_n‖_p≤‖s_n‖_p+‖t_n‖_p≤‖f‖_p+‖g‖_p, and monotone convergence gives ‖|f|+|g|‖_p≤‖f‖_p+‖g‖_p, which dominates ‖f+g‖_p. The finite-dimensional inequality still needs its own proof (convexity or Hölder), so this route reduces the problem rather than replacing the argument.

routes.title: Positive-functional construction by outer measure
routes.proofSketch: For positive L:C(K)→R define μ(U)=sup{L(f):0≤f≤1, supp f⊂U}; use partitions of unity to prove finite additivity on disjoint opens and outer regular extension to a Borel measure. Approximation of continuous f by level-set simple functions gives L(f)=∫f dμ; positivity ensures uniqueness.

routes.title: Daniell integral approach
routes.proofSketch: Treat L as a Daniell integral on the vector lattice C(K). Dini's theorem makes it continuous from below along decreasing sequences: if f_n↓0 pointwise on compact K then f_n→0 uniformly, so L(f_n)→0. Daniell's extension then gives an integral on a larger class of functions (monotone limits, then upper and lower integrals) and hence a measure on the σ-algebra it generates with L(f)=∫f dμ; since 1∈C(K), the measure is finite. Caveat: this first produces a Baire measure, and regularity on all Borel sets for non-metrizable K needs a further extension argument.

routes.title: duality/measure representation from continuous functions. State the exact real/complex and locally compact variants
routes.proofSketch: Extend L to lower semicontinuous h≥0 by L(h)=sup{L(f): f∈C(K), 0≤f≤h}; Dini's theorem gives additivity and continuity along increasing nets. Set μ*(A)=inf{L(1_U): U open, U⊇A}, an outer measure, and show via Carathéodory's criterion that Borel sets are measurable and that μ is regular. Approximating f∈C(K) uniformly by finite sums of scaled indicators of open level sets gives L(f)=∫f dμ. This is the Bourbaki-style route through semicontinuous functions; ‖L‖=L(1) for positive L, so the measure is finite.

entries.name: Prokhorov's theorem (tightness and relative compactness of probability measures on Polish spaces)
entries.description: Compactness via finite partitions and diagonal subsequences; metric/weak-convergence tightness argument; transport through distribution functions in R.

routes.title: Compactness via finite partitions and diagonal subsequences
routes.proofSketch: Given a tight family, pick compacts $K_1\subset K_2\subset\dots$ with $P_n(K_i)>1-i^{-1}$ for all $n$. The union $K_\infty$ is separable, so there is a countable class of open sets whose closures refine any open neighbourhood; form the countable class $\mathcal H$ of finite unions of $\bar A\cap K_i$. A diagonal argument gives a subsequence along which $\alpha(H)=\lim P_{n'}(H)$ exists for every $H\in\mathcal H$. Define $\beta(G)=\sup_{H\subset G}\alpha(H)$ on open sets and $\gamma(M)=\inf_{G\supset M}\beta(G)$. Seven steps show $\gamma$ is an outer measure for which closed sets are measurable and whose restriction $P$ is a probability measure (mass 1 because $K_i\in\mathcal H$), with $P(G)=\beta(G)\le\liminf P_{n'}(G)$ for open $G$, hence weak convergence.

routes.title: metric/weak-convergence tightness argument
routes.proofSketch: For the converse (relative compactness implies tightness on a complete separable metric space): first show that for open sets $G_n\uparrow S$ and $\epsilon>0$ some $n$ has $P(G_n)>1-\epsilon$ for all $P$ in the family, otherwise a weakly convergent subsequence $P_{n'}\Rightarrow Q$ would give $Q(G_n)\le\liminf P_{n'}(G_n)\le1-\epsilon$ for all $n$, impossible. Cover $S$ by balls of radius $1/k$, choose finitely many with mass $>1-\epsilon2^{-k}$, and take the closure of the totally bounded intersection over $k$: it is compact by completeness and has mass $>1-\epsilon$.

routes.title: transport through distribution functions in R
routes.proofSketch: Helly selection on the line: enumerate the rationals and by diagonalisation extract a subsequence of distribution functions converging at every rational to some $G$; set $G(x)=\inf\{G(q):q>x\}$, which is right-continuous and nondecreasing, and convergence at continuity points follows from convergence at rationals. Tightness ($\limsup_n 1-F_n(M_\epsilon)+F_n(-M_\epsilon)\le\epsilon$) is exactly the condition that every subsequential limit is a probability distribution function, ruling out escape of mass; this last equivalence is only cited, not proved, in the source.

entries.name: Radon–Nikodym theorem
entries.description: Conditional-expectation/Hilbert-space proof for finite measures; supremum construction and Hahn decomposition; maximal-function approximation.

routes.title: Conditional-expectation/Hilbert-space proof for finite measures
routes.proofSketch: For finite $\mu$ and finite positive $\lambda$, put $\phi=\lambda+\mu$. The functional $f\mapsto\lambda(f)$ is bounded on $L^2(\phi)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, so Riesz-Frechet gives $g$ with $\lambda(f)=\phi(fg)$. Testing on indicators and using Lemma 4.4 (averages) gives $0\le g\le1$ a.e. The set $B=\{g=1\}$ is $\mu$-null, which splits $\lambda=\lambda_a+\lambda_s$ with $\lambda_s\perp\mu$. Rewriting as $\lambda((1-g)f)=\mu(fg)$ and testing with $f=1_{A\cap E}(1+g+\dots+g^{n-1})$, dominated and monotone convergence give $\lambda_a(E)=\mu(1_Eh)$ with $h=1_Ag/(1-g)$. The $\sigma$-finite case is by partition, then signed and complex by decomposition.

routes.title: product-measure construction
routes.proofSketch: Take σ-finite (X,μ) and (Y,ν). Define μ×ν on measurable rectangles by μ(A)ν(B) and extend it by Carathéodory to the product σ-algebra. A monotone-class (π–λ) argument shows that for every measurable E the sections E_x are measurable and x↦ν(E_x) is measurable, and that E↦∫ν(E_x)dμ(x) and E↦∫μ(E^y)dν(y) are measures agreeing with μ×ν on rectangles; σ-finiteness and uniqueness of extension from a π-system make them equal to μ×ν. Passing from indicators to nonnegative simple functions and then to monotone limits gives Tonelli, and Fubini follows from the positive and negative parts.

routes.title: iterated-integration/measure regularity argument
routes.proofSketch: Specialize to Lebesgue measure on ℝ^{m+n}, where regularity can replace the π–λ argument. An open set U is a countable disjoint union of half-open dyadic boxes, so |U|=∫|U_x|dx by countable additivity and monotone convergence. Decreasing limits of open sets of finite measure give G_δ sets (dominated convergence), and every null set sits inside a null G_δ set, so almost every section of a null set is null. Outer regularity then covers all Lebesgue-measurable E, with almost every section measurable, and simple-function approximation gives Tonelli and Fubini for the completed measure.

routes.title: Gaussian/approximate-identity regularization
routes.proofSketch: For f,f̂∈L¹ and ε>0, Fubini and the self-dual Gaussian transform give ∫f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}e^{−πε²ξ²}dξ=(f∗G_ε)(x), where G_ε(t)=ε^{−1}e^{−πt²/ε²} is an approximate identity. As ε→0 the left side tends to ∫f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}dξ by dominated convergence (f̂∈L¹), while the right side tends to f(x) at each continuity point of f because G_ε concentrates at 0 and f∈L¹. Hence the inversion formula holds at continuity points.

routes.title: inversion via contour or Fourier integrals
routes.proofSketch: Truncate the inverse integral: S_R(x)=∫_{−R}^{R}f̂(ξ)e^{2πixξ}dξ=∫f(y)sin(2πR(x−y))/(π(x−y))dy, by Fubini and direct integration of the exponential. Since f̂∈L¹, S_R(x) converges as R→∞ to the full inverse integral. Averaging S_ρ over ρ∈[0,R] replaces the Dirichlet kernel by the Fejér kernel sin²(πRt)/(π²Rt²), a positive approximate identity (its total mass, ∫sin²u/u²du=π, can be computed by contour integration), so the averages tend to f(x) at continuity points of f. A convergent family and its Cesàro averages have the same limit, so the inverse integral equals f(x).

entries.name: Plancherel theorem
entries.description: Parseval identity on a dense class plus completion; Gaussian regularization; unitary representation of translations/Fourier transform.

routes.title: Parseval identity on a dense class plus completion
routes.proofSketch: On the Schwartz class 𝒮 the transform maps 𝒮 to itself, and the multiplication formula ∫f̂g=∫fĝ together with inversion on 𝒮 gives ⟨f̂,ĝ⟩=⟨f,g⟩, so ‖f̂‖₂=‖f‖₂. Since 𝒮 is dense in L², the transform extends uniquely to a linear isometry of L². Its range is closed and contains 𝒮, hence is all of L², so the extension is unitary; on L¹∩L² it agrees with the integral formula by approximation.

routes.title: Gaussian regularization
routes.proofSketch: Prove the isometry on L¹∩L² directly with Gaussian damping, without using inversion. For f∈L¹∩L², Fubini gives ∫|f̂(ξ)|²e^{−πεξ²}dξ=∫∫f(x)\overline{f(y)}ε^{−1/2}e^{−π(x−y)²/ε}dx dy=⟨f,f∗G_ε⟩, with G_ε a Gaussian approximate identity. Let ε↓0: the left side increases to ‖f̂‖₂² by monotone convergence and the right side tends to ‖f‖₂² because f∗G_ε→f in L². Hence the transform is isometric on L¹∩L², extends by density to L², and the identity F²f(x)=f(−x) on 𝒮 shows the extension is onto.

routes.title: unitary representation of translations/Fourier transform
routes.proofSketch: Translations τ_a on L²(ℝ) form a strongly continuous unitary group of commuting operators. By Stone's theorem and the spectral theorem for commuting unitaries (SNAG), this action is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by e^{−2πiaξ} on L²(ℝ̂,ν) for a spectral measure ν on the dual line, and the unitary intertwiner plays the role of the Fourier transform. The remaining work is to identify ν with Lebesgue measure and to show multiplicity one, for instance by testing against the Gaussian; this sketch does not carry that out.

entries.name: Isoperimetric inequality in the plane
entries.description: Variational/calculus of variations; Fourier-series proof for closed curves; Brunn–Minkowski and convex-geometric argument; symmetrization.

routes.title: Variational/calculus of variations
routes.proofSketch: Parametrize a smooth simple closed curve by arclength with length L and enclosed area A. A maximizing curve exists after compactness/regularization; first variation of A−λL shows its curvature is constant, hence the optimizer is a circle. Its area is L²/(4π), giving A≤L²/(4π). The existence and regularity step is essential and is not supplied by the Euler–Lagrange calculation alone.

routes.title: Brunn–Minkowski and convex-geometric argument
routes.proofSketch: For a planar measurable set E, apply Brunn–Minkowski to E and a small disk εB: |E+εB|^{1/2}≥|E|^{1/2}+ε√π. Approximation extends the result to finite-perimeter sets.

routes.title: symmetrization
routes.proofSketch: Repeatedly Steiner-symmetrize a bounded region: each symmetrization preserves area and does not increase perimeter. A compactness argument gives a limit invariant under every direction of symmetrization, hence a disk; lower semicontinuity of perimeter shows the disk has no larger perimeter than the original region. This proves Per(E)≥2√(π|E|), with equality only for disks up to null sets.

entries.name: Brunn–Minkowski inequality
entries.description: Induction and slicing; transport-map/Jacobian argument; Prékopa–Leindler functional inequality.

routes.title: Induction and slicing
routes.proofSketch: Hadwiger–Ohmann slicing. For boxes with sides a_i, b_i the inequality is AM–GM applied to ∏a_i/(a_i+b_i) and ∏b_i/(a_i+b_i). For finite unions of boxes, induct on the total number of boxes: if A has at least two boxes, a coordinate hyperplane separates two of them; cut A into A⁺ and A⁻ with fewer boxes, translate B so the same hyperplane splits B in the same volume ratio, apply induction to the pairs (A^±,B^±) and add. Approximate compact sets from outside by decreasing finite unions of boxes and pass to the limit; measurable sets follow by inner approximation with compact sets.

routes.title: transport-map/Jacobian argument
routes.proofSketch: Knothe–Rosenblatt transport. For compact A,B of positive volume let T:A→B be the triangular monotone map pushing the normalized uniform measure on A to that on B; its Jacobian determinant is constant, equal to |B|/|A|, and since DT is triangular with nonnegative diagonal entries t_1,…,t_n, we have ∏t_i=|B|/|A|. The map x↦x+T(x) is injective on A with image inside A+B and Jacobian ∏(1+t_i)≥(1+(∏t_i)^{1/n})^n by AM–GM. Hence |A+B|≥|A|(1+(|B|/|A|)^{1/n})^n=(|A|^{1/n}+|B|^{1/n})^n. The lack of smoothness of T is handled by approximation.

routes.title: Prékopa–Leindler functional inequality
routes.proofSketch: Prékopa–Leindler: if h((1−λ)x+λy)≥f(x)^{1−λ}g(y)^λ then ∫h≥(∫f)^{1−λ}(∫g)^λ (proved by induction on dimension from the one-dimensional case by monotone rearrangement). Apply it with f=1_A, g=1_B, h=1_{(1−λ)A+λB} to get |(1−λ)A+λB|≥|A|^{1−λ}|B|^λ. Normalize A′=A/α and B′=B/β with α=|A|^{1/n}, β=|B|^{1/n}, so |A′|=|B′|=1, and take λ=β/(α+β): then (1−λ)A′+λB′=(A+B)/(α+β), giving |A+B|≥(α+β)ⁿ.

routes.title: Affine-dependence coefficient elimination
routes.proofSketch: If x=∑_{i=1}^mλ_i x_i is a convex combination with m>d+1, the augmented vectors (x_i,1) are linearly dependent: choose a nonzero relation ∑a_i x_i=0, ∑a_i=0. Vary λ_i→λ_i−t a_i until one coefficient hits zero while all remain nonnegative; repeat until at most d+1 remain.

routes.title: linear-programming basic feasible solutions
routes.proofSketch: Cast the representation as a linear program: find λ≥0 with Σλ_i x_i=x and Σλ_i=1, which has d+1 equality constraints in the variables λ_1,…,λ_m. The feasible set is nonempty (x∈conv) and lies in the nonnegative orthant, so it is a pointed polyhedron and has a vertex. A vertex is a basic feasible solution, whose support has linearly independent constraint columns, hence at most d+1 elements.

routes.title: Radon's theorem plus induction
routes.proofSketch: Assume every d+1 of a finite family of convex sets intersect. Induct on family size; apply Radon’s theorem to points x_i chosen from intersections omitting C_i. A Radon partition yields a point lying in every C_i, contradiction otherwise. The finite-family theorem follows; topological nerve versions require additional hypotheses such as contractibility.

routes.title: minimal subfamily and affine dependence
routes.proofSketch: Take a minimal subfamily C_1,…,C_k with empty intersection. By hypothesis k≥d+2, and by minimality each ∩_{j≠i}C_j is nonempty, so pick x_i in it. These k≥d+2 points of ℝ^d are affinely dependent: Σa_ix_i=0, Σa_i=0, not all a_i zero. Split the indices into P={a_i>0} and N={a_i<0}; the point p=Σ_P a_ix_i/Σ_P a_i=Σ_N(−a_i)x_i/Σ_N(−a_i) lies in both convex hulls. For each j, either j∉P or j∉N, so all x_i of that class lie in C_j and p∈C_j by convexity. Thus p∈∩C_j, a contradiction. This inlines Radon's theorem instead of inducting on the family size.

routes.title: nerve/topological methods for generalizations
routes.proofSketch: Nerve route. In a finite family of convex sets every nonempty intersection is contractible, so the nerve N is homotopy equivalent to the union (nerve lemma), and likewise for every subfamily. A union of compact convex sets in ℝ^d has vanishing reduced homology in degrees ≥d (Alexander duality), so every induced subcomplex of N does too (the d-Leray property). If every d+1 sets meet, N has a complete d-skeleton. If N were not a full simplex, a minimal non-face σ with |σ|=k+1≥d+2 would give the induced subcomplex ∂Δ^k, which has H̃_{k−1}≠0 with k−1≥d, contradicting the Leray bound. This is the route that generalizes to topological, colorful and fractional Helly theorems.

routes.title: Affine dependence and sign partition
routes.proofSketch: For d+2 points x_i∈R^d, find a nonzero affine dependence Σa_ix_i=0 and Σa_i=0. Positive and negative coefficients both occur; normalize their absolute sums to 1. The two convex combinations then agree, so the convex hulls of the positive- and negative-coefficient point sets intersect.
