routes.title: convex-hull separation
routes.proofSketch: Suppose, for contradiction, every partition of d+2 points into two parts has disjoint convex hulls. Strict separation then supplies a hyperplane separating each pair of hulls. The sign patterns of these separating affine functionals cannot realize all required dichotomies of d+2 points in R^d (affine halfspaces have VC dimension d+1); therefore some partition has intersecting hulls. This is a separation-theorem proof of Radon, but it is less elementary and its separation/dimension argument must be stated fully.

entries.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
entries.description: Augmenting paths/residual graph; linear-programming duality; circulation/polyhedral integrality.

routes.title: Augmenting paths/residual graph
routes.proofSketch: Run augmenting paths until none remains. Let S be vertices reachable from source in residual graph. Every edge S→Sᶜ is saturated and every edge Sᶜ→S carries zero flow, so flow value equals cut capacity. Weak duality bounds any flow by every cut, proving optimality; integer capacities give an integral max flow.

routes.title: linear-programming duality
routes.proofSketch: Write max flow as a linear program in the arc flows x_e with 0≤x_e≤c_e and conservation at inner vertices. Its dual assigns potentials p_v with p_t−p_s≥1 and arc variables y_{uv}≥max(0,p_v−p_u), minimizing Σc_ey_e. Strong LP duality equates the two optima. The constraint matrix is a network matrix, hence totally unimodular, so the dual has an optimal solution that is integral with potentials in {0,1} after shifting p_s=0; the set S={v: p_v=0} then defines an s–t cut whose capacity equals the dual value.

routes.title: circulation/polyhedral integrality
routes.proofSketch: Add a return arc t→s of unbounded capacity: flows of value k correspond to circulations carrying k on this arc. By Hoffman's circulation theorem (itself a consequence of Farkas' lemma), a feasible circulation with lower bound k on the return arc exists iff every vertex set S has (lower bounds into S) ≤ (upper bounds out of S); testing sets with s∈S, t∉S says exactly that every s–t cut has capacity ≥k. The polyhedron of circulations has a totally unimodular constraint matrix, so integer capacities give an integral maximum flow.

routes.title: Laplacian cofactor and determinant expansion
routes.proofSketch: Delete one row and column of the graph Laplacian L. By Cauchy–Binet, det(L̂) sums squared determinants of incidence submatrices indexed by edge sets of size n−1. Such determinant is ±1 exactly for a spanning tree and 0 otherwise, so the cofactor counts spanning trees.

routes.title: electrical-network spanning-tree identity
routes.proofSketch: Kirchhoff's route: regard G as a network of unit resistors. Potentials φ for a unit current from u to v solve Lφ=e_u−e_v, and Cramer's rule gives the effective resistance R_{uv}=det L̂_{(u,v)}/det L̂_{(u)}, with one or two rows and columns deleted. The deletion–contraction recursion τ(G)=τ(G−e)+τ(G/e) for spanning-tree counts is matched by the matrix determinant lemma det(M+bbᵀ)=det M+bᵀadj(M)b applied to L̂(G)=L̂(G−e)+bbᵀ, whose second term is det L̂(G/e). Induction on edges (allowing disconnected graphs, where both sides vanish) then gives det L̂=τ(G).

routes.title: all-minors/forest counting
routes.proofSketch: Use Chaiken's all-minors extension. Write L=NNᵀ with N an oriented vertex–edge incidence matrix. By Cauchy–Binet, for vertex sets I,J of equal size, det L[Iᶜ,Jᶜ]=Σ_F det N[Iᶜ,F]·det N[Jᶜ,F] over edge sets F of size n−|I|. Each minor of N is ±1 exactly when F is a forest in which every component contains exactly one vertex of the deleted set, and 0 otherwise. For I=J the signs square away, so the principal minor counts spanning forests rooted at I; for |I|=1 this is the matrix-tree theorem.

entries.name: Hall's marriage theorem, infinite-set version
entries.description: Finite-subset compactness/König lemma for countable locally finite cases; maximal matching and augmenting paths; choice/Zorn argument under stated cardinal assumptions.

routes.title: Finite-subset compactness/König lemma for countable locally finite cases
routes.proofSketch: Let (A_i)_{i∈I} be finite sets satisfying Hall's condition on every finite subfamily. For finite F⊂I let X_F⊂∏A_i be the set of choice functions injective on F: X_F is nonempty by the finite Hall theorem and closed in the product of finite discrete spaces. Since X_F∩X_G⊇X_{F∪G}, the family has the finite intersection property, and Tychonoff compactness gives a point of ∩X_F, an injective choice function. For countable families, König's lemma or diagonal extraction replaces Tychonoff. Finiteness of each A_i is essential.

routes.title: maximal matching and augmenting paths
routes.proofSketch: Finite Hall by augmenting paths: take a maximum matching M and suppose some set a is unmatched. Let X be the sets reachable from a by alternating paths. If no augmenting path exists, every neighbour of X is matched to a set of X other than a, so |N(X)|=|X|−1, violating Hall's condition; hence M saturates every set. This proves only the finite theorem; passing to infinite families needs compactness or choice, which this route does not supply.

routes.title: choice/Zorn argument under stated cardinal assumptions
routes.proofSketch: Zorn on shrinking the sets, assuming each A_i is finite. Order the families (A′_i)_{i∈I} with A′_i⊆A_i satisfying Hall's condition by reverse inclusion. A chain has a lower bound (intersect along the chain): each finite subfamily involves finitely many finite sets, on which the chain stabilizes, so Hall's condition survives. A minimal family has every |A′_i|=1: if a≠b lie in A′_i, deleting either would violate Hall, giving two tight subfamilies, and the standard Halmos–Vaughan counting argument on their union and intersection yields a contradiction. The singletons then form an SDR. Without finiteness of the A_i this fails.

routes.title: Minimal-bad-sequence proof
routes.proofSketch: Assume a bad sequence of finite trees, and choose lexicographically a minimal bad sequence (each term has minimal size among choices that can extend the prefix). Replace infinitely many terms by their proper rooted subtrees; the subsequence of roots’ child forests is well-quasi-ordered by induction/product closure, yielding an earlier tree embedding into a later one, contradiction. Graph-minor theorem is much deeper; tree wqo alone is not its proof.

routes.title: tree embedding/wqo argument
routes.proofSketch: Prove Kruskal's tree theorem via Higman's lemma: finite words over a well-quasi-order are well-quasi-ordered by subsequence embedding. View a rooted tree as a root followed by the finite word of its subtrees. In a minimal bad sequence of trees, the set of proper subtrees that occur is well-quasi-ordered by minimality, so by Higman the words of subtrees are well-quasi-ordered; this yields i<j with T_i embeddable in T_j. Tree embedding is a special case of the minor relation, so this gives well-quasi-order for finite forests under minors, which is much weaker than the graph-minor theorem.

routes.title: algebraic proof via graph-minor structure (advanced)
routes.proofSketch: The statement for arbitrary finite graphs is the Robertson–Seymour graph-minor theorem, whose proof is structural rather than algebraic. Outline: take a minimal bad sequence G_1,G_2,…; since G_1 is not a minor of any later G_j, all G_j with j≥2 exclude G_1 as a minor. The graph-minor structure theorem describes such graphs as clique-sums of pieces that are nearly embeddable in a surface of bounded genus, with a bounded number of apices and vortices of bounded width. Well-quasi-order for these pieces, via tree decompositions and a labelled-minor strengthening, then yields a contradiction (Graph Minors XX). Only this outline is given; the full argument spans many long papers.

routes.title: Homology/degree
routes.proofSketch: Assume a continuous injection f:U⊂R^n→R^n has image not open at f(x). Local homology at x is H_n(U,U\{x})≅Z, while at a boundary point of f(U) the corresponding local homology in the target complement vanishes; the homeomorphism U≅f(U) induced by injectivity contradicts this. This uses local compactness/degree or homology machinery.

routes.title: local homology and orientation
routes.proofSketch: Local-degree route. For x∈U choose a closed ball B⊂U around x; K=f(B) is homeomorphic to a ball, so its complement in Sⁿ is acyclic (an Alexander-duality lemma, quoted rather than reproved). This identifies the local homology H_n(B,B∖x)≅ℤ with H_n(ℝⁿ,ℝⁿ∖f(x))≅ℤ, so f has local degree ±1 at x. Combining this with the acyclicity shows that f(x) cannot be a boundary point of f(B); the details of that step are the standard Alexander-duality argument and are not reproduced here. Hence f(U) is open, and f is an open injective map, so a homeomorphism onto its image. The sign of the local degree is locally constant.

routes.title: contradiction using compactness and boundary/sphere separation
routes.proofSketch: Jordan–Brouwer route. Fix a closed ball B⊂U and set Σ=f(∂B)≅S^{n−1}. By Jordan–Brouwer separation ℝⁿ∖Σ has exactly two components, a bounded C_in and an unbounded C_out. The compact set f(B) is homeomorphic to a ball, so it does not separate ℝⁿ: ℝⁿ∖f(B) is connected, unbounded and lies in ℝⁿ∖Σ, hence lies in C_out. Therefore C_in⊆f(B)∖Σ=f(int B). Conversely f(int B) is connected and disjoint from Σ, so it lies in one component, which must be C_in since C_in⊆f(int B). Thus f(int B)=C_in is open. As balls around any point work, f is an open map and so a homeomorphism onto f(U).

entries.name: Euler characteristic of a finite chain complex equals alternating homology dimension
entries.description: Rank-nullity cancellations; split each chain group into boundaries, homology representatives, and complements; homological algebra exact-sequence argument.

routes.title: Rank-nullity cancellations
routes.proofSketch: Over a chain complex of vector spaces, write $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$ and $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$. Since $H_k=Z_k/B_k$ one has $\dim Z_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k$. Because $\partial^2=0$, $C_k/Z_k\cong B_{k-1}$, so $\dim C_k=\dim Z_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Combining, $\dim C_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Multiply by $(-1)^k$ and sum over $k$; the boundary terms telescope, leaving $\sum(-1)^k\dim C_k=\sum(-1)^k\dim H_k$.

routes.title: homological algebra exact-sequence argument
routes.proofSketch: For a chain complex of finitely generated abelian groups with cycles $Z_n$, boundaries $B_n$ and homology $H_n=Z_n/B_n$ there are short exact sequences $0\to Z_n\to C_n\to B_{n-1}\to 0$ and $0\to B_n\to Z_n\to H_n\to 0$. Additivity of rank on short exact sequences gives $\operatorname{rank}C_n=\operatorname{rank}Z_n+\operatorname{rank}B_{n-1}$ and $\operatorname{rank}Z_n=\operatorname{rank}B_n+\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Substitute, multiply by $(-1)^n$ and sum: boundary ranks cancel, giving $\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}C_n=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Applied to cellular chains this gives $\chi(X)=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X)$.

routes.title: Iterative decomposition into alternating chains
routes.proofSketch: Given injections f:A→B and g:B→A, let A₀=A\g(B), A_{n+1}=g(f(A_n)), and C=⋃A_n. Map a∈C by f(a), and a∉C by the unique inverse g^{-1}(a). The pieces are disjoint and cover, and this piecewise map is a bijection A→B.

routes.title: maximal invariant subset construction
routes.proofSketch: Look for a maximal subset of A that f carries compatibly. Call X⊆A admissible if g(B∖f(X))∩X=∅, i.e. no point of X is the g-image of an element outside f(X). Admissible sets are closed under arbitrary unions, so there is a largest one, X₀. Maximality forces X₀=A∖g(B∖f(X₀)): otherwise a point outside both could be added to X₀. Define h=f on X₀ and h=g^{−1} on A∖X₀=g(B∖f(X₀)). Then h is injective and its image is f(X₀)∪(B∖f(X₀))=B.

routes.title: Boolean-algebra/fixed-point formulation
routes.proofSketch: View the construction as a fixed point. Φ(X)=A∖g(B∖f(X)) is monotone on the complete lattice 𝒫(A), so by the Knaster–Tarski theorem it has a fixed point X₀=Φ(X₀) (its greatest fixed point is the maximal admissible set of the previous route). The identity A∖X₀=g(B∖f(X₀)) is Banach's decomposition lemma: A splits as X₀⊔g(B′) and B as f(X₀)⊔B′ with B′=B∖f(X₀). Gluing f on X₀ with g^{−1} on g(B′) gives the bijection. The same argument runs in complete Boolean algebras (the Sikorski–Tarski versions), which is the form used for generalizations.

routes.title: Henkin term-model construction
routes.proofSketch: For a consistent theory, extend the language with countably many fresh constants and Henkin witness axioms, preserving consistency, then complete it by deciding each sentence. The quotient of closed terms by provable equality is a model; induction on formulas verifies the truth lemma, so every consistent sentence has a model and semantic consequence implies provability.

routes.title: semantic tableaux
routes.proofSketch: Systematic tableaux. Enlarge the language by countably many fresh constants and fix a fair order of rule applications, so every non-literal formula on a branch is eventually expanded and every universal formula is instantiated at every closed term. If the tableau for Σ∪{¬φ} stays open, a finished or infinite open branch is a Hintikka set, and its closed-term model satisfies all its formulas by induction on complexity. Hence Σ∪{¬φ} has a model; contrapositively, if Σ⊨φ every systematic tableau closes, and a closed tableau converts into a proof.

routes.title: sequent-calculus cut-elimination route
routes.proofSketch: Gentzen-style route in the cut-free sequent calculus LK. Given Γ⇒Δ, search for a proof bottom-up, applying every rule systematically (instantiating ∀-left and ∃-right at all terms, and using fresh constants for the eigenvariable rules). If every branch closes, the search yields a cut-free proof; otherwise an open branch defines a countermodel, with its atoms true on the left and false on the right (Schütte's semantic argument). Cut elimination (Gentzen's Hauptsatz) shows cut-free LK is no weaker than LK with cut, so completeness transfers to the usual formulations of provability.

routes.title: Gödel sentence/diagonalization
routes.proofSketch: Fix a Gödel numbering and an effectively axiomatized theory T interpreting enough arithmetic (Robinson's Q) that recursive relations, in particular the proof predicate Prf_T(y,x), are representable. The diagonal lemma gives a sentence G with T⊢G↔¬∃y Prf_T(y,⌜G⌝), 'I am not provable'. If T⊢G, a proof exists, so T⊢∃y Prf_T(y,⌜G⌝) and hence T⊢¬G: T is inconsistent. So for consistent T, G is unprovable. If T⊢¬G, T proves that G has a proof, while no actual proof exists; ω-consistency forbids this. Hence G is independent of T. (Gödel's argument needs ω-consistency for the second half; Rosser removes it.)

routes.title: Rosser sentence removing ω-consistency
routes.proofSketch: Rosser's trick: apply the diagonal lemma to 'if I have a proof, a smaller proof of my negation exists', giving a sentence R with T⊢R↔∀y(Prf_T(y,⌜R⌝)→∃z≤y Prf_T(z,⌜¬R⌝)). If T⊢R with proof number n, then T proves Prf(n̄,⌜R⌝) and hence ∃z≤n̄ Prf(z,⌜¬R⌝); but consistency means ¬R has no proof, so T proves ¬Prf(k̄,⌜¬R⌝) for each k≤n, a contradiction. If T⊢¬R with proof number m, then T proves Prf(m̄,⌜¬R⌝), so the bound is witnessed for every y>m, while for y≤m the bounded instances Prf(y,⌜R⌝) are refutable; hence T⊢R and T is inconsistent. Only plain consistency of T is used.

routes.title: computability/recursion-theoretic formulations. Treat the precise theory hypotheses as part of the theorem
routes.proofSketch: Recursion-theoretic form: suppose T is consistent, effectively axiomatized and represents all recursive functions, so true Σ₁ sentences are provable. Take the recursively inseparable r.e. sets A={e: φ_e(e)=0} and B={e: φ_e(e)=1}. If T decided every sentence 'φ_e(e)=0', the set {e: T⊢'φ_e(e)=0'} would be recursive (search for a proof of the sentence or its negation), would contain A by Σ₁-completeness, and would be disjoint from B by consistency, separating A from B, which is impossible. So some sentence of this form is undecided by T. This gives incompleteness but not the explicit Gödel sentence or the second incompleteness theorem.

entries.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic for algebraic number fields fails in general; ideal factorization restores uniqueness
entries.description: Dedekind ideal factorization; valuations/localization at prime ideals; geometry of numbers for class-group consequences. Include only as a theorem about ideals, not as a second proof of integer UFD.

routes.title: Dedekind ideal factorization
routes.proofSketch: In the ring of integers O_K of a number field, show O_K is a Dedekind domain: it is Noetherian, integrally closed, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal. For a nonzero ideal I, localize at each nonzero prime P; the DVR O_{K,P} gives I_P=P^{v_P(I)}O_{K,P}. Only finitely many exponents are nonzero, and equality can be checked after localization, giving the unique factorization I=∏P^{v_P(I)}.

routes.title: valuations/localization at prime ideals
routes.proofSketch: Localize O_K at each nonzero prime ideal P. The local ring is a discrete valuation ring, so every nonzero ideal becomes P^{v_P(I)} locally. The exponents v_P(I) are uniquely determined and vanish for all but finitely many P; intersecting the local equalities recovers I=∏P^{v_P(I)}. This is the local-valuation form of the same ideal-factorization proof, not an independent theorem-level result.

entries.name: Finite subgroups of a field's multiplicative group are cyclic
entries.description: Choose an element of maximum order and use polynomial root bounds; classify finite abelian groups and compare exponent with group size; roots of unity and the structure theorem.

routes.title: Choose an element of maximum order and use polynomial root bounds
routes.proofSketch: Let $G$ be a finite subgroup of $F^\times$. In a finite abelian group, elements of orders $n_1,n_2$ yield an element of order $\operatorname{lcm}(n_1,n_2)$. Hence if $n$ is the maximal element order, every element order divides $n$. So every element of $G$ is a root of $X^n-1$, giving $\#G\le n$ since a polynomial has at most $\deg$ roots in a field. Also $n$ divides $\#G$ by Lagrange, so $n=\#G$ and some element has order $\#G$, i.e. $G$ is cyclic.

routes.title: classify finite abelian groups and compare exponent with group size
routes.proofSketch: All proofs rest on the fact that $x^d=1$ has at most $d$ solutions in a field. Using the structure theorem for finite abelian groups: if $|G|=n$ and $G$ is not cyclic, the invariant-factor decomposition gives a $d<n$ (the exponent) with $x^d=1$ for all $x\in G$. That gives more than $d$ roots of $x^d-1$, a contradiction, so $G$ is cyclic.

routes.title: roots of unity and the structure theorem
routes.proofSketch: Apply the structure theorem to the finite abelian group $G\subset F^\times$: if $G$ is not cyclic there is $d<|G|$ with $x^d=1$ for all $x\in G$, impossible because $X^d-1$ has at most $d$ roots in a field. entries.name: Uniformization theorem for simply connected Riemann surfaces
entries.description: Classical potential-theoretic/Dirichlet methods; extremal and normal-family arguments; modern Ricci-flow uniformization. The theorem's precise sphere/plane/disk classification and hypotheses matter.

routes.title: Classical potential-theoretic/Dirichlet methods
routes.proofSketch: Potential-theoretic route. Exhaust X by relatively compact regular domains and use Perron's method for the Dirichlet problem to decide whether X carries a Green's function. If it does (hyperbolic case), take the Green's function g with a logarithmic pole at p; X simply connected gives a harmonic conjugate g*, so F=exp(−(g+ig*)) is a single-valued holomorphic map X→𝔻, which one shows to be bijective. If X is non-compact without a Green's function, a harmonic function with a single logarithmic pole at p and controlled growth gives a biholomorphism onto ℂ; compact X is handled separately by producing a meromorphic function with one simple pole (Dirichlet principle), mapping X onto the Riemann sphere. The parabolic and compact cases are only indicated here.

routes.title: extremal and normal-family arguments
routes.proofSketch: Riemann-mapping-style extremal argument for the hyperbolic case. Fix p∈X and consider the family 𝓕 of injective holomorphic maps h:X→𝔻 with h(p)=0; assume 𝓕≠∅ (a first such map comes from a Green's function or an embedding theorem). Montel's theorem makes 𝓕 normal, and a maximizer of |h′(p)| exists, injective by Hurwitz. If the maximizer missed a point of 𝔻, Koebe's square-root-and-Möbius construction would give a map in 𝓕 with larger derivative at p, a contradiction; so the maximizer is a biholomorphism onto 𝔻. The cases ℂ and the sphere need a different argument.

routes.title: modern Ricci-flow uniformization. The theorem's precise sphere/plane/disk classification and hypotheses matter
routes.proofSketch: Ricci-flow route (Hamilton, Chow) for the compact case. On a compact surface evolve the metric by the normalized Ricci flow ∂_tg=(r̄−R)g. Hamilton proved long-time existence and convergence to a constant-curvature metric when the Euler characteristic is ≤0, and Chow completed the case χ>0 (the sphere). The limit metric is conformal to the original, and the universal cover of a constant-curvature surface is the sphere, the plane or the disk with its model metric. Non-compact simply connected surfaces such as ℂ and 𝔻 are not covered by this sketch.

routes.title: K-theory and cobordism
routes.proofSketch: The symbol of an elliptic operator defines a class in K⁰(T*M). Topological pushforward (built from Thom isomorphism and Bott periodicity) gives its topological index. Show the analytic index is invariant under symbol homotopy and bordism and agrees on generators; this identifies analytic and topological indices. Cobordism and K-theory are the conceptual proof framework; full details are substantial.

routes.title: heat-kernel/supertrace proof
routes.proofSketch: For a Dirac-type operator D, McKean–Singer gives ind(D⁺)=Str(e^{−tD²}) for every t>0. As t→0, the heat-kernel diagonal has a local asymptotic expansion; all non-top-degree terms cancel in the supertrace and the remaining coefficient is the characteristic-form density. Integrating gives the index formula.

routes.proofSketch: An elliptic differential operator is Fredholm, and its index depends only on its stable homotopy class of principal symbol. entries.name: Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields (Weil theorem)
entries.description: Jacobian/endomorphism eigenvalues; intersection theory on C×C; Stepanov–Bombieri polynomial method; Deligne's general Weil-conjectures route.

routes.title: Jacobian/endomorphism eigenvalues
routes.proofSketch: For an abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb F_q$, the Frobenius endomorphism $\pi$ satisfies $|A(\mathbb F_{q^m})|=\prod(1-a_i^m)$, where $a_i$ are the eigenvalues of $\pi$ on $T_\ell A$: $\pi-1$ is étale, so its kernel $A(\mathbb F_q)$ has size $\deg(\pi-1)=P_\pi(1)$. The Rosati involution attached to a polarization satisfies $\pi^\dagger\pi=q$ (Lemma 1.2), and a positivity argument in the semisimple algebra $\mathbb Q[\pi]$ (Lemma 1.3) then gives $|a_i|=q^{1/2}$. For a curve $C$ with Jacobian $J$, the Lefschetz-type formula $(\Gamma_\alpha\cdot\Delta)=1-\mathrm{Tr}(\alpha')+\deg\alpha$ (Prop. 11.2) applied to the Frobenius of $C$ shows $N=1-\sum a_i+q$ for the eigenvalues $a_i$ of $\pi_J$. Since $|a_i|=q^{1/2}$ there are $2g$ of them, so $|N-q-1|\le 2g\,q^{1/2}$.

routes.title: intersection theory on C×C
routes.proofSketch: On $V=C_1\times C_2$ one has $C_1^2=C_2^2=0$, $C_1\cdot C_2=1$. For a divisor $D$ with $d_1=D\cdot C_1$, $d_2=D\cdot C_2$, the class $D-d_2C_1-d_1C_2$ is orthogonal to the ample-type class $C_1+C_2$ (self-intersection $2>0$), so the Hodge index theorem gives $(D-d_2C_1-d_1C_2)^2\le0$, i.e. $D^2\le 2d_1d_2$. Defining the defect $\mathrm{def}(D)=2d_1d_2-D^2\ge0$, positivity of $\mathrm{def}(mD+nD')$ in $m,n$ yields $|D\cdot D'-d_1d_2'-d_2d_1'|\le(\mathrm{def}D\,\mathrm{def}D')^{1/2}$. For a morphism $f$ the adjunction formula gives $\mathrm{def}(\Gamma_f)=2g_2\deg f$. Applying this to the diagonal ($\mathrm{def}=2g$) and the Frobenius graph ($\mathrm{def}=2gq$) on $C\times C$ gives $|(\Delta\cdot\Gamma_\pi)-q-1|\le 2gq^{1/2}$, and $(\Delta\cdot\Gamma_\pi)$ is the number of rational points.

routes.title: Stepanov–Bombieri polynomial method
routes.proofSketch: Assuming $q$ is a perfect square, $|C(\mathbb F_q)|$ is the number of intersection points of $C_1=\{(z,\mathrm{Frob}_{\sqrt q}z)\}$ and its transpose $C_2$ on $C\times C$. Choose a rational point $P_\infty$ and let $R_n$ be the functions on $C$ with a pole of order at most $n$ only at $P_\infty$; Riemann's inequality gives $\dim R_n\ge n+1-g$. Take $V=R_\ell\otimes R_m\subset k(C\times C)$, of dimension at least $(\ell+1-g)(m+1-g)$. Its restriction to $C_1$ has dimension at most $\ell+m\sqrt q+1$ and to $C_2$ at most $\ell\sqrt q+m+1$; for $m$ slightly larger than $\ell$ the second restriction map is not injective. If $\ell<\sqrt q$ the first restriction is injective (distinct pole orders at $P_\infty$), so a nonzero $f\in V$ vanishes on $C_2$ but not on $C_1$. Its restriction to $C_1$ vanishes on $C_1\cap C_2$, which has $|C(\mathbb F_q)|$ points, and has at most $\ell+m\sqrt q$ poles. Hence $|C(\mathbb F_q)|\le\ell+m\sqrt q$; the choice $m=\sqrt q+2g$, $\ell\approx\frac{g}{g+1}\sqrt q+g+1$ gives the weak bound.

routes.title: Deligne's general Weil-conjectures route
routes.proofSketch: Grothendieck's trace formula expresses $Z(X_0,t)$ through $\det(1-F^*t,H^i_c)$. Theorem 1.6 (weights are $q^{i/2}$) is reduced to Lemma 1.7 (eigenvalues have complex conjugates of absolute value $q^{i/2}$): rationality and a Hankel-determinant/Fatou argument show the polynomials $P_i$ are rational with integer coefficients and independent of $\ell$. The key estimate (Theorem 3.2, inspired by Rankin) takes a sheaf with a symplectic form whose monodromy is open in $\mathrm{Sp}$ and shows it is pure: for the $2k$-th tensor power, the local factors have positive coefficients, and its $L$-function has only the pole $1/q^{k\beta+1}$ by invariant theory, so Rankin's positivity lemma bounds $|\alpha|\le q_x^{\beta/2+1/(2k)}$; letting $k\to\infty$ and using the symplectic duality gives $|\alpha|=q_x^{\beta/2}$. Lefschetz pencils later supply the needed monodromy hypothesis.

routes.title: Reidemeister-move skein relation
routes.proofSketch: Define the bracket recursively by ⟨L⟩=A⟨L₀⟩+A⁻¹⟨L∞⟩ and ⟨L⊔○⟩=−(A²+A⁻²)⟨L⟩. Check the three Reidemeister moves: II and III preserve the bracket, while I multiplies by a writhe-dependent factor. Normalize by (−A³)^{−w(L)} to obtain an ambient-isotopy invariant (then change variables for Jones V).

routes.title: Chern–Simons/topological quantum field theory. State the exact normalization and link equivalence
routes.proofSketch: Witten's heuristic: take SU(2) Chern–Simons theory at level k and define the invariant of a link as the path-integral expectation of Wilson loops in the fundamental representation, with q=e^{2πi/(k+2)}. Isotopy invariance is expected because the action is metric-independent and gauge invariant, so the expectation value depends on the link only up to a framing correction (the writhe normalization). The skein relation comes from the two-dimensional space of conformal blocks of the four-punctured sphere, which yields the Jones polynomial V(t) with t=q^{±1}. The path integral itself is not mathematically defined; the rigorous version is the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction, essentially the quantum-group route.

routes.title: Jacobi-field comparison and exponential coordinates

Constant sectional curvature makes this scalar equation identical to that in the model sphere/Euclidean/hyperbolic space; matching initial data makes exponential-coordinate metrics locally isometric. Parallel-frame/Cartan proofs integrate the same structure equations.

routes.title: Frobenius/integrability of parallel frames
routes.proofSketch: Frobenius route. On the frame bundles O(M) and O(S_κ) of M and the model space, the canonical forms θ^i and Levi-Civita connection forms ω^i_j satisfy dθ^i=−ω^i_j∧θ^j and dω^i_j=−ω^i_k∧ω^k_j+κθ^i∧θ^j (constant curvature κ on both). The 1-forms θ^i−θ̃^i and ω^i_j−ω̃^i_j on O(M)×O(S_κ) define a Pfaffian system whose exterior derivatives lie in the ideal it generates, exactly because the curvature equations coincide. Frobenius' theorem gives integral manifolds, which project to local isometries M→S_κ.

routes.title: Cartan connection/structure equations
routes.proofSketch: Cartan-geometry route. Combine the canonical and connection forms into a 𝔤-valued 1-form Θ on O(M), where 𝔤=𝔰𝔬(n+1), 𝔢(n) or 𝔰𝔬(n,1) is the Lie algebra of the isometry group of the model space of curvature κ. The torsion-free and constant-curvature-κ conditions are equivalent to the Maurer–Cartan equation dΘ+½[Θ,Θ]=0. A Maurer–Cartan form on a simply connected open set is g^{−1}dg for a map g into the group G, unique up to left translation, and the induced map M→G/H is a local isometry.

routes.title: Elliptic PDE and Green operators
routes.proofSketch: On a compact Riemannian manifold, ellipticity gives Green operator G on the orthogonal complement of harmonic forms and ΔG=GΔ=I−H. For closed α, α=Hα+dδGα, so its class has harmonic representative; if harmonic α is exact, ⟨α,α⟩=⟨α,dβ⟩=⟨δα,β⟩=0, proving uniqueness.

routes.title: Hilbert-space orthogonal decomposition
routes.proofSketch: Hilbert-space (Weyl) route. For closed α, let ω be the L²-orthogonal projection of α onto the orthogonal complement of the closure of dΩ^{k−1}, i.e. the L²-minimizer of ‖α−η‖ over η in that closure. Then δω=0 weakly (ω⊥dβ for all β) and dω=0 weakly (dα=0 and α−ω lies in the closure of exact forms), so Δω=0 weakly and Weyl's lemma for the elliptic operator Δ makes ω smooth. Rellich compactness and the Gårding-type estimate show that dΩ^{k−1} is closed in L², so α−ω is exact and [α]=[ω]. Uniqueness follows because a harmonic exact form is orthogonal to itself.

routes.title: heat-flow convergence to harmonic representatives
routes.proofSketch: Heat-flow route. Solve ∂_tα_t=−Δα_t with α_0=α closed. Since Δ commutes with d, α_t stays closed, and α_t−α=−d∫_0^tδα_s ds is exact, so [α_t]=[α]. By the spectral theorem for Δ on a compact manifold (discrete spectrum, eigenforms φ_λ), α_t=Σe^{−λt}⟨α,φ_λ⟩φ_λ, which converges in C^∞ as t→∞ to the projection of α onto ker Δ, the harmonic part Hα. Hence Hα lies in the class of α. For uniqueness, a harmonic exact form dβ has ‖dβ‖²=⟨β,δdβ⟩=0.

entries.name: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
entries.description: Degree/mod-2 homology; Tucker's lemma and combinatorial antipodal labeling; equivariant topology.

routes.title: Degree/mod-2 homology
routes.proofSketch: Suppose f(x)≠f(−x) for all x (for n=1 this is the intermediate value theorem; take n≥2). Then g(x)=(f(x)−f(−x))/‖f(x)−f(−x)‖ is an odd map S^n→S^{n−1}. Restricted to the equator S^{n−1}, g is an odd self-map of S^{n−1}, which has odd degree (Borsuk): it descends to RP^{n−1}→RP^{n−1} and pulls the generator w∈H¹(RP^{n−1};ℤ₂) back to itself, so w^{n−1}≠0 is preserved and the map has degree 1 mod 2. But g on the equator extends over the upper hemisphere into S^{n−1}, so it is null-homotopic with degree 0, a contradiction.

references.label: Matoušek, Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem
references.locator: Chapter 1, degree/mod-2 and combinatorial Tucker proof

routes.title: Tucker's lemma and combinatorial antipodal labeling
routes.proofSketch: Combinatorial route via Tucker's lemma: if T is a triangulation of the n-ball Bⁿ that is antipodally symmetric on the boundary and λ labels vertices with ±1,…,±n so that λ(−v)=−λ(v) on the boundary, then some edge has labels summing to 0. Suppose f(x)≠f(−x) everywhere and let g(x)=f(x)−f(−x), an odd map. Pull back to the upper hemisphere ≅Bⁿ and label each vertex by the index and sign of the coordinate of g of largest absolute value. The labeling is odd on the boundary, so a complementary edge {v,w} exists, with g_i(v)>0>g_i(w) at maximal coordinates. As the mesh tends to 0, uniform continuity forces ‖g(v)‖_∞→0, and a limit point x gives g(x)=0, a contradiction.

references.label: Matoušek, Using the Borsuk–Ulam Theorem
references.locator: Chapter 1, degree/mod-2 and combinatorial Tucker proof

routes.title: equivariant topology
routes.proofSketch: Equivariant route via the ℤ₂-index. For a free ℤ₂-space X let w₁(X)∈H¹(X/ℤ₂;ℤ₂) classify the double cover, and let h(X)=max{k: w₁(X)^k≠0}. A ℤ₂-map X→Y induces X/ℤ₂→Y/ℤ₂ pulling w₁(Y) back to w₁(X), so h(X)≤h(Y). For X=S^n we have X/ℤ₂=RP^n and w₁^n≠0, so h(S^n)=n; for Y=S^{n−1}, h(Y)≤n−1 since H^n(RP^{n−1};ℤ₂)=0. A ℤ₂-map S^n→S^{n−1} would give n≤n−1. This is the statement that no such map exists, which is equivalent to Borsuk–Ulam.

entries.name: Noether's theorem (continuous symmetry yields a conserved quantity)
entries.description: Euler–Lagrange variational identity; Hamiltonian/symplectic moment-map formulation; current conservation via differential forms. Specify the finite-dimensional or field-theoretic version.

routes.title: Euler–Lagrange variational identity
routes.proofSketch: For a one-parameter variational symmetry with infinitesimal generator η and Lagrangian L, differentiate the invariance identity at the identity and use Euler–Lagrange equations: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇·η−B)=0. Hamiltonian moment-map and differential-form currents are corresponding formulations. Field-theoretic versions require boundary terms and regularity assumptions.

references.label: Olver, Applications of Lie Groups to Differential Equations

routes.title: Hamiltonian/symplectic moment-map formulation
routes.proofSketch: Hamiltonian route. After the Legendre transform a symmetry becomes a one-parameter group of canonical transformations generated by a function J, so the flow of X_J preserves H. Then dJ/dt={J,H}=±X_J(H)=0 along the Hamiltonian flow, since H is constant along X_J. For a cotangent-lifted action the moment map is J_ξ(q,p)=p·ξ_Q(q), the same quantity as ∂L/∂q̇·η in the Lagrangian picture. The Lagrangian and Hamiltonian statements correspond under the Legendre map when it is regular; the divergence term B needs separate handling.

routes.title: current conservation via differential forms. Specify the finite-dimensional or field-theoretic version
routes.proofSketch: Field-theoretic route with differential forms. Invariance of the action up to a boundary term means 𝓛_{pr v}(L dⁿx)=dη for an (n−1)-form η. The first variation formula gives 𝓛_{pr v}(L dⁿx)=E(L)·Q dⁿx+dθ, where E(L) are the Euler–Lagrange expressions, Q the characteristic of v, and θ the boundary form. On solutions E(L)=0, so d(θ−η)=0: J=θ−η is a closed (n−1)-form, the Noether current. Stokes' theorem gives conservation of its flux through time slices; for n=1 it reduces to dQ/dt=0.
